questions.q: Which standard amino acid has no stereocenter at its α-carbon?
o: Alanine
Alanine's α-carbon has four different groups, including a CH₃ side chain, so it's chiral.
Proline
Proline's ring makes it stiff, not symmetric. Its α-carbon is still chiral.
Glycine
Correct: its side chain is H, so the α-carbon has two identical H atoms.
Cysteine
Cysteine is chiral. It's just unusual because it's labeled R instead of S.
questions.note: Glycine is the only achiral standard amino acid.
questions.x: A stereocenter (also called a chiral center) is a carbon holding four different groups. Every amino acid's α-carbon (the central carbon) holds an H, an amino group, a carboxyl group and a side chain. In glycine, the side chain is just another H. So its α-carbon holds two identical H atoms, and it can't be a stereocenter. Every other standard amino acid, even proline with its ring, has four different groups there, so they're all chiral.

questions.q: Amino acids incorporated into human proteins by ribosomes have which configuration at the α-carbon?
o: L
Correct: ribosomes build proteins only from L-amino acids.
D
D-amino acids show up in bacterial cell walls, but ribosomes don't put them in human proteins.
A racemic mix of D and L
Translation picks one mirror image only, so it's never a 50:50 mix.
R in every case
L/D and R/S are different systems, and most L-amino acids are actually S.
questions.note: Trap: D/L (Fischer) is not the same as R/S (CIP).
questions.x: Ribosomes only put L-amino acids into human proteins. The enzymes that load amino acids onto tRNA, and the ribosome itself, are 'handed' in shape, so they only fit the L version, a bit like a right hand only fitting a right glove. D-amino acids do exist in nature, for example in bacterial cell walls, but other enzymes make those, not ribosomes. Also watch out: L and D are a separate labeling system from R and S, so L doesn't mean R.

questions.q: Almost every chiral L-amino acid has S absolute configuration. Which L-amino acid is the exception, with R configuration?
o: Serine
The CH₂OH carbon has (O, H, H), which ranks below COOH's (O, O, O), so L-serine stays S.
Methionine
Its first side-chain atom is a carbon with (C, H, H), below COOH, so it stays S.
Glycine
Glycine isn't chiral at all, so it gets no R or S label.
Cysteine
Correct: the S in CH₂SH outranks the carboxyl's O atoms, flipping the label to R.
questions.note: Sulfur at the first side-chain atom is what changes the priority order.
questions.x: R and S labels come from ranking the four groups on the stereocenter by atomic number (the CIP rules). You compare the atoms touching the stereocenter first, and if two tie, you look at what's attached to them. In cysteine, the side-chain carbon carries (S, H, H) and the carboxyl carbon carries (O, O, O). Sulfur (atomic number 16) beats oxygen (8) at that first comparison, so the side chain jumps ahead of the carboxyl. The shape is the same as every other L-amino acid, but the swapped ranking flips the label to R.

questions.q: Which pair of amino acids both carry a negatively charged side chain at physiological pH?
o: Asparagine and glutamine
These are the amide versions of Asp and Glu. Amides don't ionize, so they stay neutral.
Aspartate and glutamate
Correct: both side-chain carboxyls (pKₐ ≈ 4) have lost their protons at pH 7.4.
Lysine and arginine
These are the basic amino acids. They're charged at pH 7.4, but positive.
Serine and threonine
Their OH groups (pKₐ above 13) keep their protons, so they're neutral.
questions.x: A side chain is negatively charged at body pH (about 7.4) only if it has an acid group that gives up its proton easily. pKₐ tells you how easily: when the pH is above a group's pKₐ, the group has lost its proton. Aspartate and glutamate have side-chain carboxyl groups (COOH) with pKₐ ≈ 4. pH 7.4 is way above 4, so those groups are COO⁻, charge −1. Asparagine and glutamine look almost the same, but they end in an amide (CONH₂), which doesn't ionize, so they're polar but neutral.

questions.q: An enzyme needs a residue that can donate a proton and accept one back near pH 7. Which side chain is best suited?
o: Lysine
Lysine's pKₐ ≈ 10.5 keeps it almost always protonated at pH 7, so it can't accept a proton back.
Histidine
Correct: its pKₐ ≈ 6 means both forms are present near neutral pH.
Arginine
Arginine's pKₐ ≈ 12.5 means it basically never loses its proton at pH 7.
Aspartate
Aspartate's pKₐ ≈ 3.9 means it has almost always lost its proton at pH 7.
questions.note: A good acid-base catalyst has a pKₐ close to the working pH.
questions.x: To hand a proton off and take one back, a group needs to spend real time in both forms: with the proton and without it. That happens when its pKₐ is close to the pH, because at pH = pKₐ you have a 50:50 mix. Histidine's side chain (an imidazole ring) has pKₐ ≈ 6, the closest of any standard side chain to pH 7. Lysine, arginine and aspartate have pKₐ values far from 7, so each is stuck almost entirely in one form and can only go one way.

questions.q: Lysine has pKₐ values of 2.2 (α-COOH), 9.0 (α-NH₃⁺) and 10.5 (side chain). What is its net charge at pH 7.0?
o: This treats both amines as having lost their protons, but pH 7 is below both of their pKₐ values.
This forgets the side-chain amine, which is still protonated below pH 10.5.
Correct: both amines are protonated (+1 each) and the carboxyl isn't (−1): −1 + 1 + 1 = +1.
This keeps the carboxyl protonated, but pH 7 is far above its pKₐ of 2.2.
questions.x: Add up the charge of each group. Rule: a group keeps its proton when the pH is below its pKₐ. The α-COOH has pKₐ 2.2. pH 7 is above that, so it has lost its proton: COO⁻, charge −1. The α-NH₃⁺ has pKₐ 9.0 and the side-chain NH₃⁺ has pKₐ 10.5. pH 7 is below both, so both keep their protons: +1 each. Net charge = −1 + 1 + 1 = +1. Forgetting the side-chain amine gives 0.

questions.q: Glycine has pKₐ values of 2.3 and 9.7. What is its isoelectric point?
o: Neutral pH for water isn't the pI. The pI depends on the molecule's pKₐ values.
That's the amino group's pKₐ. The pI sits between the two pKₐ values, not on one.
This adds the two pKₐ values (2.3 + 9.7 = 12.0) but forgets to divide by 2.
questions.x: The isoelectric point (pI) is the pH where the molecule's net charge is zero. Glycine has two groups that can lose a proton, so its neutral form exists between the two pKₐ values, and the pI is their average. Formula: pI = (pKₐ₁ + pKₐ₂) ÷ 2. Values: pKₐ₁ = 2.3, pKₐ₂ = 9.7. Plug in: pI = (2.3 + 9.7) ÷ 2 = 12.0 ÷ 2 = 6.0. The pI depends on the molecule's own pKₐ values, so it isn't automatically 7.

questions.q: Glutamate has pKₐ values of 2.2 (α-COOH), 4.2 (side chain) and 9.7 (α-NH₃⁺). What is its pI?
o: Correct: the neutral form sits between 2.2 and 4.2, so pI = 6.4 ÷ 2 = 3.2.
This averages all three pKₐ values, which isn't how pI works.
This uses only the α-groups and ignores the acidic side chain.
This averages the side-chain and amino pKₐ values, the rule for a basic amino acid.
questions.note: Acidic amino acid: average the two lowest pKₐ values.
questions.x: The pI is the average of the two pKₐ values on either side of the neutral form. So first find when glutamate is neutral. Fully protonated it's +1. After the α-COOH loses its proton (pKₐ 2.2) it's 0. After the side-chain COOH loses its proton (pKₐ 4.2) it's −1. So the neutral form sits between 2.2 and 4.2. Formula: pI = (pKₐ below + pKₐ above) ÷ 2. Plug in: pI = (2.2 + 4.2) ÷ 2 = 6.4 ÷ 2 = 3.2. The extra acid group pulls the pI way down.

questions.q: Arginine has pKₐ values of 2.2 (α-COOH), 9.0 (α-NH₃⁺) and 12.5 (side chain). What is its pI?
o: This averages only the α-groups and ignores the basic side chain.
This averages all three pKₐ values, which isn't how pI works.
Correct: the neutral form sits between 9.0 and 12.5, so pI = 21.5 ÷ 2 = 10.75.
That's the side chain's pKₐ. The pI lies between two pKₐ values, not on one.
questions.note: Basic amino acid: average the two highest pKₐ values.
questions.x: Find the neutral form first, then average the two pKₐ values on either side of it. Fully protonated arginine is +2 (α-COOH 0, α-NH₃⁺ +1, side chain +1). After pKₐ 2.2 it's +1. After pKₐ 9.0 it's 0. After pKₐ 12.5 it's −1. So the neutral form sits between 9.0 and 12.5. Formula: pI = (pKₐ below + pKₐ above) ÷ 2. Plug in: pI = (9.0 + 12.5) ÷ 2 = 21.5 ÷ 2 = 10.75. Basic amino acids have high pI values because the extra positive group has to lose its proton before the molecule is neutral.

questions.q: A histidine side chain has pKₐ 6.0. At pH 7.0, roughly what percentage of these side chains are protonated?
o: A 100 : 1 ratio would need the pH to be 2 units above the pKₐ, not 1.
Correct: base ÷ acid = 10¹ = 10, so protonated = 1 ÷ 11 ≈ 9%.
50% happens only when the pH equals the pKₐ, here 6.0.
This flips the ratio. pH above the pKₐ favors the unprotonated form.
questions.note: Each pH unit above the pKₐ shifts the base:acid ratio 10-fold.
questions.x: Use the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKₐ + log([base] ÷ [acid]). Values: pH = 7.0, pKₐ = 6.0. Plug in: 7.0 = 6.0 + log(ratio), so log(ratio) = 7.0 − 6.0 = 1. Log just reads off the exponent of 10, so the ratio is 10¹ = 10. That's 10 unprotonated side chains for every 1 protonated. The protonated share is 1 out of 10 + 1 = 11 total: 1 ÷ 11 ≈ 0.09, about 9%. The tempting 91% flips it: when pH is above pKₐ, the unprotonated form wins.

questions.q: A fully protonated amino acid is titrated with NaOH. The curve shows three buffering regions centered at pH 2.2, 9.0 and 10.5. Which amino acid is it?
o: Glutamate
Glutamate's extra pKₐ is near 4.2, not 10.5.
Histidine
Histidine's extra pKₐ is near 6.0, not 10.5.
Alanine
Alanine's side chain can't lose a proton, so it shows only two buffering regions.
Lysine
Correct: an extra pKₐ near 10.5 matches lysine's side-chain amino group.
questions.x: Each flat part (buffering region) of a titration curve sits at one pKₐ, so three flat parts means three groups that can lose a proton. Every amino acid has an α-COOH (pKₐ about 2) and an α-NH₃⁺ (pKₐ about 9 to 10). That accounts for 2.2 and 9.0. The extra one at 10.5 must be the side chain, and a side-chain pKₐ near 10.5 belongs to lysine's side-chain amino group (its ε-amino group). Glutamate's side chain would buffer near 4.2 and histidine's near 6.0.

questions.q: While titrating glycine with NaOH, the solution passes through the isoelectric point. What is observed at that point?
o: The pH changes sharply with a small amount of added base
Correct: the pI is an equivalence point, where buffering is weakest.
The pH resists change most strongly
The pH resists change most at a pKₐ, not at the pI.
The pH equals the pKₐ of the amino group
The pI is halfway between the two pKₐ values, not at the amino group's.
Most molecules carry a net charge of +1
At the pI most molecules are the neutral zwitterion, not +1.
questions.note: Flat parts of the curve are pKₐ values; steep parts are equivalence points.
questions.x: On a titration curve, the flat parts are at the pKₐ values. There, a group is half protonated and half not, so it soaks up added base and the pH barely moves (that's buffering). Glycine's pI comes right after the first group is fully done, when nearly every molecule is the zwitterion (net 0) and the second group hasn't started yet. With no half-and-half pair around to buffer, a tiny bit of base makes the pH jump. So the pI is a steep spot, not a flat one.

questions.q: How many equivalents of OH⁻ must be added to fully protonated glycine to reach its isoelectric point?
o: At 0.5 equivalents the pH equals pKₐ₁. That's the middle of a buffering region.
Correct: removing the carboxyl proton gives the zwitterion, net charge 0.
At 1.5 equivalents the pH equals pKₐ₂, the amino group's pKₐ.
At 2.0 equivalents both protons are gone, so the net charge is −1.
questions.x: Fully protonated glycine (⁺H₃N–CH₂–COOH) has net charge +1: COOH is 0 and NH₃⁺ is +1. Each equivalent of OH⁻ pulls off one proton per molecule, lowering the charge by 1. Formula: net charge = starting charge − equivalents added. To get from +1 to 0, you need 1 equivalent: +1 − 1 = 0. The carboxyl proton leaves first, giving the zwitterion, which is the pI. The half amounts (0.5 and 1.5) are where the pH equals the pKₐ values.

questions.q: How is a peptide bond formed between two amino acids?
o: Hydrolysis of the carboxyl group by water
Hydrolysis breaks peptide bonds. It doesn't make them.
Oxidation of two side-chain thiols
That makes a disulfide bond between cysteines, not a peptide bond.
Condensation of a carboxyl group with an amino group, releasing water
Correct: it's a dehydration reaction that forms an amide.
Esterification between two hydroxyl groups
Peptide bonds are amides with nitrogen, not esters with oxygen.
questions.x: A peptide bond is an amide (a C–N bond next to a C=O). It forms when the carboxyl group (COOH) of one amino acid joins the amino group (NH₂) of the next. The OH from the carboxyl and an H from the amine leave together as a water molecule. A reaction that joins two pieces and releases water is called condensation (or dehydration). Hydrolysis is the reverse: adding water to break the bond. Disulfide bonds and esters are different links that don't join the backbone.

questions.q: Why is rotation about the peptide C–N bond restricted?
o: Bulky side chains physically block the rotation
Side chains sit on the α-carbons. The lock comes from the bond's electrons.
The bond is a full C=N double bond
It's a blend of single and double, only partly double, which is why it's in between in length.
Hydrogen bonds from water lock the bond in place
Water doesn't cause this. The flatness is built into the amide itself.
Resonance gives the bond partial double-bond character
Correct: the nitrogen's lone pair spreads into the C=O, giving partial double-bond character.
questions.x: The nitrogen in a peptide bond has a lone pair (two unshared electrons) that it shares with the neighboring C=O. Chemists call this resonance: the real bond is a blend of a C–N single bond and a C=N double bond, with roughly 40% double-bond character. That makes the bond shorter than a normal single bond, and it can't twist without breaking that partial double bond. So the six atoms of the peptide group stay locked in one flat plane. It's only partly double, not a full double bond.

questions.q: Which description best fits the geometry of most peptide bonds in proteins?
o: Planar and cis
Cis is uncommon. It shows up mainly right before proline.
Trans and freely rotating
Trans is right, but partial double-bond character stops free rotation.
Planar and trans
Correct: trans puts the α-carbons on opposite sides, so they don't clash.
Nonplanar with tetrahedral nitrogen
The amide nitrogen is flat, not tetrahedral, because of resonance.
questions.x: Two things set the shape. First, resonance (the nitrogen sharing its lone pair with the C=O) makes the peptide group flat and stops it from rotating. Second, of the two flat arrangements, trans puts the two neighboring α-carbons on opposite sides of the bond, so they don't bump into each other. Cis puts them on the same side, which crowds them. So almost every peptide bond is planar and trans. Cis shows up mainly right before proline, whose ring makes the two arrangements closer in energy.

questions.q: Backbone conformations are described by the φ and ψ angles. Which bonds do these angles describe?
o: The peptide C–N bond and the C=O bond
Both of these have double-bond character and don't rotate freely.
N–Cα and Cα–C(carbonyl)
Correct: these single bonds sit on either side of the α-carbon and can rotate.
Only bonds within the side chains
Side-chain twists are called χ angles, not φ and ψ.
The disulfide S–S bonds
Disulfide bonds link side chains. They aren't part of the backbone.
questions.x: The peptide bond itself is flat and stiff, so a protein's backbone can only bend at the two single bonds on either side of each α-carbon (the central carbon of each amino acid). φ (phi) is the twist around the N–Cα bond, and ψ (psi) is the twist around the Cα–C(=O) bond. Together, the φ and ψ pair at each residue sets the backbone's path. Twists in side-chain bonds have a different name, χ (chi). A Ramachandran plot shows which φ/ψ pairs fit without atoms bumping into each other.

questions.q: A peptide sequence written as Met-Gly-Ser by convention means what?
o: Met is at the N-terminus and Ser is at the C-terminus
Correct: sequences are written from the N-terminus to the C-terminus.
Met is at the C-terminus and Ser is at the N-terminus
This flips the standard convention.
Gly forms both peptide bonds through its side chain
Peptide bonds are backbone bonds, and glycine's side chain is just H.
The residues can be in any order
Order is the primary structure. Change it and you have a different peptide.
questions.x: Peptides are always written starting from the N-terminus (the end with a free amino group) on the left, and ending at the C-terminus (the end with a free carboxyl group) on the right. So in Met-Gly-Ser, Met is at the N-terminus and Ser is at the C-terminus. This matches how ribosomes build proteins: they start at the N-terminus and add each new amino acid to the C-terminal end. Order matters, so Ser-Gly-Met would be a different peptide.

questions.q: Complete hydrolysis of a tripeptide into free amino acids uses how many water molecules?
o: One water breaks only one of the two peptide bonds.
Correct: a tripeptide has 3 − 1 = 2 peptide bonds, and each needs one water.
There are three amino acids but only two bonds between them.
Four would be for five amino acids (5 − 1 = 4). Each bond uses one water.
questions.note: n residues → n − 1 peptide bonds.
questions.x: Hydrolysis uses one water molecule for each peptide bond it breaks. So count the bonds, not the amino acids. A straight chain of n amino acids has n − 1 bonds between them, like 3 beads on a string with 2 gaps. Formula: bonds = n − 1. Value: n = 3. Plug in: bonds = 3 − 1 = 2. One water per bond, so 2 × 1 = 2 water molecules. Counting the amino acids instead of the bonds gives the tempting wrong answer of 3.

questions.q: Peptide bond hydrolysis has ΔG < 0, yet proteins persist in neutral water for years without enzymes. Why?
o: Hydrolysis is endergonic at neutral pH
Hydrolysis is favorable. It's making peptide bonds that takes energy.
Water cannot reach the peptide bond
Backbones on a protein's surface are fully exposed to water.
The activation energy for uncatalyzed hydrolysis is very high
Correct: the reaction is favorable but very slow without a catalyst.
Peptide bonds re-form spontaneously as fast as they break
Re-forming is the unfavorable direction, so it can't keep pace with breaking.
questions.note: Thermodynamics says if a reaction can go; kinetics says how fast.
questions.x: ΔG (the free energy change) tells you whether a reaction is favorable, not how fast it goes. Peptide bond hydrolysis is favorable (ΔG < 0), but to get there the molecules have to climb a very high energy hill first. That hill is the activation energy. Because it's so high, a peptide bond in plain neutral water takes years to break. Enzymes called proteases lower the hill, so the same reaction happens in a fraction of a second. They don't change ΔG.

questions.q: Which amino acid has its side chain covalently bonded to its own α-amino nitrogen?
o: Proline
Correct: its side chain loops back to the backbone nitrogen, forming a ring.
Lysine
Lysine's side-chain amine sits free at the end of a four-carbon chain.
Histidine
Histidine's ring is separate from the backbone nitrogen.
Tryptophan
Tryptophan's ring hangs off the β-carbon, not the α-nitrogen.
questions.x: Proline's side chain is three carbons long, and it curls back and bonds to its own α-amino nitrogen. That closes a five-membered ring that includes the backbone nitrogen. This ring locks one of the backbone angles in place, and once proline is in a chain its nitrogen has no H left to donate in a hydrogen bond. That's why proline breaks α-helices. Histidine and tryptophan also have rings, but theirs hang off the side chain and don't touch the backbone nitrogen.

questions.q: Which amino acid has the most hydrophobic side chain?
o: Serine
Serine's OH group makes it polar.
Glutamine
Glutamine has a polar amide side chain.
Aspartate
Aspartate is negatively charged at body pH, so it loves water.
Leucine
Correct: its branched side chain is all carbon and hydrogen.
questions.x: 'Hydrophobic' means water-avoiding. A side chain is hydrophobic when it's made only of carbon and hydrogen, with no polar groups (like OH or C=O) and no charges. Leucine's side chain is a branched chain of carbons and hydrogens, so it avoids water and tends to hide in the middle of a folded protein. Serine has an OH, glutamine has an amide, and aspartate carries a negative charge. All three get along well with water.

questions.q: A protein kinase phosphorylates a side-chain hydroxyl. Which residue could it target?
o: Alanine
Alanine's CH₃ side chain has no OH to take a phosphate.
Threonine
Correct: serine, threonine and tyrosine have the OH groups kinases use.
Phenylalanine
Phenylalanine is tyrosine without the OH group.
Valine
Valine's side chain is only carbon and hydrogen.
questions.x: A kinase is an enzyme that moves a phosphate group from ATP onto a protein. It needs an OH group on the side chain to attach that phosphate to. The three standard amino acids with OH side chains are serine, threonine and tyrosine, so those are the usual targets. Threonine is the only one of those listed here. Phenylalanine is the tempting wrong choice because it looks just like tyrosine, but it's missing the OH.

questions.q: N-linked glycosylation attaches an oligosaccharide to a side-chain nitrogen. Which residue receives it?
o: Serine
Serine gets O-linked sugars through its OH group, not N-linked ones.
Asparagine
Correct: N-linked sugars attach to the amide nitrogen of asparagine.
Glutamate
Glutamate's side chain is a carboxylate. It has no nitrogen.
Lysine
Lysine has a side-chain nitrogen, but it isn't the N-linked sugar acceptor.
questions.x: 'N-linked' tells you the sugar attaches to a nitrogen. The residue that gets it is asparagine, on the nitrogen of its side-chain amide (CONH₂). This happens in the rough ER, and usually only when the asparagine sits in the pattern Asn, then any amino acid, then Ser or Thr. The other common type, O-linked glycosylation, attaches sugars to the oxygen of a serine or threonine OH, mostly in the Golgi. Match the atom (N or O) to the residue.

questions.q: Protein concentration is often estimated from absorbance at 280 nm. Which side chain contributes most to this absorbance?
o: Histidine
Histidine's small ring absorbs very little at 280 nm.
Leucine
Leucine has no ring, so it doesn't absorb at 280 nm.
Serine
Serine has no ring of double bonds to absorb UV at 280 nm.
Tryptophan
Correct: its double-ring indole absorbs strongly near 280 nm.
questions.note: Trp and Tyr cause the A280 signal.
questions.x: Proteins absorb UV light at 280 nm mainly because of side chains with big aromatic rings. Those rings have alternating double bonds (a conjugated system), and the bigger that system, the closer to 280 nm it absorbs. Tryptophan's indole, a double ring, absorbs the most. Tyrosine comes next, and phenylalanine adds only a little. Histidine's ring is too small to absorb much at 280 nm, and side chains without rings, like leucine and serine, don't absorb there at all.

questions.q: In a folded protein at pH 7, a lysine side chain sits next to a glutamate side chain. What interaction do they most likely form?
o: A salt bridge
Correct: positive NH₃⁺ and negative COO⁻ attract each other.
A disulfide bond
Only cysteine SH groups form disulfide bonds.
A hydrophobic interaction
Both side chains are charged, not water-avoiding.
A peptide bond
Peptide bonds join backbone groups during translation, not side chains.
questions.x: At pH 7, lysine's side chain has its extra proton (NH₃⁺, positive) and glutamate's side chain has lost its proton (COO⁻, negative). Opposite charges attract, so these two pull together. That attraction is called a salt bridge, a type of ionic bond inside a protein. Disulfide bonds only form between two cysteines. Hydrophobic interactions need water-avoiding side chains, and these two are charged. Peptide bonds only join backbone groups.

questions.q: Which point mutation is most conservative, least likely to alter protein structure?
o: Leucine → aspartate
This puts a charged side chain where a water-avoiding one was.
Glycine → tryptophan
This swaps the smallest side chain for the bulkiest one.
Leucine → isoleucine
Correct: both are branched, water-avoiding side chains of the same size.
Lysine → glutamate
This flips the side-chain charge from + to −.
questions.x: A conservative mutation swaps one amino acid for another that's similar in size, shape and chemistry, so the protein barely notices. Leucine and isoleucine are a near-perfect match. They have the same atoms (they're isomers), and both have branched, water-avoiding side chains. Only the branch point differs. Swaps that change charge, polarity or size a lot, like leucine to aspartate or glycine to tryptophan, are much more likely to mess up the structure.

questions.q: In sickle-cell hemoglobin, a surface glutamate in β-globin is replaced by valine. Why does deoxyhemoglobin S polymerize?
o: The valine forms disulfide bonds between hemoglobin molecules
Valine has no SH group, so it can't form disulfide bonds.
The mutation oxidizes heme iron to Fe³⁺
The swap doesn't change the iron's charge.
The mutation prevents α and β chains from assembling
HbS still forms normal α₂β₂ tetramers.
The valine creates a hydrophobic surface patch that binds a pocket on neighboring hemoglobins
Correct: a sticky water-avoiding contact links deoxy HbS into fibers.
questions.x: In sickle-cell hemoglobin (HbS), a glutamate on the outside of the protein is replaced by valine. Glutamate is charged and loves water. Valine is water-avoiding, so it makes a sticky spot on the surface. When hemoglobin lets go of its oxygen (the deoxy form), that sticky valine fits into a matching water-avoiding pocket on a neighboring hemoglobin. Molecule after molecule sticks together into long fibers that bend red blood cells into a sickle shape. The hemoglobin still assembles normally and its iron stays Fe²⁺.

questions.q: A mixture of Asp (pI 2.8), Gly (pI 6.0) and Lys (pI 9.7) is electrophoresed at pH 6.0. Which moves toward the anode?
o: Glycine
At its pI glycine has no net charge, so it stays near where it started.
Lysine
Lysine is positive at pH 6.0, so it moves toward the cathode.
Aspartate
Correct: pH 6.0 is above Asp's pI, so it's negative and moves to the + electrode.
None of them; all are zwitterions
Only glycine is neutral at this pH. The other two move.
questions.note: pH > pI → negative; pH < pI → positive.
questions.x: The anode is the positive electrode, so only negative molecules move toward it. To find each molecule's charge, compare the pH to its pI (the pH where its net charge is zero). If pH is above the pI, the molecule has lost extra protons and is negative. If pH is below the pI, it's holding extra protons and is positive. At pH 6.0, aspartate (pI 2.8) is negative and moves to the anode. Lysine (pI 9.7) is positive and moves to the cathode. Glycine (pI 6.0) has no net charge and stays put.

questions.q: In isoelectric focusing, a protein with pI 5.5 is loaded where the gel pH is 8. How does it move?
o: Toward the cathode, stopping where pH = 5.5
A negative protein moves away from the cathode, not toward it.
Toward the anode, stopping where pH = 5.5
Correct: it's negative at pH 8 and moves to lower pH until its charge is zero.
Toward the anode until it reaches the end of the gel
It stops once the local pH equals its pI and its charge becomes zero.
It stays at the loading point
It's negative at pH 8, so it moves.
questions.x: In isoelectric focusing (IEF), the gel has a pH gradient: low pH at the anode (+) and high pH at the cathode (−). This protein starts at pH 8, which is above its pI of 5.5, so it's negative. Negative molecules move toward the anode, which also means toward lower pH. As the pH drops, the protein picks up protons and its negative charge shrinks. At pH 5.5 its net charge hits zero, so the field stops pushing it, and it stops there instead of running off the gel.

questions.q: Estimate the net charge of the tripeptide Lys-Glu-His at pH 7.0 (side-chain pKₐ values: Lys 10.5, Glu 4.2, His 6.0).
o: This forgets the N-terminal amino group, which is still protonated.
Correct: N-terminus +1, Lys +1, Glu −1, C-terminus −1, His about 0.
This counts His as protonated, but pH 7 is above its pKₐ of 6.
This ignores the two negative charges from Glu and the C-terminus.
questions.note: Remember the termini when counting charges in a peptide.
questions.x: Count every group that can carry a charge, including the two ends of the peptide. Rule: a group keeps its proton when pH is below its pKₐ. At pH 7: the N-terminal amine (pKₐ ≈ 8) keeps its proton, +1. Lys (10.5) keeps its proton, +1. Glu (4.2) has lost its proton, −1. The C-terminal carboxyl (≈ 3.5) has lost its proton, −1. His (6.0) is only about 9% protonated, so it adds about 0. Total: +1 + 1 − 1 − 1 + 0 = 0.

questions.q: What is the net charge of the tripeptide Gly-Lys-Asp at pH 1?
o: At pH 1 both carboxyls hold their protons, so there's no negative charge to cancel anything.
This misses that the Lys side chain is also protonated.
Correct: the N-terminus and Lys are +1 each, and both carboxyls are neutral COOH.
Asp's carboxyl becomes neutral, not positive, when it picks up a proton.
questions.x: pH 1 is extremely acidic, lower than every pKₐ in this peptide, so every group keeps its proton. For amines that means NH₃⁺, +1. For carboxyls that means COOH, which is neutral, 0. The groups that can carry charge are the N-terminal amine (+1), the Lys side-chain amine (+1), the Asp side-chain carboxyl (0) and the C-terminal carboxyl (0). Total: +1 + 1 + 0 + 0 = +2. Adding a proton to a carboxyl makes it neutral, never positive.

questions.q: Which amino acid has a thioether (C–S–C) side chain?
o: Methionine
Correct: its side chain is CH₂CH₂–S–CH₃, sulfur between two carbons.
Cysteine
Cysteine has a thiol (SH), not a thioether.
Serine
Serine has an OH group and no sulfur.
Threonine
Threonine has an OH group and no sulfur.
questions.x: A thioether is a sulfur atom sitting between two carbons, C–S–C. It's the sulfur version of an ether. Methionine's side chain is CH₂CH₂–S–CH₃, so its sulfur has a carbon on each side. Cysteine also has sulfur, but its side chain ends in SH, which is called a thiol (sulfur bonded to a carbon and a hydrogen). That H is what lets two cysteines form a disulfide bond. Methionine's sulfur has no H, so it can't. Serine and threonine have no sulfur at all.

questions.q: Which amino acid is polar but uncharged at physiological pH?
o: Glutamate
Glutamate is negatively charged at pH 7.4.
Isoleucine
Isoleucine is uncharged, but it's not polar.
Glutamine
Correct: its amide side chain is polar and doesn't gain or lose protons.
Lysine
Lysine is positively charged at pH 7.4.
questions.x: Polar means the side chain has uneven charge sharing, so it can hydrogen-bond with water. Charged means it has actually gained or lost a proton. Glutamine's side chain ends in an amide (CONH₂). Its C=O and N–H bonds make it polar, but amides don't gain or lose protons in water, so it stays uncharged. Glutamate and lysine are polar too, but they carry a charge at pH 7.4 (negative and positive). Isoleucine is just carbon and hydrogen, so it isn't polar at all.

questions.q: An aspartate side chain has pKₐ 3.9. At pH 4.9, what is the ratio of deprotonated to protonated side chains?
o: Correct: pH − pKₐ = 1, so [A⁻] ÷ [HA] = 10¹ = 10.
This flips the ratio. pH above pKₐ favors the deprotonated form.
A 1 : 1 ratio only happens when pH = pKₐ.
100 : 1 would need the pH to be 2 units above the pKₐ.
questions.x: Use the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKₐ + log([A⁻] ÷ [HA]), where [A⁻] is the form without the proton (COO⁻) and [HA] is the form with it (COOH). Values: pH = 4.9, pKₐ = 3.9. Plug in: 4.9 = 3.9 + log(ratio), so log(ratio) = 4.9 − 3.9 = 1. Log just reads off the exponent of 10, so ratio = 10¹ = 10. That's 10 deprotonated side chains for every 1 protonated. pH above pKₐ always favors the deprotonated form, so 1 : 10 is backwards.

questions.q: Which form of alanine is most abundant in water at pH 7?
o: H₂N–CH(CH₃)–COOH
The fully uncharged form is barely present in water at any pH.
⁺H₃N–CH(CH₃)–COOH
This +1 form only wins below about pH 2.3.
H₂N–CH(CH₃)–COO⁻
This −1 form only wins above about pH 9.7.
⁺H₃N–CH(CH₃)–COO⁻
Correct: the amino group is protonated and the carboxyl isn't, making a zwitterion.
questions.x: Check each group against pH 7. The carboxyl group has pKₐ ≈ 2.3, and pH 7 is above that, so it has lost its proton: COO⁻. The amino group has pKₐ ≈ 9.7, and pH 7 is below that, so it keeps its proton: NH₃⁺. That gives ⁺H₃N–CH(CH₃)–COO⁻, a zwitterion: a molecule with one + and one − charge that cancel to net 0. The fully uncharged drawing you see in textbooks is barely present in water at any pH.

questions.q: The α-COOH of an amino acid has pKₐ ≈ 2, far lower than acetic acid (pKₐ ≈ 4.8). What best explains this?
o: Resonance between the carboxyl and the side chain
The side chain isn't connected to the carboxyl by alternating double bonds.
The nearby positively charged α-NH₃⁺ stabilizes the carboxylate
Correct: the nearby positive NH₃⁺ stabilizes COO⁻, so the proton leaves more easily.
Water hydrogen-bonds more strongly to the amino acid
Water alone can't explain a gap of almost 3 pKₐ units.
The amino acid's larger size spreads the charge out
Size isn't the cause. The nearby positive NH₃⁺ is.
questions.x: An acid is stronger (lower pKₐ) when the form left behind after it loses its proton, its conjugate base, is more stable. In an amino acid, the positively charged NH₃⁺ group sits right next to the carboxyl. It pulls electron density toward itself through the bonds (an inductive effect), and its + charge directly attracts the − charge of COO⁻. Both make COO⁻ more comfortable, so the carboxyl lets go of its proton more easily. That drops its pKₐ from about 4.8 (acetic acid) to about 2.

questions.q: A neighboring histidine lowers an active-site cysteine's thiol pKₐ from 8.3 to 6.5. What is the main effect at pH 7.4?
o: The cysteine is mostly protonated and unreactive
Lowering the pKₐ below 7.4 favors losing the proton, not keeping it.
The cysteine is mostly thiolate and a stronger nucleophile
Correct: pH above pKₐ favors S⁻, which is a far stronger nucleophile than SH.
The cysteine forms a disulfide bond with histidine
Histidine has no SH group, so no disulfide can form.
The cysteine gains a positive charge
Losing a proton from SH gives a negative S⁻, not a positive charge.
questions.x: Lowering a pKₐ means the group loses its proton at a lower pH. At pH 7.4, the new pKₐ of 6.5 is below the pH, so most of the cysteine has lost its proton. Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKₐ + log([S⁻] ÷ [SH]). Values: pH = 7.4, pKₐ = 6.5. Plug in: log(ratio) = 7.4 − 6.5 = 0.9, so the ratio is 10⁰·⁹ ≈ 7.9. Thiolate share = 7.9 ÷ (7.9 + 1) = 7.9 ÷ 8.9 ≈ 0.89, about 89%. The thiolate (S⁻) is a much stronger nucleophile (electron-pair donor) than SH.

questions.q: Why is β-mercaptoethanol added to protein samples before SDS-PAGE?
o: To hydrolyze peptide bonds into smaller fragments
It's a reducing agent, not an enzyme that cuts peptide bonds.
To give each protein a uniform negative charge
Giving the uniform negative charge is SDS's job.
To stabilize the native folded state
It's used to help unfold proteins fully, not to keep them folded.
To reduce disulfide bonds so subunits separate
Correct: it breaks S–S bonds that SDS alone can't.
questions.x: SDS-PAGE separates proteins by size. SDS is a detergent that unfolds proteins and coats them with negative charge, but it only breaks weak, noncovalent bonds. It can't break disulfide bonds (S–S), which are covalent. β-mercaptoethanol is a reducing agent: it breaks each S–S bond into two separate SH groups. That lets chains linked by disulfides come apart, and loops held by disulfides open up, so each chain runs at the spot set by its own mass.

questions.q: A protein runs as one 100 kDa band on SDS-PAGE without reducing agent and as one 50 kDa band with reducing agent. What is the best conclusion?
o: It has two identical 50 kDa subunits joined by disulfide bonds
Correct: only reduction splits it, and one band means the chains are the same size.
It is a noncovalent dimer of 50 kDa subunits
SDS alone would split a noncovalent dimer, giving 50 kDa without reducing agent.
It is a 100 kDa monomer that the reducing agent degrades
Reducing agents don't cut peptide bonds.
It has two different subunits of 60 and 40 kDa
Two different chains would give two bands after reduction.
questions.x: SDS alone breaks weak, noncovalent bonds. So whatever is still stuck together without a reducing agent must be linked by covalent bonds. Here, the protein stays at 100 kDa with SDS alone, then drops to 50 kDa once a reducing agent breaks its disulfide bonds. So the pieces were held together by disulfides. Only one band shows up after reduction, so every chain is the same size. Number of chains = 100 kDa ÷ 50 kDa = 2. That's two 50 kDa chains linked by disulfide bonds.

questions.q: Which residue is most likely buried in the core of a water-soluble globular protein?
o: Lysine
Charged lysine usually sits on the surface, touching water.
Glutamate
Charged glutamate prefers the surface, where water can reach it.
Phenylalanine
Correct: its water-avoiding ring hides from water in the core.
Arginine
Arginine's charged side chain prefers the surface.
questions.x: When a protein folds in water, its water-avoiding (hydrophobic) side chains bunch together in the middle, the core, out of contact with water. This is called the hydrophobic effect. Phenylalanine's side chain is a ring of only carbon and hydrogen, so it's water-avoiding and usually ends up buried. Lysine, glutamate and arginine are charged. Charged groups love being surrounded by water, so they usually sit on the protein's surface.

questions.q: A 20-residue segment is predicted to form a single membrane-spanning α-helix. Which residues should it be rich in?
o: Aspartate, glutamate and lysine
Charged residues are very unfavorable inside the oily membrane.
Serine, asparagine and glutamine
These polar side chains want to be near water.
Proline and glycine
These two break up or weaken α-helices.
Leucine, isoleucine and valine
Correct: water-avoiding side chains fit against the oily lipid tails.
questions.x: The inside of a cell membrane is made of fatty acid tails: a layer about 30 Å thick that's basically oil. An α-helix rises about 1.5 Å per residue. Formula: helix length = 1.5 Å × number of residues. Plug in: 1.5 Å × 20 = 30 Å, just enough to cross. The side chains facing those oily tails have to be water-avoiding too. Leucine, isoleucine and valine are water-avoiding and good at forming helices. Charged residues hate being in the oily layer, and proline and glycine break helices.

questions.q: Which standard amino acid has two stereocenters?
o: Serine
Serine's side-chain carbon (CH₂OH) has two matching H atoms.
Valine
Valine's side-chain carbon has two matching CH₃ groups.
Threonine
Correct: both its α-carbon and its β-carbon have four different groups.
Leucine
Leucine's branch carbon has two matching CH₃ groups, so only the α-carbon is chiral.
questions.note: Thr and Ile each have two chiral centers.
questions.x: A carbon is a stereocenter only if all four of its groups are different. Every amino acid except glycine has one at the α-carbon. Threonine has a second one in its side chain: its β-carbon holds an OH, a CH₃, an H and the α-carbon, all different. (Isoleucine also has two.) Serine, valine and leucine each have a side-chain carbon with two matching groups (two H's or two CH₃'s), so only their α-carbon is a stereocenter.

questions.q: Which amino acid differs from phenylalanine only by a para-hydroxyl group on the ring?
o: Tryptophan
Tryptophan has a double-ring indole, not a benzene ring with an OH.
Tyrosine
Correct: tyrosine is phenylalanine with an OH at the para position.
Histidine
Histidine has a five-membered ring with two nitrogens.
Serine
Serine has an OH but no ring at all.
questions.x: Tyrosine is phenylalanine with one extra OH group on the ring, on the carbon straight across from where the ring attaches (the para position). In fact, the body makes tyrosine by adding that OH to phenylalanine, using an enzyme called phenylalanine hydroxylase. The OH makes tyrosine more polar and gives kinases a spot to attach phosphate. Tryptophan and histidine have rings too, but different ones. Serine has an OH but no ring.

questions.q: The N-terminal α-NH₃⁺ in a peptide has pKₐ ≈ 8, lower than in a free amino acid (≈ 9.6). Why?
o: There is no adjacent carboxylate to stabilize the protonated amine
Correct: in a free amino acid, the nearby COO⁻ helps the NH₃⁺ hold its proton.
The peptide bond makes the amine a stronger base
A lower pKₐ for NH₃⁺ means a weaker base, not a stronger one.
The N-terminal amine is part of the peptide bond
The N-terminal amine is free. Only the amines inside the chain are in peptide bonds.
Side chains donate electrons to the terminal amine
Pushing electrons onto the amine would raise its pKₐ, not lower it.
questions.x: In a free amino acid, the NH₃⁺ group has a negative COO⁻ right next door. That negative neighbor attracts the positive NH₃⁺ and helps it hold its proton, which pushes its pKₐ up to about 9.6. In a peptide, the N-terminal residue's carboxyl has been turned into a neutral peptide bond (an amide). The helpful negative neighbor is gone, so the NH₃⁺ lets go of its proton more easily, and its pKₐ drops to about 8. A lower pKₐ here means a weaker base, not a stronger one.

questions.q: Amino acids can accept protons and also donate them. What is this property called?
o: Hydrophobic
Hydrophobic describes how something behaves in water, not proton transfer.
Chiral
Chiral is about mirror-image handedness, not proton transfer.
Amphoteric
Correct: they can act as both acids and bases.
Aromatic
Aromatic describes special rings, not proton transfer.
questions.x: A substance that can act as either an acid (giving away a proton) or a base (taking one) is called amphoteric. Amino acids have a carboxyl group, which can give away a proton, and an amino group, which can take one. In acid, they pick up a proton and become positive. In base, they lose one and become negative. That's why they exist as zwitterions and can buffer at more than one pH. Hydrophobic, chiral and aromatic describe totally different properties.

questions.q: Free histidine has pKₐ values of 1.8, 6.0 and 9.2. At which pH would it buffer best?
o: 3.9 is about 2 units from every pKₐ, so buffering there is poor.
Correct: buffering is strongest at a pKₐ, and 6.0 is the side chain's pKₐ.
7.6 is histidine's pI, a steep spot where buffering is weak.
11.0 is almost 2 units above the highest pKₐ, so little buffer is left.
questions.note: Trap: the pI is where buffering is weakest.
questions.x: A buffer resists pH change best when the pH equals a group's pKₐ. At that point the group is half protonated and half not, so it can soak up added acid or added base equally well. Histidine's pKₐ values are 1.8, 6.0 and 9.2, and 6.0 is the only choice sitting right on one of them. 7.6 is a trap: it's histidine's pI, (6.0 + 9.2) ÷ 2 = 15.2 ÷ 2 = 7.6, which is a steep spot on the titration curve where buffering is weakest.

questions.q: Trypsin cleaves on the C-terminal side of Lys and Arg (except before Pro). How many fragments does it make from Ala-Lys-Gly-Arg-Phe-Lys?
o: This misses one of the two cut sites inside the chain.
Correct: cuts after the 2nd-position Lys and the Arg give Ala-Lys, Gly-Arg and Phe-Lys.
The last Lys is the C-terminus, so there's no bond after it to cut.
Trypsin doesn't cut after every residue, only after Lys and Arg.
questions.x: Trypsin cuts the bond right after a Lys or Arg, unless the next residue is Pro. Go through Ala-Lys-Gly-Arg-Phe-Lys one residue at a time. Lys (2nd) is followed by Gly: cut. Arg (4th) is followed by Phe: cut. Lys (6th) is the last residue, so there's no bond after it to cut. That's 2 cuts. Formula: fragments = cuts + 1. Plug in: 2 + 1 = 3 fragments: Ala-Lys, Gly-Arg and Phe-Lys.

questions.q: Glycine is common in tight turns and flexible loops. Which property of glycine explains this?
o: Its tiny side chain allows backbone angles that other residues cannot adopt
Correct: with only H as a side chain, glycine has the most bending freedom.
Its side chain forms strong hydrogen bonds
Glycine's side chain is just an H, which can't form hydrogen bonds.
It cannot form peptide bonds on one side
Glycine forms normal peptide bonds on both sides.
It is charged at physiological pH
Glycine's side chain has no charge.
questions.x: Glycine's side chain is just a single hydrogen. Every other amino acid has at least a carbon there, and that carbon bumps into the backbone when the chain tries to bend sharply. Glycine has nothing to bump, so it can take on backbone angles that other residues can't. That flexibility lets the chain make tight U-turns, which is why glycine shows up in turns and loops. The same floppiness makes glycine bad at forming steady α-helices.

questions.q: Alanine (pKₐ values 2.3 and 9.7) is in a solution at pH 9.7. What is its average net charge?
o: A full −1 needs the pH well above 9.7.
Correct: half the molecules are zwitterions (0) and half are −1.
Zero is the average charge at the pI (6.0), not at 9.7.
+0.5 is the average charge at the other pKₐ, 2.3.
questions.note: At any pKₐ, the group is half protonated.
questions.x: At pH = pKₐ, that group is exactly half protonated. pH 9.7 equals the amino group's pKₐ, so half the NH₃⁺ groups (+1) have turned into NH₂ (0). The carboxyl (pKₐ 2.3) is far below pH 9.7, so it's fully COO⁻ (−1). Formula: average charge = sum of each group's average charge. Values: carboxyl = −1; amino group = (+1 × 0.5) + (0 × 0.5) = +0.5. Plug in: −1 + 0.5 = −0.5. In other words, half the molecules are 0 and half are −1.

questions.q: What does a protein's primary structure refer to?
o: Its α-helices and β-sheets
Those are secondary structures.
The overall 3D fold of one chain
That's tertiary structure.
How multiple subunits are arranged
That's quaternary structure.
Its amino acid sequence linked by peptide bonds
Correct: primary structure is the order of amino acids in the chain.
questions.x: Primary structure is simply the order of amino acids in the chain, linked by peptide bonds and written from the N-terminus to the C-terminus. It's the only level held together by covalent backbone bonds, and it decides everything else. Secondary structure is local shapes like α-helices and β-sheets. Tertiary structure is the full 3D fold of one chain. Quaternary structure is how several chains fit together.

questions.q: What chiefly stabilizes α-helices and β-sheets?
o: Ionic bonds between side chains
Side-chain bonds mainly hold tertiary structure.
Hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups
Correct: secondary structure is defined by backbone hydrogen bonds.
Disulfide bonds between cysteines
Disulfides are covalent links that hold tertiary or quaternary structure.
Peptide bonds between adjacent residues
Peptide bonds make up primary structure.
questions.x: α-helices and β-sheets are secondary structure, and they're held together by hydrogen bonds between backbone groups: the C=O of one amino acid and the N–H of another. Every amino acid has the same backbone, so almost any sequence can form these shapes. Bonds that involve side chains, like salt bridges, water-avoiding packing and disulfides, mainly hold tertiary and quaternary structure. Peptide bonds are primary structure.

questions.q: In an α-helix, the backbone C=O of residue n hydrogen-bonds to the N–H of which residue?
o: An n + 2 bond would make a very tight turn, not an α-helix.
Correct: this n → n + 4 pattern gives about 3.6 residues per turn.
Neighboring residues are too close to hydrogen-bond across the helix.
A residue on a neighboring strand
Bonds to a neighboring strand describe a β-sheet.
questions.x: In an α-helix, the C=O of each residue (call it n) hydrogen-bonds to the N–H of the residue four places later, n + 4. The helix turns 100° per residue, so after about 3.6 residues it completes a full turn (3.6 × 100° = 360°). That puts residue n + 4 almost directly above residue n, one turn up, where its N–H can line up with the C=O below. Bonds between separate strands lying side by side describe β-sheets, not helices.

questions.q: How are side chains arranged in an α-helix?
o: They point into the center of the helix
The middle of an α-helix is already filled with backbone atoms.
They lie flat in a plane above and below
That alternating up-and-down pattern describes β-strands.
They form the hydrogen bonds that hold the helix
The helix is held by backbone hydrogen bonds, not side chains.
They project outward from the helix axis
Correct: they point out, away from the tightly packed backbone.
questions.x: In an α-helix, the backbone coils tightly to form the middle of the helix, with no space left inside. The hydrogen bonds holding the helix run up and down between backbone groups. So the side chains have nowhere to go but out: they stick outward from the helix's axis, like bristles on a round brush or spokes on a wheel. That lets them interact with water, membranes or other parts of the protein. Side chains alternating above and below a flat plane describes a β-strand.

questions.q: What defines an antiparallel β-sheet?
o: Adjacent strands run in opposite N-to-C directions
Correct: antiparallel means neighboring strands point opposite ways.
Adjacent strands run in the same N-to-C direction
Strands running the same way make a parallel β-sheet.
Hydrogen bonds form within a single strand
β-sheet hydrogen bonds form between strands, not within one.
Side chains lie in the plane of the sheet
Side chains point above and below the sheet, not in its plane.
questions.x: Every strand in a β-sheet has a direction, from its N-terminal end to its C-terminal end. If neighboring strands run in opposite directions, the sheet is antiparallel. If they run the same way, it's parallel. Either way, the hydrogen bonds connect backbone C=O and N–H groups on different strands. In antiparallel sheets those bonds line up straight across, which makes them a bit more stable. Where the side chains point has nothing to do with the name.

questions.q: Along a single β-strand, how do successive side chains point?
o: All point to the same face of the sheet
Back-to-back residues alternate sides, so they don't all face one way.
They spiral around the strand every 3.6 residues
Spiraling every 3.6 residues describes an α-helix.
They alternate above and below the plane of the sheet
Correct: the pleated backbone flips each side chain to the opposite face.
They point toward the hydrogen-bonded neighboring strand
The backbone C=O and N–H face the neighboring strands, not the side chains.
questions.note: A sheet can have one hydrophobic face and one polar face.
questions.x: A β-strand is stretched out and pleated, like a folded paper fan. Each α-carbon sits on a fold, alternately a little above and a little below the sheet, and its side chain points out on that side. So side chains alternate: one up, the next down, then up again. Residues 1, 3, 5 share one face and 2, 4, 6 share the other. If water-avoiding and water-loving residues alternate, the sheet ends up with one greasy face and one water-loving face. Spiraling every 3.6 residues describes an α-helix.

questions.q: Which two residues are especially common in β-turns?
o: Leucine and isoleucine
Bulky water-avoiding residues prefer helices and buried strands.
Lysine and arginine
Charge alone doesn't make a residue good at tight turns.
Phenylalanine and tryptophan
Big ring-shaped side chains are too bulky for tight turns.
Glycine and proline
Correct: glycine's flexibility and proline's built-in kink suit tight turns.
questions.x: A β-turn is a tight U-turn that flips the chain's direction over about four residues. That needs unusual backbone angles. Glycine fits because its side chain is just an H, so nothing gets in the way when the backbone bends sharply. Proline fits because its ring locks the backbone into a built-in kink that matches the turn's shape. So these two are opposites, the floppiest and the stiffest, yet both love turns. Bulky residues like leucine or tryptophan crowd the backbone in such a tight space.

questions.q: What does a protein's tertiary structure describe?
o: The sequence of amino acids
That's primary structure.
Local helices and sheets only
That's secondary structure.
The overall three-dimensional fold of a single polypeptide
Correct: it's how the helices, sheets and loops of one chain pack together.
How two or more chains assemble
That's quaternary structure.
questions.x: Tertiary structure is the complete 3D shape of one chain: how its helices, sheets and loops fold up and pack against each other. It's held together mostly by side-chain interactions. Those include water-avoiding side chains clustering in the core, hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and disulfide bonds. The sequence is primary structure, local helices and sheets alone are secondary, and the way separate chains fit together is quaternary.

questions.q: Which protein has quaternary structure?
o: Myoglobin
Myoglobin is a single chain.
Hemoglobin
Correct: it's built from four chains, two α and two β.
Ribonuclease A
Ribonuclease A is a single chain held by internal disulfides.
A 30-residue monomeric peptide
One chain can't have quaternary structure.
questions.x: Quaternary structure only exists when a protein is made of two or more separate chains (subunits) that fit together. Hemoglobin is built from four chains, two α and two β (written α₂β₂). Its chains talk to each other, which is what lets it pick up oxygen cooperatively. Myoglobin and ribonuclease A are each a single chain, so tertiary is their highest level. A peptide with one chain can't have quaternary structure no matter how it folds.

questions.q: What is the main driving force for a soluble protein to fold with nonpolar residues in its core?
o: Water gains entropy when nonpolar groups are buried
Correct: burying nonpolar groups frees the caged water around them (the hydrophobic effect).
Hydrogen bonds form between nonpolar side chains
Nonpolar side chains can't form hydrogen bonds.
The polypeptide chain gains conformational entropy
Folding lowers the chain's own entropy.
Disulfide bonds form between all buried residues
Few residues are cysteines, and many proteins fold with no disulfides.
questions.x: Water can't hydrogen-bond with water-avoiding (nonpolar) side chains. So water molecules next to them get stuck in neat, cage-like arrangements, which lowers water's entropy (its freedom or disorder). When the protein folds and tucks those side chains into its core, that water is set free and its entropy goes up. That favorable change is called the hydrophobic effect, and it's the main force behind folding. The chain itself actually loses entropy when it folds, so that can't be the driver.

questions.q: Folded proteins are typically only about 20 to 60 kJ/mol more stable than the unfolded state, despite many favorable interactions. Why?
o: Folding has a positive ΔG that ATP hydrolysis overcomes
Most proteins fold on their own, without ATP.
Noncovalent interactions contribute no energy
Each interaction is weak, but together they add up to a lot.
The chain's large loss of conformational entropy offsets most of those interactions
Correct: stability is a small difference between two large opposing terms.
Folded proteins are held only by covalent bonds
Folding relies mainly on noncovalent forces, not covalent bonds.
questions.x: Folding has two big effects pulling in opposite directions. On the plus side, the chain forms many weak interactions (lowering ΔH) and frees caged water (raising water's entropy). On the minus side, the chain goes from countless floppy shapes to just one, losing a huge amount of its own entropy. Plug into ΔG = ΔH − TΔS and those large terms nearly cancel. What's left is a small net ΔG, around 20 to 60 kJ/mol. That's why one mutation or a bit of heat can unfold a protein.

questions.q: A small enzyme is unfolded with urea and a reducing agent. When both are removed slowly, it refolds and regains full activity. What does this show?
o: The amino acid sequence contains the information for the native fold
Correct: it refolds correctly with nothing but its sequence to guide it.
Chaperones are always needed for folding
No chaperones were present, and it still refolded.
Disulfide bonds determine the sequence
The sequence comes from the gene. Disulfides form during folding.
Denaturation breaks peptide bonds
Getting full activity back shows the chain was never cut.
questions.x: Urea unfolds the protein, and the reducing agent breaks its disulfide bonds, so nothing is left but the amino acid chain itself. When both are slowly removed, the enzyme refolds, re-forms the right disulfides and works perfectly again, with no help from anything else. So the sequence alone holds all the information needed to reach the correct fold. This is Anfinsen's famous experiment with ribonuclease A. Chaperones help folding in cells, but they don't supply the information.

questions.q: A denatured, reduced enzyme is reoxidized while still in 8 M urea, and then the urea is removed. Activity stays very low. Why?
o: Urea hydrolyzed peptide bonds during reoxidation
Urea breaks noncovalent interactions, but it doesn't cut peptide bonds.
Oxidation converted cysteine into methionine
Oxidizing cysteine SH groups makes disulfides, not methionine.
The enzyme lost its primary structure
The sequence is unchanged. The problem is wrong cysteine pairing.
Disulfides formed randomly in the unfolded chain, trapping non-native structures
Correct: oxidizing before folding locks in mismatched cysteine pairs.
questions.x: Disulfide bonds need to form after the chain folds, so the right cysteines are next to each other. Here, they formed while the chain was still unfolded in urea, so cysteines paired at random. Ribonuclease A has 8 cysteines. The number of ways to pair them into 4 disulfides is 7 × 5 × 3 × 1 = 105, and only 1 is correct. So only about 1 in 105, roughly 1%, of molecules get it right. The wrong pairs are covalent, so removing urea can't fix them, and activity stays low.

questions.q: What do molecular chaperones mainly do?
o: Provide the structural information that specifies the native fold
The information for the fold is in the amino acid sequence.
Bind exposed hydrophobic regions to prevent misfolding and aggregation
Correct: they shield sticky regions so the chain can fold, but the sequence decides the shape.
Form permanent covalent bonds with their client proteins
Chaperones hold on briefly and noncovalently, then let go.
Catalyze peptide bond formation on the ribosome
Peptide bonds are made by the ribosome, not chaperones.
questions.x: Unfolded or half-folded chains have water-avoiding patches showing that would normally be tucked inside. In a crowded cell, those sticky patches can glom onto other proteins and form clumps (aggregates). Chaperones, like Hsp70 and the barrel-shaped GroEL, grab those exposed patches. That keeps the chain from clumping and gives it more chances to fold correctly. They don't decide the final shape; the sequence still does that.

questions.q: How does a high concentration of urea denature proteins?
o: It hydrolyzes peptide bonds
Urea doesn't break covalent backbone bonds.
It disrupts hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions
Correct: it steals hydrogen bonds and weakens the hydrophobic effect, leaving the sequence intact.
It reduces disulfide bonds
Urea isn't a reducing agent, so it can't break disulfides.
It permanently adds groups to side chains
Urea unfolding is usually reversible and noncovalent.
questions.x: Urea unfolds proteins in two ways. First, it's full of N–H and C=O groups, so it hydrogen-bonds to the protein's own C=O and N–H groups, stealing the partners that held the fold together. Second, it makes water friendlier to water-avoiding side chains, which weakens the hydrophobic effect that drives folding. Both effects are noncovalent, so peptide bonds and disulfide bonds stay intact. That's why removing urea often lets the protein refold. To break disulfides you need a separate reducing agent.

questions.q: An enzyme solution is boiled for 10 minutes. Which level of structure is most likely still intact?
o: Secondary
Heat breaks the backbone hydrogen bonds that hold helices and sheets.
Tertiary
The 3D fold is lost on boiling.
Quaternary
Contacts between subunits are noncovalent and fall apart.
Primary
Correct: heat breaks noncovalent interactions, not peptide bonds.
questions.x: Heat gives molecules enough energy to break weak, noncovalent interactions: hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and the hydrophobic effect. Those are what hold secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure, so boiling unravels all three. Peptide bonds are covalent and very slow to break without a catalyst, so 10 minutes of boiling leaves the amino acid sequence untouched. Denaturing destroys a protein's shape, not its sequence.

questions.q: How do strongly acidic or basic conditions denature a protein?
o: They change side-chain ionization, disrupting salt bridges and hydrogen bonds
Correct: changed charges break the electrostatic interactions holding the fold.
They break disulfide bonds by reduction
Changing the pH doesn't act as a reducing agent.
They convert L-amino acids to D-amino acids instantly
Flipping L to D is slow and isn't how pH unfolds proteins.
They remove water from the protein core
pH works through charge, not by drying out the core.
questions.x: A protein's fold depends partly on charged side chains attracting each other (salt bridges) and on hydrogen bonds. Very low pH adds protons, so negative groups like COO⁻ on Asp and Glu become neutral COOH. Very high pH removes protons, so positive groups like NH₃⁺ on Lys become neutral NH₂. Either way, salt bridges lose a partner, hydrogen-bond patterns change, and the protein ends up with lots of charges of one sign that push each other apart. The fold falls apart without any covalent bond breaking.

questions.q: In SDS-PAGE, what mainly determines how far a protein moves?
o: Its isoelectric point
pI is the basis of isoelectric focusing, not SDS-PAGE.
Its native three-dimensional shape
SDS unfolds proteins, wiping out differences in shape.
Its molecular mass
Correct: SDS gives equal charge per mass, so smaller chains move farther.
Its intrinsic net charge
SDS's negative charge drowns out the protein's own charge.
questions.x: SDS is a negatively charged detergent. It unfolds proteins and coats them evenly, with roughly the same amount of SDS per unit of length. So every chain gets about the same negative charge for its size and the same stretched-out rod shape. The gel acts like a sieve: smaller chains slip through its pores faster and travel farther. That leaves mass as the main thing deciding how far a protein moves. Its own charge and its folded shape no longer matter.

questions.q: Thermal unfolding shows a wild-type protein with a melting temperature (Tm) of 52 °C and a point mutant with Tm 44 °C. What is the best conclusion?
o: The mutation stabilizes the folded state
Stabilizing mutations raise the Tm, not lower it.
The mutant has higher catalytic activity
Tm measures stability, not activity.
The mutant cannot fold at any temperature
It has a Tm, so it's folded below 44 °C.
The mutation destabilizes the folded state
Correct: a lower Tm means less heat is needed to unfold it.
questions.x: The melting temperature (Tm) is the temperature where half the protein molecules are unfolded. A higher Tm means the protein takes more heat to unfold, so it's more stable. The mutant's Tm dropped from 52 °C to 44 °C, a change of 52 − 44 = 8 °C. Less heat is needed to unfold it, so the mutation made the folded state less stable. Tm says nothing directly about how fast the enzyme works, and having a Tm at all means the mutant is folded below 44 °C.

questions.q: How do prions cause disease?
o: A small DNA genome encodes a toxic protein
Prions contain no DNA or RNA.
Point mutations spread from cell to cell
Prions copy a shape, not a sequence change.
A misfolded, β-sheet-rich protein converts normally folded copies into the misfolded form
Correct: the misfolded shape spreads by converting normal copies, with no DNA or RNA.
The prion protein is hydrolyzed into toxic peptides
Prions are known for resisting breakdown.
questions.x: Prions are infectious proteins with no DNA or RNA at all. The normal prion protein (PrP) is mostly α-helix. The disease form has the same sequence but is folded wrong, rich in β-sheet. When the bad form touches a normal copy, it acts as a template and flips that copy into the bad shape too. Each newly flipped copy can then flip others, so the misfolding spreads. The bad form piles up into clumps that enzymes can't break down, which damages brain cells. What spreads is a shape, not a gene.

questions.q: A region of a protein folds on its own into a compact unit and often has its own function. What is it called?
o: A subunit
A subunit is a separate chain, not part of one chain.
A domain
Correct: domains are parts of one chain that fold on their own.
A primary sequence
The primary sequence is the order of residues, not a folded unit.
A β-turn
A β-turn is a short U-turn in the chain, not a working unit.
questions.x: A domain is a section of a single chain that folds up on its own into a compact, stable unit, and it often has its own job, like binding DNA or ATP. Many proteins are built from several domains strung together, like modules. Don't mix it up with a subunit: a subunit is a whole separate chain, and fitting subunits together is quaternary structure. A domain is part of one chain, so it belongs to tertiary structure.

questions.q: Why are disulfide bonds much more common in secreted proteins than in cytosolic ones?
o: The cytosol is a reducing environment, while the ER lumen and extracellular space are oxidizing
Correct: the cytosol keeps cysteines as SH, while the ER and outside the cell favor S–S.
Cytosolic proteins contain no cysteine
Cytosolic proteins have cysteines, usually as free SH groups.
Disulfides form only at low temperature
Temperature isn't what controls disulfide formation.
Ribosomes in the cytosol cannot translate cysteine codons
All ribosomes read cysteine codons.
questions.x: Making a disulfide bond is an oxidation: two SH groups give up their hydrogens (and electrons) to become S–S. So it only happens where the surroundings are oxidizing. The cytosol is kept reducing by a small molecule called glutathione, which breaks any disulfides that form, so cytosolic cysteines stay as free SH. Proteins headed out of the cell fold inside the ER, which is oxidizing, and enzymes there help build disulfides. Outside the cell is oxidizing too, so the bonds last.

questions.q: Adding 1 M NaCl most weakens which interaction in a folded protein?
o: Peptide bonds in the backbone
Salt doesn't affect covalent peptide bonds.
Disulfide bonds
Disulfides are covalent and need a reducing agent to break.
Salt bridges between charged side chains
Correct: dissolved ions screen the attraction between opposite charges.
Hydrophobic packing in the core
Moderate salt tends to strengthen water-avoiding packing, if anything.
questions.x: A salt bridge is the attraction between a positive and a negative side chain. When you add lots of salt, the dissolved Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions crowd around each charged side chain and partly cancel its charge. This is called screening. With the charges muffled, the two side chains attract each other much less. Salt can't touch covalent bonds like peptide bonds or disulfides, and it doesn't weaken water-avoiding packing in the core; if anything, salt makes that a bit stronger.

questions.q: What does a Ramachandran plot show?
o: Which combinations of φ and ψ backbone angles are sterically allowed
Correct: the allowed regions match α-helix and β-sheet shapes.
How absorbance changes with wavelength
That's an absorption spectrum.
How reaction rate depends on substrate concentration
That's a Michaelis-Menten plot.
How net charge changes with pH
That's a titration curve.
questions.x: A protein's backbone can twist at two bonds around each α-carbon. The twist angles are called φ (phi) and ψ (psi). A Ramachandran plot graphs φ against ψ and shows which combinations are allowed, meaning atoms don't crash into each other. Most combinations are blocked. The allowed regions match the shapes of α-helices and β-sheets. Glycine, with its tiny side chain, can reach more of the plot; proline, with its ring, can reach less.

questions.q: Adding high concentrations of ammonium sulfate makes a protein come out of solution. What is this called, and why does it happen?
o: Salting in; the salt shields charges and increases solubility
Salting in happens at low salt and makes proteins more soluble.
Denaturation; the salt breaks peptide bonds
Salting out is usually reversible and leaves the chain intact.
Reduction; sulfate breaks disulfide bonds
Sulfate isn't a reducing agent.
Salting out; the salt ions take up water needed to solvate the protein
Correct: the salt ions tie up the water the protein needs to stay dissolved.
questions.x: At high concentrations, ammonium sulfate ions grab a lot of water molecules to surround themselves. That leaves too little water to surround the protein molecules. Without enough water around them, the proteins' water-avoiding patches stick to each other, and the proteins clump together and fall out of solution. This is called salting out. It usually doesn't damage the protein, so it's used to purify and concentrate proteins. Salting in is the opposite effect, at low salt, where a little salt actually helps proteins dissolve.

questions.q: At what pH is a protein typically least soluble in water?
o: Two units below its pI
Here the protein is positive, and the molecules push each other apart.
At its isoelectric point
Correct: with no net charge, molecules don't repel and they clump together.
Two units above its pI
Here the protein is negative, and the molecules push each other apart.
At pH 7 regardless of pI
Solubility depends on each protein's own pI, not on pH 7.
questions.x: When protein molecules all carry the same kind of net charge, they push each other away and stay spread out in water. At the pI, the protein's positive and negative charges balance out, so its net charge is zero. With nothing pushing the molecules apart, their sticky spots let them clump together and fall out of solution. So a protein is least soluble at its own pI. Every protein has a different pI, so it isn't automatically pH 7.

questions.q: In size-exclusion chromatography, which protein elutes first?
o: The smallest protein
Small proteins enter the pores and get delayed.
The largest protein
Correct: big proteins can't enter the pores and take the shortest path.
The most positively charged protein
Size exclusion separates by size, not charge.
The protein with the lowest pI
pI matters in ion exchange, not size exclusion.
questions.x: Size-exclusion chromatography (also called gel filtration) uses a column packed with porous beads. Small proteins can slip into the pores, so they wander through a lot of extra space and take longer to get out. Large proteins are too big for the pores. They can only travel through the gaps between the beads, which is a short, direct route, so they come out first. Charge and pI don't matter here; they matter in ion-exchange chromatography.

questions.q: How does native PAGE differ from SDS-PAGE in what it separates by?
o: Native PAGE separates by mass alone
Separating by mass alone needs SDS to remove charge and shape differences.
Native PAGE separates only by pI
Separating only by pI is isoelectric focusing.
Native PAGE always denatures the proteins
Native PAGE is designed to keep proteins folded.
Native PAGE separates by size, charge and shape
Correct: without SDS, proteins keep their own charge and folded shape.
questions.x: In SDS-PAGE, the detergent SDS unfolds every protein and coats it with the same amount of negative charge per unit mass, so mass is the only thing left that matters. Native PAGE skips the SDS. Proteins stay folded, keep their own charge and keep any partner chains attached. So how far they move depends on three things together: their charge (how hard the field pulls them), their size, and their shape (how easily they squeeze through the gel). That's why native PAGE can show working enzymes and intact complexes.

questions.q: A cation-exchange column has negatively charged beads. At pH 7, which protein binds most strongly?
o: A protein with pI 9.5
Correct: below its pI it's positive and sticks to the negative beads.
A protein with pI 4.5
It's negative at pH 7, so the negative beads push it away.
A protein with pI 7.0
It's about neutral at pH 7, so it barely binds.
A protein with pI 5.5
It's negative at pH 7, so it washes straight through.
questions.x: A cation-exchange column has negative beads, so it grabs positive proteins (cations). A protein is positive when the pH is below its pI. At pH 7, the protein with pI 9.5 is 2.5 units below its pI, so it's clearly positive and sticks tightly to the negative beads. Proteins with pI below 7 (4.5 and 5.5) are negative at pH 7 and get pushed away. The protein with pI 7.0 is roughly neutral and barely sticks.

questions.q: Gel filtration gives a native mass of 150 kDa. SDS-PAGE shows one 50 kDa band whether or not reducing agent is added. What is the protein's structure?
o: A disulfide-linked trimer
Disulfide-linked chains would stay together without reducing agent.
A 150 kDa monomer
A single 150 kDa chain would run near 150 kDa on SDS-PAGE.
A noncovalent trimer of 50 kDa subunits
Correct: 150 ÷ 50 = 3, and SDS alone separates them, so no disulfides.
A noncovalent dimer of 75 kDa subunits
75 kDa chains would run as a 75 kDa band, not 50 kDa.
questions.x: Gel filtration keeps the protein folded, so it measures the whole assembly: 150 kDa. SDS-PAGE unfolds it and measures each chain: 50 kDa, in a single band, so every chain is the same size. Number of chains = 150 kDa ÷ 50 kDa = 3. The 50 kDa band shows up even without reducing agent, which means SDS alone pulled the chains apart. SDS only breaks noncovalent contacts, so there are no disulfides between chains. Answer: three 50 kDa chains held together noncovalently.

questions.q: A protein is heated in 8 M urea with no reducing agent. Which bonds remain intact?
o: Hydrogen bonds only
Hydrogen bonds are among the first to go.
Salt bridges and disulfide bonds
Disulfides survive, but salt bridges are noncovalent and get broken.
Hydrophobic interactions and peptide bonds
Peptide bonds survive, but urea and heat break up the water-avoiding core.
Peptide bonds and disulfide bonds
Correct: both are covalent, and heat and urea only break noncovalent forces.
questions.x: Heat and urea only break weak, noncovalent interactions: hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and the water-avoiding packing in the core. Covalent bonds need special chemistry to break. Peptide bonds (the backbone) need hydrolysis, and disulfide bonds (S–S links) need a reducing agent. No reducing agent was added here, so both covalent bond types survive. That's why fully unfolding a protein with disulfides takes urea plus a reducing agent.

questions.q: An α-helix has leucines spaced every 3 to 4 residues and charged residues elsewhere. What is this helix likely to be?
o: Fully hydrophobic, able to span a membrane
Charged residues around most of the helix rule out crossing a membrane.
Unable to form a helix
Leucine and charged residues are both fine in helices.
Amphipathic, with one hydrophobic face
Correct: residues 3 to 4 apart line up on one side of a 3.6-residue helix.
A β-strand
That spacing fits a helix. β-strands alternate every 2 residues.
questions.x: An α-helix has 3.6 residues per turn, so residues 3 or 4 apart end up on the same side of the helix. Leucines placed every 3 to 4 residues therefore line up as a water-avoiding stripe down one face, while the charged residues fill in the other faces. A helix with one water-avoiding face and one water-loving face is called amphipathic. These helices often lie flat on a membrane surface or pair up with another helix, as in leucine zippers.

questions.q: Silk fibroin is built from repeating Gly-Ala-Gly-Ala segments arranged in β-sheets. Why does this sequence suit tightly stacked sheets?
o: Glycine and alanine form disulfide cross-links
Neither glycine nor alanine has sulfur, so no disulfides.
Small side chains let neighboring sheets pack closely together
Correct: tiny H and CH₃ side chains let neighboring sheets pack tightly.
Their charged side chains form salt bridges between sheets
Glycine and alanine side chains have no charge.
These residues force the chain into an α-helix
The structure is a β-sheet, and small residues pack well in sheets.
questions.x: In a β-sheet, each strand's side chains alternate sides: one points up, the next points down. In silk's Gly-Ala-Gly-Ala repeat, every glycine (side chain H) ends up on one face and every alanine (side chain CH₃) on the other. Both are tiny, so both faces of the sheet are almost flat. Flat sheets can stack very tightly against each other, packed with weak contacts. That dense stacking is what makes silk so strong, with no disulfides or charges needed.

questions.q: How does ethanol denature proteins?
o: It solvates nonpolar side chains, weakening the hydrophobic effect
Correct: a less polar solvent weakens the push to bury the water-avoiding core.
It hydrolyzes peptide bonds
Ethanol doesn't cut the backbone.
It oxidizes cysteines to form extra disulfides
Ethanol isn't an oxidizing agent here.
It removes all metal cofactors by chelation
Ethanol doesn't grab metal ions.
questions.x: Ethanol is less polar than water and has a small greasy part (its CH₃CH₂ group). That means it can surround water-avoiding side chains much more comfortably than water can. The hydrophobic effect, which drives proteins to fold, depends on water hating exposed water-avoiding surfaces. With ethanol around, exposing the core doesn't cost as much, so the folded shape loses its advantage and the protein unfolds. Ethanol doesn't cut, oxidize or grab metals from proteins.

questions.q: Heavy metal ions such as Hg²⁺ and Pb²⁺ inactivate many proteins. What is the main mechanism?
o: They hydrolyze peptide bonds
Metal ions at these levels don't cut the backbone.
They convert lysine into arginine
Metals can't turn one amino acid into another.
They bind cysteine thiols and disrupt structure
Correct: these metals grip sulfur tightly and warp the fold.
They raise the pH above 12
Metal salts don't make solutions strongly basic.
questions.x: Heavy metal ions like Hg²⁺ (mercury) and Pb²⁺ (lead) have a strong attraction to sulfur. In chemistry terms, they're 'soft' acids, and cysteine's sulfur is a 'soft' base, and soft pairs with soft very tightly.
