When these metals latch onto cysteine SH groups, they can block an active site, bridge two cysteines in the wrong way, or kick zinc out of zinc-binding sites. Any of those distorts the protein's shape and switches it off.

questions.q: Cooked egg white stays solid after cooling and does not return to a clear liquid. Why?
o: Unfolded proteins aggregate through exposed hydrophobic regions
Correct: tangled clumps can't refold, so the change is permanent.
Cooking hydrolyzes the proteins into free amino acids
Free amino acids would dissolve. Peptide bonds survive cooking.
Heat converts the proteins into carbohydrates
Heat doesn't turn proteins into carbohydrates.
The proteins form new peptide bonds with each other
Heat doesn't make new peptide bonds between proteins.
questions.x: Heating egg white unfolds its proteins, so the water-avoiding side chains that were tucked inside get exposed. Those sticky patches grab onto other unfolded proteins, building a tangled 3D network. The network scatters light (so it turns white) and holds water in place (so it turns solid). When it cools, the chains are trapped in that tangle and can't find their way back to their original folds. The peptide bonds are all still intact; the change is in shape and clumping.

questions.q: How do cells mark misfolded cytosolic proteins for destruction?
o: They phosphorylate them for export out of the cell
Phosphorylation is an on/off switch, not a disposal tag.
They add mannose-6-phosphate to send them to mitochondria
Mannose-6-phosphate sends proteins to lysosomes, and it's added in the Golgi.
They glycosylate them in the cytosol
Glycosylation mostly happens in the ER and Golgi, not the cytosol.
They attach polyubiquitin chains for degradation by the proteasome
Correct: polyubiquitin tags them for the proteasome to destroy.
questions.x: Cells tag misfolded proteins in the cytosol with a chain of small proteins called ubiquitin. Enzymes called ubiquitin ligases attach one ubiquitin after another to a lysine on the bad protein, building a polyubiquitin chain. That chain is a 'destroy me' label. The proteasome, a barrel-shaped protein shredder, recognizes the label, unfolds the protein and chops it into short pieces. Mannose-6-phosphate is a different tag, added in the Golgi to send enzymes to lysosomes.

questions.q: About how many residues make up one turn of an α-helix?
o: Two residues per repeat fits a stretched-out β-strand.
Correct: 360° ÷ 100° per residue = 3.6 residues per turn.
Close, but 4 is the hydrogen-bond spacing (n to n + 4), not residues per turn.
About 10 is base pairs per turn of B-DNA.
questions.x: In an α-helix, each residue turns the chain 100° around the helix's axis. Formula: residues per turn = 360° ÷ rotation per residue. Value: rotation per residue = 100°. Plug in: 360° ÷ 100° = 3.6 residues per turn. Each residue also rises 0.15 nm, so one full turn rises 3.6 × 0.15 nm = 0.54 nm. Don't confuse this with 4: the hydrogen bonds link residue n to n + 4, but that's a different number. 10 per turn is DNA, not proteins.

questions.q: How do the hydrogen bonds in a β-sheet differ from those in an α-helix?
o: They form between side chains rather than backbone groups
Both structures use backbone C=O and N–H hydrogen bonds, not side chains.
They form between strands that may be far apart in sequence
Correct: sheet bonds link separate strands, which can be far apart in the sequence.
They are covalent bonds
Hydrogen bonds are noncovalent in both structures.
They form only between residues four apart
The n to n + 4 pattern belongs to the α-helix.
questions.x: Both α-helices and β-sheets are held by the same kind of bond: a hydrogen bond between a backbone C=O and a backbone N–H. The difference is who the partners are. In a helix, the partners are always close: residue n bonds to residue n + 4 in the same coil. In a sheet, the bonds link strands lying side by side, and those strands can be far apart in the sequence, or even on different chains. That's how sheets can tie together distant parts of a protein.

questions.q: A protein is rich in lysine and arginine and has few acidic residues. What is its pI most likely to be?
o: Well below 7
Acidic residues lower the pI. Basic residues raise it.
Well above 7
Correct: many basic groups need a high pH before the net charge reaches zero.
Exactly 7
The pI depends on what the protein is made of, not a fixed 7.
Impossible to estimate from composition
Composition gives a good estimate of the pI.
questions.x: The pI is the pH where a protein's positive and negative charges balance out. Lysine and arginine side chains are positive and hold onto their protons until high pH (pKₐ about 10.5 and 12.5). A protein loaded with them, and with few negative Asp or Glu to cancel them, is strongly positive at pH 7. To get it to net zero, you have to raise the pH until many of those groups lose their protons, which only happens well above 7. So its pI is high.

questions.q: What is the net charge of a protein in a buffer whose pH is below the protein's pI?
o: Negative
Net negative happens when the pH is above the pI.
Zero
Net zero happens only when the pH equals the pI.
It depends only on the protein's mass
Charge depends on pH compared with pI, not on mass.
Positive
Correct: pH below pI means extra protons, so net positive.
questions.x: Compare the buffer pH to the protein's pI. When the pH is below the pI, the solution has more protons (H⁺) than the protein needs to be neutral. Its groups pick up extra protons: COO⁻ becomes neutral COOH, and amines stay NH₃⁺. So the protein ends up net positive. At pH equal to the pI, it's net zero. Above the pI, it's net negative. This one rule predicts behavior in electrophoresis and ion-exchange columns.

questions.q: What composition is typical of intrinsically disordered protein regions, which lack a stable fold?
o: High in charged and polar residues, low in bulky hydrophobic residues
Correct: with no water-avoiding core to bury, there's little push to fold.
High in leucine, isoleucine and phenylalanine
These bulky water-avoiding residues usually drive a folded core.
Many cysteines forming disulfides
Disulfides tend to lock a structure in place, not loosen it.
Composed entirely of glycine
Disordered regions have mixed compositions, not pure glycine.
questions.x: Proteins fold mainly because water-avoiding side chains want to hide together in a core. Intrinsically disordered regions are stretches that never settle into one stable shape. They have few bulky water-avoiding residues like leucine, isoleucine and phenylalanine, so there's little to bury and little push to fold. They're rich in charged and polar residues instead, and lots of the same charge makes the chain repel itself and stay floppy. Many of these regions only take a shape when they bind a partner.

questions.q: Why do cells make more heat shock proteins after a rise in temperature?
o: Heat shock proteins generate heat to restore body temperature
They help proteins fold. They don't make heat.
Heat converts other proteins into heat shock proteins
Heat shock proteins come from their own genes, not from other proteins.
More proteins partly unfold and need chaperones to refold or avoid aggregation
Correct: heat shock proteins are chaperones that respond to unfolding stress.
They break down all heat-damaged DNA
Heat shock proteins work on proteins, not DNA.
questions.x: When temperature rises, many proteins start to partly unfold. That exposes their water-avoiding patches, which can stick to other proteins and form clumps. Cells respond by making more heat shock proteins. Most of these are chaperones, like Hsp70, that grab exposed sticky patches, help proteins refold, and keep them from clumping. The name tells you when they're made (after a heat shock), not what they do. They work on proteins, not DNA, and they don't make heat.

questions.q: Wild-type and mutant proteins are unfolded with urea. The midpoints of unfolding are 4.0 M urea for wild type and 2.0 M for the mutant. What does this show?
o: The mutant's folded state is more stable
A more stable protein would need more urea to unfold, not less.
The mutant binds urea covalently
Urea works through noncovalent effects, not covalent binding.
The mutant has twice as many residues
Unfolding midpoints reflect stability, not chain length.
The mutant's folded state is less stable
Correct: less urea is needed to unfold half of the mutant molecules.
questions.x: The unfolding midpoint is the urea concentration where half the protein molecules are unfolded. A more stable protein can take more urea before it gives way. The wild type reaches its midpoint at 4.0 M urea, but the mutant gets there at only 2.0 M, so the mutant's folded state is less stable. A simple model puts numbers on it: stability ≈ m × midpoint. With a typical m of about 5 kJ/mol per M, the wild type is about 5 × 4.0 = 20 kJ/mol and the mutant about 5 × 2.0 = 10 kJ/mol.

questions.q: Which process changes a protein's primary structure?
o: Heat denaturation
Heat leaves peptide bonds intact.
Treatment with 6 M urea
Urea only breaks noncovalent interactions.
Proteolytic cleavage of a precursor
Correct: cutting peptide bonds changes the covalent sequence.
Shifting the pH from 7 to 3
Adding protons changes charge, not sequence.
questions.x: Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids, held together by covalent peptide bonds. So only something that breaks or makes peptide bonds can change it. Proteolytic cleavage does exactly that: an enzyme cuts specific peptide bonds, as when proinsulin is trimmed into insulin, or an inactive zymogen like trypsinogen is cut to make active trypsin. Heat, urea and pH changes only break weak interactions or change charges, so the sequence stays the same.

questions.q: Many DNA-binding transcription factors contain a helix-turn-helix. What kind of structural element is it?
o: A primary sequence that is always identical
Motifs are defined by shape, and their sequences vary.
A supersecondary motif in which one helix fits into the DNA major groove
Correct: two helices joined by a turn form a common DNA-binding motif.
A quaternary arrangement of four subunits
It forms within a single chain, not from four subunits.
A covalent link between protein and DNA
The binding is noncovalent.
questions.x: A motif (also called supersecondary structure) is a small, recurring arrangement of a few helices or strands that shows up in many proteins. The helix-turn-helix is two α-helices connected by a short turn, all within one chain. One of the helices, called the recognition helix, fits into the major groove of DNA, where its side chains touch the edges of the base pairs and read the sequence. The binding is noncovalent, so the protein can let go when it needs to.

questions.q: What stabilizes the fold of a classic zinc-finger domain?
o: Zn²⁺ held by cysteine and histidine side chains
Correct: the zinc ion holds together a fold too small to have a real core.
Zn²⁺ forming peptide bonds
Metal ions don't form peptide bonds.
A disulfide between two zinc atoms
Disulfides form between cysteine sulfurs, not between metals.
Hydrophobic packing alone, with zinc acting only as a catalyst
Zinc here holds the structure; it doesn't catalyze anything.
questions.x: A classic zinc finger is tiny, about 30 residues: a short β-hairpin and an α-helix. That's too small to have a real water-avoiding core, so it needs something else to hold its shape. A zinc ion (Zn²⁺) does the job. It's gripped by two cysteines in the hairpin and two histidines in the helix, tying the two parts together like a staple. Take the zinc away and the finger unfolds. Here zinc is structural, not catalytic, and disulfides only form between cysteine sulfurs, never between metals.

questions.q: How can phosphorylating a serine change a protein's conformation?
o: It changes serine's α-carbon configuration
Phosphorylation doesn't change the α-carbon's 3D arrangement.
It breaks the peptide bond next to the serine
The backbone stays intact.
It adds a bulky negative charge that forms new electrostatic interactions
Correct: the phosphate's −2 charge can rearrange nearby contacts.
It adds a positive charge that attracts carboxylates
Phosphate groups are negative, not positive.
questions.x: Phosphorylation swaps serine's neutral OH for a bulky phosphate group that carries about a −2 charge at body pH. That new negative charge changes the neighborhood. It can pair up with nearby positive Lys or Arg side chains (forming new salt bridges), push away nearby negative Asp or Glu, and create spots for other proteins to bind. Those changes can shift a loop or a whole domain, switching the protein on or off. The backbone and the α-carbon's shape aren't touched.

questions.q: Which engineered change is most likely to raise a protein's thermal stability?
o: Adding a disulfide bond between two residues that are close in the native fold
Correct: a covalent cross-link limits the unfolded chain and stabilizes the fold.
Replacing a buried leucine with aspartate
Burying a charge in the water-avoiding core destabilizes the protein.
Placing several glycines in the middle of an α-helix
Glycine's floppiness weakens helices.
Removing a surface salt bridge by mutating both residues to alanine
Losing a helpful interaction lowers stability.
questions.x: Stability is how much more energy the unfolded state has than the folded state. A disulfide bond between two residues that already sit close together in the folded protein doesn't strain the folded shape. But it ties the unfolded chain into a loop, cutting down the number of floppy shapes it can take (lowering its entropy). That makes unfolding less rewarding, so the protein stays folded at higher temperatures. Burying a charge, adding floppy glycines to a helix, or removing a salt bridge all do the opposite.

questions.q: Which residue binds the heme iron on its proximal side in myoglobin and hemoglobin?
o: Cysteine
Cysteine binds heme iron in cytochrome P450, not in globins.
Lysine
Lysine isn't the iron's partner in globins.
Glutamate
Glutamate isn't the iron's partner in globins.
Histidine
Correct: a histidine ring nitrogen binds Fe²⁺ at the fifth position.
questions.x: In myoglobin and hemoglobin, the iron (Fe²⁺) at the center of each heme is held in the ring by four nitrogens. A fifth bond comes from below the ring, from a nitrogen on a histidine side chain called the proximal histidine. Oxygen binds on the opposite side, the sixth position. A second histidine on that side (the distal histidine) doesn't touch the iron; it just hydrogen-bonds to the O₂. Cysteine is the iron's partner in a different family of enzymes, cytochrome P450.

questions.q: Collagen has glycine at every third position (Gly-X-Y). Why is glycine needed there?
o: Glycine forms disulfide bonds between the three chains
Disulfide bonds need cysteine's sulfur. Glycine has no sulfur at all.
Only glycine is small enough to fit in the crowded center of the triple helix
Correct: every third residue sits in the crowded middle of the helix, where only glycine's tiny H fits.
Glycine's charged side chain forms salt bridges
Glycine's side chain is just an H atom. It carries no charge, so it can't form salt bridges.
Glycine is the residue that becomes hydroxylated
Proline and lysine get the -OH groups added. Glycine has nothing to add one to.
questions.x: Collagen is made of three protein chains twisted around each other into a tight rope called a triple helix. In that rope, every third amino acid points straight into the middle, where the three chains press together. There's almost no room there. Glycine is the only amino acid whose side chain is just a single hydrogen atom, so it's the only one small enough to fit. Put anything bigger there and the helix can't close properly, which is what happens in some forms of brittle bone disease (osteogenesis imperfecta). The extra -OH groups collagen gets are added to proline and lysine, not glycine.

questions.q: Why does vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) weaken connective tissue?
o: Vitamin C is a structural residue within collagen chains
Vitamin C helps an enzyme. It never becomes part of the collagen chain.
Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases need ascorbate, so collagen triple helices are less stable
Correct: the hydroxylases need ascorbate, so less hydroxyproline forms and the triple helix is unstable.
Vitamin C is needed to form peptide bonds in collagen
Ribosomes make peptide bonds, and they don't need vitamin C to do it.
Vitamin C directly cross-links collagen fibrils
Lysyl oxidase makes the cross-links between fibrils. Vitamin C doesn't do that itself.
questions.x: Vitamin C (ascorbate) is a helper for the enzymes that add -OH groups to proline and lysine in new collagen. Those enzymes, prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, use an iron atom that has to stay in its Fe²⁺ form, and vitamin C keeps it that way. Without vitamin C, collagen ends up short on hydroxyproline, which normally helps hold the triple helix together, and short on hydroxylysine, which is needed for cross-links between collagen molecules. The collagen that results is weak. That's why scurvy causes bleeding gums, easy bruising and wounds that won't heal.

questions.q: A permanent wave treatment for hair first reduces and then reoxidizes which bonds in α-keratin?
o: Peptide bonds
Mild reducing agents can't cut peptide bonds. Cutting them would destroy the hair, not curl it.
Hydrogen bonds only
Water resets hydrogen bonds. A perm lasts because it changes covalent bonds.
Glycosidic bonds
Glycosidic bonds join sugars. Keratin is a protein.
Disulfide bonds
Correct: reduce the S–S bonds, curl the hair, then oxidize to form new S–S bonds in new spots.
questions.x: Hair is made mostly of α-keratin, a protein full of cysteine. Cysteines on neighboring chains link up through disulfide bonds (S–S bonds), and those bonds hold hair's shape. A perm uses a reducing lotion first, which breaks each S–S bond into two -SH groups so the strands can slide. The hair is wrapped around curlers, and then an oxidizing lotion makes new S–S bonds between cysteines that are now next to each other. That locks in the curl. Hydrogen bonds also matter for hair's shape, but water alone resets them, which is why a style from a blow-dryer fades in humid air.

questions.q: Microfilaments of the cytoskeleton are polymers of which protein?
o: Actin
Correct: single G-actin units link up into F-actin, which is what microfilaments are.
Tubulin
Tubulin builds microtubules, the thickest filaments, not microfilaments.
Keratin
Keratin is one of the intermediate filament proteins.
Collagen
Collagen is outside the cell. It isn't part of the cytoskeleton.
questions.x: The cytoskeleton is the cell's internal scaffolding. It has three kinds of filaments, and each is built from a different protein. Microfilaments are made of actin. Microtubules are made of tubulin. Intermediate filaments are made from proteins like keratin, vimentin and lamins. Single actin units, called G-actin (G for globular), carry ATP and link up into long chains called F-actin (F for filament). Collagen isn't part of the cytoskeleton at all. It sits outside the cell.

questions.q: Microtubules are built from α/β-tubulin heterodimers. Which nucleotide do these dimers bind to support polymerization?
o: ATP
ATP goes with actin. Tubulin uses GTP.
cAMP
cAMP is a signaling molecule inside cells, not a building fuel for filaments.
GTP
Correct: GTP-tubulin adds to growing microtubules, and turning GTP into GDP helps them come apart.
NADH
NADH carries electrons in metabolism. It doesn't bind cytoskeletal proteins.
questions.x: Microtubules are built from pairs of tubulin proteins (α and β), and each pair carries GTP, the guanine version of ATP. A tubulin pair holding GTP adds easily to the growing end, called the plus end. Soon after it joins, the β-tubulin breaks its GTP down to GDP, and GDP-tubulin holds on less tightly. As long as fresh GTP-tubulin keeps arriving, a 'GTP cap' protects the end. If the cap is lost, the microtubule falls apart fast. This switching between growing and shrinking is called dynamic instability. Actin is the filament that uses ATP.

questions.q: Which motor protein carries cargo from axon terminals back toward the neuron cell body?
o: Kinesin
Most kinesins walk toward the plus end, which carries cargo out to the terminal, the wrong way.
Myosin II
Myosin II walks on actin and powers muscle contraction, not axon transport.
Tubulin
Tubulin builds the track. It isn't the motor that walks on it.
Dynein
Correct: dynein walks toward the minus end, and the minus ends face the cell body.
questions.note: Kinesin goes out (+ end); dynein comes back (− end).
questions.x: In an axon, all the microtubules point the same way: their minus ends face the cell body and their plus ends face the axon terminal. Motor proteins walk along these microtubules in one direction only. Most kinesins walk toward the plus end, so they carry cargo out to the terminal. That's called anterograde transport. Dynein walks toward the minus end, so it carries cargo back to the cell body. That's called retrograde transport. Cargo heading back from the terminal therefore rides on dynein.

questions.q: In the cross-bridge cycle, what happens when ATP binds the myosin head?
o: Myosin performs the power stroke
The power stroke comes later, when Pi is released. ATP binding makes the head let go.
Troponin releases Ca²⁺
Ca²⁺ levels are set by the sarcoplasmic reticulum, not by ATP binding to myosin.
Myosin detaches from actin
Correct: ATP binding makes myosin let go of actin. No ATP means the heads stay stuck, as in rigor mortis.
Actin depolymerizes
The actin filaments stay intact. Muscle shortens because filaments slide, not because they fall apart.
questions.x: Muscle contracts by a repeating cycle. Myosin heads on the thick filament grab the actin thin filament, pull it, let go and reset. A myosin head stuck to actin with nothing bound to it stays stuck. When ATP binds the head, the head lets go of actin. Next, ATP is split into ADP and phosphate (Pi), which re-cocks the head like pulling back a spring. The cocked head grabs actin again, and releasing Pi fires the power stroke. After death, ATP runs out, so the heads can't let go. That's why muscles stiffen in rigor mortis.

questions.q: Which step in the myosin cycle is most closely linked to the power stroke?
o: Binding of ATP to the head
ATP binding makes the head let go of actin. It doesn't produce force.
Release of Pi after the head binds actin
Correct: releasing Pi after the head grabs actin is what swings the head and pulls the filament.
Hydrolysis of ATP while detached
Splitting ATP re-cocks the head while it's detached. It stores energy but doesn't move anything yet.
Release of Ca²⁺ from troponin
Ca²⁺ leaving troponin turns cycling off and lets the muscle relax.
questions.x: Each turn of the myosin cycle goes in this order. ATP binds and the head lets go of actin. ATP is split into ADP and Pi while the head is free, which re-cocks it, storing energy like a pulled-back spring. The cocked head grabs actin. Then Pi is released, and that's the moment the head swings and pulls the thin filament: the power stroke. Finally ADP leaves. So splitting ATP stores the energy, but the step that actually moves the filament is Pi release.

questions.q: Why is hemoglobin's O₂-binding curve sigmoidal while myoglobin's is hyperbolic?
o: Hemoglobin binds O₂ cooperatively among its four subunits
Correct: O₂ binding at one heme makes the other hemes grab O₂ more easily.
Hemoglobin has a higher O₂ affinity at all pressures
It's the other way around: myoglobin holds O₂ more tightly than hemoglobin does.
Myoglobin contains no heme
Myoglobin has one heme. Without it, it couldn't bind O₂ at all.
Hemoglobin binds O₂ covalently
O₂ binds the iron reversibly in both proteins. It has to come off in tissues.
questions.x: Hemoglobin has four subunits, each with its own heme (the iron-containing group that holds O₂), and those subunits affect each other. When O₂ binds one heme, the whole protein shifts from a low-grip shape (the T state, for tense) toward a high-grip shape (the R state, for relaxed). That makes the other hemes grab O₂ more easily. This teamwork is called positive cooperativity, and it makes the curve S-shaped (sigmoidal). Myoglobin is a single chain with just one heme, so there's nothing to cooperate with, and its curve is a simple bend (hyperbolic).

questions.q: Which change in actively contracting muscle helps hemoglobin release more O₂?
o: A fall in temperature
Cooling makes hemoglobin hold O₂ tighter. Working muscle actually warms up.
A fall in CO₂
Working muscle makes more CO₂, not less. Less CO₂ would tighten the grip.
A fall in pH
Correct: lower pH favors hemoglobin's low-grip T state, so it releases more O₂. This is the Bohr effect.
A fall in 2,3-BPG
Less 2,3-BPG tightens hemoglobin's grip on O₂, so less is released.
questions.x: Working muscle makes CO₂, acid (H⁺) and heat. More H⁺ means a lower pH. H⁺ attaches to parts of hemoglobin that favor its low-grip T state, so hemoglobin loosens its hold on O₂. That's called the Bohr effect. On the graph, the O₂ curve shifts to the right, and more O₂ is released in the muscle at the same O₂ pressure. A fall in temperature, CO₂ or 2,3-BPG would all do the opposite: they'd tighten hemoglobin's grip.

questions.q: Why does fetal hemoglobin (α₂γ₂) have a higher O₂ affinity than adult hemoglobin?
o: It binds 2,3-BPG less tightly
Correct: HbF binds the grip-loosening molecule 2,3-BPG weakly, so it holds O₂ more tightly.
It contains twice as many hemes
Both have four chains and four hemes. More hemes would mean more capacity, not tighter grip.
It binds O₂ covalently
O₂ binds reversibly in both. Fetal hemoglobin still has to let go of O₂ in fetal tissues.
It lacks cooperativity
Fetal hemoglobin still shows cooperativity. Its S-shaped curve just sits farther left.
questions.x: 2,3-BPG is a small molecule in red blood cells that sits in a pocket in the middle of hemoglobin and holds it in its low-grip T state. In adult hemoglobin, that pocket is lined with positive charges that hold onto 2,3-BPG, which is negative. Fetal hemoglobin uses γ chains instead of β chains, and the γ chains have fewer positive charges in that pocket. So fetal hemoglobin holds 2,3-BPG weakly, spends more time in its high-grip state, and binds O₂ more tightly. That lets the fetus pull O₂ away from the mother's hemoglobin across the placenta.

questions.q: A mutant hemoglobin has a P50 of 12 mmHg, compared with 26 mmHg for normal hemoglobin. What does this mean?
o: It binds O₂ more weakly
Weaker binding would need more pressure to get half full, so P50 would go up, not down.
It carries twice as much O₂ per molecule
P50 tells you how tightly O₂ is held, not how much O₂ fits. Each hemoglobin still holds four.
It has lost all cooperativity
P50 is one point on the curve. It doesn't tell you the curve's shape.
It binds O₂ more tightly and unloads less in tissues
Correct: a lower P50 means half full at lower pressure. Tighter grip, left shift, less O₂ released in tissues.
questions.x: P50 is the O₂ pressure at which hemoglobin is half full (50% saturated). A lower P50 means it gets half full at a lower pressure, so it's grabbing O₂ more easily. That's a tighter grip, and on the graph the curve shifts left. Normal hemoglobin has P50 = 26 mmHg; this mutant has P50 = 12 mmHg, so it holds O₂ more tightly. That helps in the lungs, but it's bad in the tissues: plugging into the Hill equation, normal hemoglobin drops about 21% of its O₂ between the lungs (100 mmHg) and tissues (40 mmHg), while the mutant drops only about 3%.

questions.q: A binding protein has a measured Hill coefficient of 1.0. What does this indicate?
o: Positive cooperativity
Positive cooperativity gives n greater than 1, like hemoglobin's 2.8.
No cooperativity between binding sites
Correct: n = 1 means the sites don't affect each other, giving a simple curve like myoglobin's.
Negative cooperativity
Negative cooperativity gives n less than 1.
Exactly one binding site per molecule
n measures how the sites affect each other, not how many there are.
questions.x: The Hill coefficient, written n, tells you whether a protein's binding sites help or hinder each other. If n = 1, the sites act independently: filling one doesn't change how easily the others fill. That gives a simple bend-shaped (hyperbolic) curve, like myoglobin's. If n is bigger than 1, the sites help each other (positive cooperativity), like hemoglobin with n ≈ 2.8. If n is less than 1, they get in each other's way (negative cooperativity). The Hill coefficient isn't a count of binding sites.

questions.q: Carbon monoxide occupies some hemes in hemoglobin. Why does it cut O₂ delivery more than the loss of those sites alone would?
o: CO oxidizes all iron to Fe³⁺
CO binds Fe²⁺ as it is. It doesn't oxidize the iron to Fe³⁺.
The remaining hemes gain O₂ affinity and release less O₂ in tissues
Correct: CO pushes hemoglobin toward its high-grip state, so the remaining hemes hold O₂ tighter and release less.
CO breaks hemoglobin into monomers
Hemoglobin stays as four chains. The chains need to stay together for this effect to happen.
CO lowers O₂ affinity at the remaining hemes
A looser grip would release more O₂, not less. CO actually tightens the grip.
questions.x: Carbon monoxide (CO) sticks to the iron in heme about 200 times more tightly than O₂ does, so every heme holding CO is a seat O₂ can't use. That alone cuts how much O₂ the blood carries. But there's a second problem. Because hemoglobin's four subunits work together, CO on some hemes pushes the whole protein toward its high-grip R state. The hemes that still carry O₂ now hold it more tightly, so the curve shifts left and they release less O₂ in the tissues. That's why CO poisoning is worse than just losing the same number of hemes.

questions.q: Which parts of an antibody form its antigen-binding site?
o: The constant region of the heavy chains only
The heavy-chain constant region forms the stem (Fc). It talks to immune cells, not the target.
The disulfide hinge region
The hinge lets the arms flex. It doesn't touch the target.
The light chain constant region only
The light-chain constant region is the same in many antibodies, so it can't match each target.
The variable regions of the heavy and light chains
Correct: the variable regions of a heavy and a light chain together form the binding site at each tip.
questions.x: An antibody is a Y-shaped protein made of two heavy (long) chains and two light (short) chains. Each tip of the Y holds an antigen-binding site, the spot that grabs the target. That site is built from the variable regions of one heavy chain and one light chain together. 'Variable' means these regions differ from one antibody to the next. Each has loops shaped to fit one particular part of the target, called an epitope. The stem of the Y, the constant (Fc) region, doesn't bind the target. It signals immune cells and other defense proteins.

questions.q: Antibodies coat a bacterium so that macrophages engulf it more readily. What is this process called?
o: Opsonization
Correct: phagocytes grab the stems (Fc regions) of the antibodies coating the bacterium and eat it.
Neutralization
Neutralization blocks a germ or toxin from attaching to your cells.
Agglutination
Agglutination is antibodies clumping targets together.
Class switching
Class switching is a change inside a B cell that changes which antibody class it makes.
questions.x: Opsonization means coating a germ so it's easier for immune cells to eat. Antibodies grab the bacterium with their tips, which leaves their stems (the Fc regions) sticking out. Macrophages and other eating cells (phagocytes) have receptors that grab those stems, which tells them to swallow the bacterium. Neutralization is different: antibodies block a virus or toxin from attaching to your cells. Agglutination is antibodies clumping several targets together. All three start with antibodies binding a target, but only opsonization depends on phagocytes recognizing the stems.

questions.q: The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor opens a cation pore when acetylcholine binds. What kind of protein is it?
o: A voltage-gated ion channel
Voltage-gated channels open when the membrane voltage changes. This one opens when acetylcholine binds.
A G protein-coupled receptor
Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors are GPCRs. Nicotinic ones are channels.
A ligand-gated ion channel
Correct: acetylcholine binding opens the pore directly.
A receptor tyrosine kinase
Receptor tyrosine kinases add phosphates to proteins. They don't form pores.
questions.x: A ligand-gated ion channel is a protein that is both a receptor and a gate. When a chemical messenger (the ligand) binds it, the gate opens right away and ions flow through. The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor works exactly like this. It's made of five subunits arranged around a central pore. When acetylcholine binds, the pore opens, Na⁺ rushes in (and a little K⁺ leaks out), and the cell's inside becomes less negative (depolarizes). Muscarinic receptors bind the same acetylcholine but work differently: they're G protein-coupled receptors with no pore.

questions.q: Which cell adhesion molecules need Ca²⁺ to bind identical molecules on neighboring cells?
o: Integrins
Integrins mostly bind proteins in the material around cells, not identical integrins.
Selectins
Selectins need Ca²⁺ too, but they bind sugars on other cells, not identical selectins.
Aquaporins
Aquaporins are water channels. They don't stick cells together.
Cadherins
Correct: cadherins need Ca²⁺ and bind the same kind of cadherin on the next cell.
questions.x: Cell adhesion molecules are proteins that stick cells to each other or to the material around them. Cadherins stick to the same kind of cadherin on the neighboring cell, which is called like-to-like (homophilic) binding. They need calcium ions (Ca²⁺): Ca²⁺ stiffens the outer part of the cadherin so it can hold on. Take the Ca²⁺ away and the cells come apart. Cadherins build adherens junctions and desmosomes, two kinds of cell-to-cell anchors. Integrins mostly bind the material between cells, and selectins bind sugars.

questions.q: Which transmembrane proteins link extracellular matrix proteins such as fibronectin to the actin cytoskeleton?
o: Cadherins
Cadherins stick cells to other cells, not to the matrix.
Selectins
Selectins make brief contacts by binding sugars on other cells.
Integrins
Correct: integrins connect matrix proteins like fibronectin to actin inside the cell.
Connexins
Connexins form gap junctions, channels that join two cells' insides.
questions.x: Integrins are proteins that cross the cell membrane and connect the outside of the cell to its skeleton inside. Each one is made of two different chains, α and β. The outside part grabs proteins in the extracellular matrix (the mesh of protein around cells), such as fibronectin, laminin and collagen. The inside part connects, through helper proteins, to actin filaments. Integrins also pass signals both ways: grabbing the matrix sends signals into the cell, and signals inside the cell can make integrins grab harder. Cadherins connect cell to cell, not cell to matrix.

questions.q: Leukocytes roll along blood vessel walls before leaving the blood. Which adhesion molecules bind carbohydrate ligands to make this rolling possible?
o: Cadherins
Cadherins hold tissue cells together by binding each other, not sugars.
Selectins
Correct: selectins bind sugar groups, making quick on-and-off bonds that cause rolling.
Integrins
Integrins handle the later firm stop, and they bind proteins, not sugars.
Collagens
Collagen is a structural protein in the matrix, not a receptor on cells.
questions.x: When there's an infection, white blood cells (leukocytes) need to leave the blood and get into the tissue. First they slow down by rolling along the blood vessel wall. Selectins make this possible. Selectins are lectins, proteins that bind specific sugar groups on other cells' surface proteins. These bonds are weak and break quickly, so the cell grabs, lets go, and grabs again, which makes it tumble slowly instead of rushing past. After that, integrins take over to stop the cell firmly so it can squeeze out of the vessel.

questions.q: What happens when a growth factor binds a receptor tyrosine kinase?
o: The receptors dimerize and phosphorylate each other's tyrosines
Correct: two receptors pair up and add phosphates to each other's tyrosines, which then recruit signaling proteins.
A heterotrimeric G protein swaps GDP for GTP
That's how GPCRs signal, through three-part G proteins.
A pore opens to let Na⁺ into the cell
That describes a ligand-gated ion channel.
The receptor enters the nucleus to act as a transcription factor
Moving into the nucleus is what steroid hormone receptors do.
questions.x: A receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) is a receptor with an enzyme built into its inside part. The enzyme is a kinase, meaning it adds phosphate groups, and it adds them to tyrosine, one of the amino acids. When a growth factor binds, it pulls two receptors together (dimerization). Side by side, each receptor's kinase adds phosphates to tyrosines on its partner. Those phosphorylated tyrosines act like docking spots for signaling proteins such as Grb2, which leads on to Ras and a chain of kinases that tells the cell to grow and divide. Swapping GDP for GTP on a three-part G protein is how GPCRs work instead.

questions.q: How does an activated G protein-coupled receptor turn on its G protein?
o: It phosphorylates the G protein on tyrosine
GPCRs swap nucleotides on the G protein. They don't add phosphates to it.
It hydrolyzes the G protein's GTP
Breaking down GTP turns the G protein OFF, and Gα does that itself.
It promotes exchange of GDP for GTP on the Gα subunit
Correct: the receptor makes Gα swap GDP for GTP, and GTP-bound Gα goes on to act.
It cleaves the G protein into active fragments
The G protein isn't cut. Its parts separate and later rejoin.
questions.x: A G protein is an on/off switch made of three parts: Gα, Gβ and Gγ. It's off when Gα holds GDP and on when Gα holds GTP. When a messenger binds a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), the receptor changes shape and pries GDP out of Gα. GTP is far more common in the cell than GDP, so GTP slides into the empty spot. Now Gα is on. It separates from Gβγ, and both pieces can go switch on enzymes or channels. The signal ends when Gα breaks its own GTP back down to GDP.

questions.q: Activating a Gq-coupled receptor leads directly to which events?
o: Phospholipase C activation, producing IP₃ and DAG and releasing Ca²⁺
Correct: Gq turns on phospholipase C, which makes IP₃ (releases Ca²⁺) and DAG (turns on PKC).
Adenylyl cyclase activation, raising cAMP
Raising cAMP through adenylyl cyclase is the Gs pathway.
Adenylyl cyclase inhibition, lowering cAMP
Lowering cAMP by blocking adenylyl cyclase is the Gi pathway.
Opening of a ligand-gated Na⁺ channel
Gq works through enzymes. It doesn't open a ligand-gated channel directly.
questions.x: The type of Gα decides what a GPCR does. Gq switches on an enzyme called phospholipase C, which cuts a membrane lipid called PIP₂ into two messengers: IP₃ and DAG. IP₃ floats to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), the cell's calcium store, and opens channels that let Ca²⁺ out into the cell. DAG stays in the membrane and, together with Ca²⁺, switches on protein kinase C. Gs and Gi work differently: they raise or lower cAMP by turning adenylyl cyclase up or down.

questions.q: Cholera toxin modifies Gαs so that it can no longer hydrolyze GTP. What happens in intestinal cells?
o: cAMP falls because adenylyl cyclase is inhibited
Gαs turns adenylyl cyclase up, not down. Stuck on, it raises cAMP.
IP₃ stays high because phospholipase C stays on
Phospholipase C and IP₃ belong to the Gq pathway, not Gs.
The receptor can no longer bind its ligand
The toxin acts on the G protein inside the cell. The receptor binds its ligand normally.
cAMP stays high because adenylyl cyclase stays on
Correct: Gαs stuck with GTP keeps adenylyl cyclase on, so cAMP stays high.
questions.x: Gαs normally turns itself off by breaking down its GTP to GDP. Cholera toxin sticks a chemical tag (an ADP-ribose group) onto Gαs that blocks this. So Gαs stays in its 'on' GTP form, and it keeps telling adenylyl cyclase to make cAMP. cAMP stays high. In intestinal cells, high cAMP opens chloride channels called CFTR. Cl⁻ pours into the gut, Na⁺ and water follow, and the result is severe watery diarrhea.

questions.q: What motor drives the bending of cilia and flagella in eukaryotic cells?
o: Myosin pulling on actin filaments
Myosin and actin drive muscle, not cilia. The cilium's core is made of microtubules.
Dynein sliding neighboring microtubule doublets past each other
Correct: dynein arms slide neighboring doublets, and because the doublets are tied together, sliding becomes bending.
A rotary motor powered by a proton gradient
A spinning motor powered by a proton flow is the bacterial flagellum.
Kinesin walking toward the minus end
Most kinesins walk toward the plus end, and they carry cargo rather than bend the cilium.
questions.x: Inside a eukaryotic cilium or flagellum is a core called the axoneme. It's a ring of nine pairs of microtubules (doublets) around two single microtubules in the middle, the '9 + 2' pattern. Dynein motors attached to one doublet walk along the doublet next to it, using ATP. If the doublets were free, they'd just slide past each other. But they're tied together by linking proteins, so the sliding force makes the whole thing bend instead. Bacterial flagella are a totally different machine: they spin like propellers, driven by a flow of protons.

questions.q: Which plasma protein is most responsible for oncotic (colloid osmotic) pressure and also carries fatty acids and many drugs?
o: Hemoglobin
Hemoglobin stays inside red blood cells. It isn't a plasma protein.
Albumin
Correct: albumin is the most plentiful plasma protein and carries fatty acids and many drugs.
Fibrinogen
Fibrinogen is a clotting protein, present in much smaller amounts.
Immunoglobulin G
IgG is an antibody. It defends against germs and isn't the main source of oncotic pressure.
questions.x: Albumin is the most plentiful protein in blood plasma, the liquid part of blood. Oncotic pressure is the pull that proteins in the blood create to draw water back into the capillaries, the tiniest blood vessels. It depends on how many protein particles are stuck inside the vessel, and since albumin is by far the most common, it makes most of that pull. Albumin also works as a delivery truck: it carries fatty acids, bilirubin, calcium and many drugs. When albumin is low, water leaks out of the vessels into the tissues, causing swelling (edema).

questions.q: How does calmodulin pass a rise in cytosolic Ca²⁺ on to target enzymes?
o: Calmodulin pumps Ca²⁺ out of the cell
Separate pump proteins move Ca²⁺ out. Calmodulin is a small floating protein, not a pump.
Calmodulin phosphorylates its targets directly
Calmodulin switches on kinases, but it isn't a kinase itself.
Calmodulin hydrolyzes GTP to time the signal
Breaking down GTP as a timer is how G proteins work.
Ca²⁺ binding changes calmodulin's shape so it binds and activates target proteins
Correct: Ca²⁺ binding reshapes calmodulin so it grabs and switches on target proteins.
questions.x: Calmodulin is a small protein that senses calcium. It has four spots that bind Ca²⁺. When Ca²⁺ in the cell rises, those spots fill and calmodulin changes shape, uncovering greasy (water-avoiding) patches. Those patches let it wrap around target proteins, such as CaM kinases, and switch them on. Calmodulin isn't an enzyme itself. Think of it as a messenger that only delivers the signal when Ca²⁺ is around. When Ca²⁺ is pumped away, calmodulin lets go of Ca²⁺ and of its targets.

questions.q: How do enzymes speed up reactions?
o: They lower the activation energy by stabilizing the transition state
Correct: holding the transition state tightly lowers the energy hill, so more molecules react each second.
They make ΔG of the reaction more negative
ΔG depends only on the start and end points. Enzymes don't change it.
They raise the temperature of the solution
Enzymes work at the cell's normal temperature. They don't heat anything.
They shift the equilibrium toward products
Enzymes get you to the same equilibrium, just faster.
questions.x: Every reaction has to climb an energy hill before it can go downhill to products. The top of the hill is called the transition state, and the height of the climb is the activation energy. An enzyme's active site holds onto the transition state more tightly than it holds the starting molecule (the substrate), and that lowers the top of the hill. With a lower hill, many more molecules make it over each second, so the reaction speeds up. Enzymes don't change the overall energy difference between start and finish (ΔG), and they don't change where the equilibrium ends up. They only change the speed.

questions.q: An enzyme is added to a reaction mixture that is already at equilibrium. What happens?
o: More product forms
More product would mean a new equilibrium constant, and catalysts can't change it.
More reactant forms
Catalysts don't favor either direction, so no extra reactant forms.
The equilibrium concentrations do not change
Correct: the enzyme speeds the forward and backward reactions equally, so the amounts stay the same.
The reaction stops
At equilibrium, the reaction keeps running both ways. It doesn't stop.
questions.x: At equilibrium, the reaction is still running both ways, but the forward rate equals the backward rate, so the amounts don't change. An enzyme lowers the energy hill for both directions by the same amount, because both directions pass through the same top of the hill (the transition state). So both rates speed up by the same factor and stay equal. The amounts of reactant and product stay exactly where they were. Where equilibrium sits depends on ΔG°, and enzymes don't change ΔG°.

questions.q: A stable compound is made to resemble an enzyme reaction's transition state. Compared with the substrate, how does it bind?
o: More weakly
The active site is shaped to fit the transition state best, so a mimic fits better, not worse.
With the same affinity
If the enzyme bound the transition state no better than the substrate, it couldn't speed anything up.
Only at an allosteric site
A transition-state mimic binds the active site, not a separate regulatory site.
More tightly
Correct: active sites hold the transition state most tightly, so a stable mimic binds more tightly than the substrate.
questions.x: An enzyme works by holding the transition state, the unstable in-between shape at the top of the energy hill, more tightly than it holds the starting molecule. Its active site is shaped to fit the transition state best. A stable compound built to look like the transition state can make all those same snug contacts without ever reacting. So it binds the active site more tightly than the substrate does, often by a huge margin. That's why these 'transition-state analogs' make powerful competitive inhibitors and useful drugs.

questions.q: Crystal structures show an enzyme's active site changing shape when substrate binds. Which model does this support?
o: Lock and key
Lock and key assumes a rigid site that doesn't change shape.
Concerted model
The concerted model is about subunits of a multi-part protein switching together.
Induced fit
Correct: the substrate binding causes the enzyme to change shape for a better fit.
Fluid mosaic model
The fluid mosaic model describes cell membranes, not enzymes.
questions.x: There are two classic pictures of how a substrate fits into an enzyme. In the lock-and-key model, the active site is rigid and already shaped exactly like the substrate. In the induced-fit model, the active site is flexible: when the right substrate binds, the enzyme changes shape around it, lining up the parts that do the chemistry. Crystal structures showing the active site reshaping when substrate binds are direct evidence for induced fit.

questions.q: Which enzyme class joins two molecules using energy from ATP hydrolysis?
o: Lyases
Lyases make or break bonds without ATP, water or electron transfer.
Ligases
Correct: ligases join two molecules and pay for it with ATP, like DNA ligase.
Hydrolases
Hydrolases split bonds by adding water. They don't join molecules.
Isomerases
Isomerases rearrange one molecule. They can't join two.
questions.x: Enzymes are sorted into classes by the kind of reaction they run. Ligases join two molecules with a new bond, and they pay for it by breaking down ATP (or a similar molecule like GTP). DNA ligase, which seals breaks in DNA, is a classic example. Lyases can also make or break bonds, but without ATP, without water and without moving electrons. Hydrolases use water to split bonds. Isomerases rearrange the atoms within a single molecule.

questions.q: Hexokinase moves a phosphate from ATP to glucose. Which enzyme class does it belong to?
o: Transferases
Correct: kinases move a phosphate group from ATP to another molecule, which makes them transferases.
Ligases
Using ATP doesn't make an enzyme a ligase. Hexokinase doesn't join two molecules.
Hydrolases
No bond is split with water here.
Oxidoreductases
No electrons are moved between molecules.
questions.note: Trap: kinases are transferases even though they use ATP.
questions.x: A kinase is an enzyme that moves a phosphate group from ATP onto another molecule. That makes every kinase a transferase, the class of enzymes that move a chemical group from one molecule to another. Hexokinase takes the last phosphate off ATP and puts it on glucose, giving glucose-6-phosphate and ADP. It does use ATP, but it isn't a ligase, because a ligase uses ATP's energy to join two separate molecules into one. Here, nothing is joined: a phosphate just changes hands.

questions.q: Aldolase splits fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into two trioses without using water or a redox step. Which enzyme class does it belong to?
o: Hydrolases
Hydrolases need water to split a bond, and aldolase uses none.
Oxidoreductases
No electrons move between molecules, so it isn't a redox enzyme.
Lyases
Correct: lyases break bonds without water or a redox step, just like aldolase.
Ligases
Ligases join molecules using ATP. Aldolase splits one molecule.
questions.x: A lyase is an enzyme that breaks (or makes) a bond without using water and without moving electrons. Often it creates a double bond or a new C=O in the process. Aldolase splits fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (six carbons) into two three-carbon sugars, dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. No water is added, and no electron carrier is used, so it's a lyase. A hydrolase always uses water to split a bond. Aldolase can also run backward to join the two sugars, still without ATP.

questions.q: Lactate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to lactate while oxidizing NADH to NAD⁺. Which enzyme class does it belong to?
o: Oxidoreductases
Correct: dehydrogenases move electrons (as a hydride) between molecules, which makes them oxidoreductases.
Transferases
No chemical group like a phosphate or amino group is passed along. Electrons move.
Isomerases
Lactate has two more hydrogens than pyruvate, so they aren't isomers.
Lyases
No bond is broken to make a double bond or ring. A C=O is reduced to C–OH.
questions.x: Oxidoreductases are enzymes that move electrons from one molecule to another. Every dehydrogenase is one: it moves electrons as a hydride ion (H⁻, a hydrogen carrying two electrons) to or from a carrier like NAD⁺. Lactate dehydrogenase hands a hydride from NADH to pyruvate. Pyruvate's C=O becomes lactate's C–OH, so pyruvate is reduced (it gains electrons) and NADH is oxidized to NAD⁺ (it loses them). Pyruvate and lactate differ by two hydrogens, so they aren't isomers.

questions.q: Mg²⁺ and Zn²⁺ are inorganic ions that many enzymes need for activity. What are they called?
o: Coenzymes
Coenzymes are organic molecules, often made from vitamins. Metal ions aren't coenzymes.
Substrates
Substrates are turned into products. These ions come out unchanged.
Zymogens
Zymogens are inactive enzyme precursors, not small ions.
Cofactors
Correct: cofactors include metal ions; the organic ones are called coenzymes.
questions.x: A cofactor is any non-protein helper an enzyme needs in order to work. Cofactors come in two kinds. Inorganic ones are metal ions like Mg²⁺ and Zn²⁺. Organic ones (carbon-based molecules, often made from vitamins) are called coenzymes. So Mg²⁺ and Zn²⁺ are cofactors, but not coenzymes. Cofactors also aren't used up like substrates: they come out of each reaction unchanged, ready for the next one.

questions.q: The coenzyme NAD⁺ is made from which vitamin?
o: Riboflavin (B₂)
Riboflavin makes FAD and FMN, not NAD⁺.
Niacin (B₃)
Correct: niacin supplies the nicotinamide ring of NAD⁺.
Thiamine (B₁)
Thiamine makes thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP).
Ascorbate (C)
Vitamin C keeps certain enzymes' iron in working form. It isn't part of NAD⁺.
questions.x: Many coenzymes are built from B vitamins. Niacin (vitamin B₃) supplies the nicotinamide ring of NAD⁺ and NADP⁺. In fact, NAD stands for nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, so the name gives it away. That ring is the part that picks up electrons when NAD⁺ becomes NADH. Riboflavin (B₂) makes FAD and FMN instead, and thiamine (B₁) makes thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP). Not getting enough niacin causes a disease called pellagra.

questions.q: What is a cofactor called when it is tightly or covalently bound and stays with the enzyme throughout catalysis?
o: A cosubstrate
Cosubstrates like NAD⁺ bind loosely and leave after each cycle.
A prosthetic group
Correct: a prosthetic group stays bound, like heme in cytochromes or attached FAD.
An apoenzyme
An apoenzyme is the enzyme without its cofactor, not the cofactor itself.
An allosteric effector
Allosteric effectors adjust activity from a separate site. The enzyme's chemistry doesn't depend on them.
questions.x: Coenzymes and other cofactors can be sorted by how tightly they hold on. A prosthetic group is bound tightly, sometimes by a covalent bond, and stays attached to the enzyme through the whole reaction cycle. Examples include heme in cytochromes and FAD that's permanently attached in succinate dehydrogenase. A cosubstrate is the opposite: it binds loosely, gets changed during the reaction, then leaves. NAD⁺ in most dehydrogenases works this way.

questions.q: What is an enzyme called when it lacks a required cofactor and is therefore inactive?
o: A holoenzyme
A holoenzyme is the complete, active enzyme with its cofactor.
A ribozyme
A ribozyme is an RNA molecule that acts as an enzyme.
An isozyme
Isozymes are different working versions of an enzyme that run the same reaction.
An apoenzyme
Correct: apoenzyme plus cofactor gives the active holoenzyme.
questions.x: Some enzymes need a cofactor, like a metal ion or a coenzyme, to work. The protein on its own, without that cofactor, is called an apoenzyme, and it's inactive. Once the cofactor binds, the complete, working enzyme is called a holoenzyme ('holo' means whole). So: apoenzyme + cofactor = holoenzyme. Isozymes are different proteins that run the same reaction, and ribozymes are RNA molecules that act as enzymes.

questions.q: Thiamine deficiency impairs pyruvate dehydrogenase. Which coenzyme is missing?
o: Thiamine pyrophosphate
Correct: TPP, made from vitamin B₁, is needed to pull CO₂ off pyruvate.
Biotin
Biotin helps enzymes that ADD CO₂, like pyruvate carboxylase.
Pyridoxal phosphate
PLP, from vitamin B₆, works with transaminases.
Tetrahydrofolate
Tetrahydrofolate carries one-carbon pieces for making DNA building blocks.
questions.x: Thiamine (vitamin B₁) is turned into thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), the coenzyme that helps pull CO₂ off molecules called α-keto acids. Pyruvate is one of them. Pyruvate dehydrogenase, the enzyme complex that turns pyruvate into acetyl-CoA, needs TPP for its first step. So does α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase in the citric acid cycle. Without enough thiamine, the body can't burn glucose well, which leads to beriberi or a brain disorder called Wernicke encephalopathy. Biotin is used by enzymes that add CO₂, and PLP is used by transaminases.

questions.q: What does histidine do in a serine protease catalytic triad (Ser-His-Asp)?
o: It forms a covalent acyl-enzyme bond with the substrate
Serine forms the covalent bond with the substrate. Histidine just activates it.
It binds the substrate's side chain in the specificity pocket
A separate pocket next to the active site picks the substrate. The triad's histidine doesn't.
It acts as a general base, taking the proton from serine's hydroxyl
Correct: histidine pulls the H⁺ off serine's -OH, making serine strong enough to attack.
It reduces a disulfide in the substrate
Proteases cut peptide bonds with water. They don't break disulfides.
questions.x: Serine proteases are enzymes that cut proteins, and they use three amino acids working as a team, called the catalytic triad: serine, histidine and aspartate. Serine does the attacking, but its -OH group is too weak to attack on its own. Histidine acts as a general base: it pulls the H⁺ off serine's -OH, turning serine's oxygen into a strong attacker. Serine then attacks the carbon of the peptide bond and briefly forms a covalent bond with the substrate. Aspartate's job is to hold histidine in the right position. Which proteins get cut is decided by a separate pocket, not by the triad.

questions.q: In carbonic anhydrase, a Zn²⁺ ion binds a water molecule. How does this help catalysis?
o: It reduces CO₂ to formate
The reaction adds water to CO₂. Nothing is reduced.
It forms a covalent bond to bicarbonate permanently
The bicarbonate leaves each cycle, so the enzyme can keep working.
It changes the reaction's equilibrium constant
No catalyst changes the equilibrium constant.
It lowers the water's pKₐ, giving a zinc-bound hydroxide that attacks CO₂
Correct: zinc makes its water give up H⁺ easily, leaving a hydroxide that attacks CO₂.
questions.x: Carbonic anhydrase turns CO₂ and water into bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) and H⁺. Water on its own is a weak attacker. Zn²⁺ fixes that. Zn²⁺ is a Lewis acid, meaning it pulls electron density toward itself. When water binds the zinc, the zinc tugs on its electrons, making the water much more willing to give up an H⁺. Its pKₐ drops from about 15.7 (plain water) to about 7. So at body pH, a lot of it exists as hydroxide (OH⁻) stuck to the zinc. Hydroxide is a much stronger attacker than water, and it quickly attacks CO₂ to make bicarbonate, which then leaves.

questions.q: An enzyme holds two substrates next to each other in the correct orientation. Why does this speed the reaction?
o: It makes the overall reaction more exergonic
ΔG depends only on the start and end points. Holding substrates together doesn't change it.
It provides heat to the substrates
Enzymes don't add heat. They work at the cell's normal temperature.
It reduces the entropy cost of bringing reactants together
Correct: holding the substrates together and lined up pays the entropy cost of bringing them together.
It permanently fuses the two substrates to the enzyme
The products are released and the enzyme comes out unchanged.
questions.x: For two molecules to react, they have to bump into each other and line up in exactly the right way. In a solution where everything is tumbling around, that's rare. Lining them up also costs entropy, because the molecules lose their freedom to move and spin. An enzyme grabs both substrates and holds them side by side, already lined up. The energy it gets from binding them pays that entropy cost up front. This 'proximity and orientation' effect is like raising the concentration of the reactants enormously, and it lowers the energy hill. It doesn't change ΔG.

questions.q: Chymotrypsin cleaves after large aromatic residues such as phenylalanine. What explains this specificity?
o: Its catalytic triad uses a different nucleophile than trypsin
Trypsin and chymotrypsin use the same Ser-His-Asp team and the same attacker, serine.
A deep hydrophobic S1 pocket that fits aromatic side chains
Correct: a deep, greasy pocket fits big ring-shaped side chains like phenylalanine.
Phenylalanine's side chain is positively charged
Phenylalanine's side chain is nonpolar and uncharged.
It recognizes the substrate's disulfide bonds
The pocket reads the side chain beside the cut, not disulfide bonds.
questions.x: Chymotrypsin, trypsin and elastase all cut proteins using the same three-amino-acid team (serine, histidine, aspartate). So what makes each one choose different spots to cut? A pocket next to the active site, called the S1 pocket. It holds the side chain of the amino acid just before the bond being cut. Chymotrypsin's pocket is deep and greasy (hydrophobic), so it fits big, nonpolar ring-shaped side chains like phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan. Trypsin's pocket has a negative aspartate at the bottom, so it attracts the positive lysine and arginine instead.

questions.q: An enzyme works in the lumen of the stomach. Near which pH is its activity most likely highest?
o: Correct: stomach enzymes like pepsin are built to work at the stomach's acidic pH.
7.4 is the pH of blood, not the stomach.
About pH 8 suits pancreatic enzymes in the small intestine.
No part of the digestive tract is this basic.
questions.x: Every enzyme works best at a certain pH, called its optimum pH, and that usually matches the place where it works. pH matters because it decides which parts of the enzyme carry H⁺ or not, and that affects both the active site and the enzyme's folded shape. The stomach is very acidic, because cells in its lining pump out hydrochloric acid (HCl). Pepsin, the stomach's main protein-cutting enzyme, works best near pH 2. Enzymes from the pancreas that work in the small intestine prefer about pH 8. Blood is about pH 7.4.

questions.q: An enzyme's activity rises with temperature up to a point and then drops sharply. Why?
o: Molecular motion first speeds catalysis, then heat denatures the enzyme
Correct: faster motion speeds catalysis at first, then heat unfolds the enzyme.
Substrate molecules break down at high temperature
The sharp drop comes from the enzyme unfolding, not the substrate breaking down.
The reaction's ΔG reverses sign at high temperature
A change in ΔG would shift the equilibrium. It wouldn't make a working enzyme stop.
Enzymes need cold to bind substrate
Enzymes don't need cold to bind substrate. Activity rises with warmth because reactions speed up.
questions.x: Two things happen as you warm an enzyme up. First, molecules move faster, so more of them have enough energy to get over the energy hill, and the reaction speeds up. But the enzyme's folded shape is held together by many weak attractions. Past a certain temperature, the heat shakes those attractions apart and the enzyme unfolds (denatures), so the active site falls apart. The peak of the curve is where these two effects balance. The drop after it is sharp because once unfolding starts, the whole structure tends to come apart at once.

questions.q: An enzyme's activity is bell-shaped versus pH, falling below pH 6 and above pH 9. What most likely causes the drop below pH 6?
o: Deprotonation of a lysine that must be positive
Lysine loses its H⁺ near pH 10. That fits the high-pH edge, not the low one.
Breaking of peptide bonds by acid
Mild acid can't break peptide bonds. That takes boiling in strong acid.
Protonation of an active-site histidine that must be neutral to act as a base
Correct: histidine's pKₐ ≈ 6 matches the low edge. Below it, histidine carries H⁺ and can't act as a base.
Loss of the enzyme's primary structure
pH 6 doesn't change the amino acid sequence.
questions.x: A bell-shaped activity curve usually means two groups on the enzyme each need the right H⁺ status. Each edge of the bell points to one group, and the pH at that edge is close to that group's pKₐ (the pH where it's half with H⁺, half without). The low edge is at pH 6, and histidine's pKₐ is about 6. Above pH 6, histidine is mostly neutral and can grab an H⁺ as a general base. Below pH 6, it's mostly carrying an extra H⁺ and can't. At pH 5, only 1 ÷ (1 + 10¹) = 1/11 ≈ 9% of it is neutral. A lysine losing its H⁺ near pH 10 would explain the high-pH edge instead.

questions.q: The active site residues of an enzyme are often far apart in its amino acid sequence. How do they come together?
o: Folding into tertiary structure brings them close
Correct: folding into a 3D shape brings distant amino acids together to form the active site.
Peptide bonds form between them after translation
Peptide bonds only link each amino acid to its neighbors in the chain.
The substrate pulls them together covalently
The substrate doesn't make covalent links between the enzyme's amino acids.
They are joined by disulfide bonds in every enzyme
Many enzymes have no disulfide bonds at all.
questions.x: An active site isn't built from amino acids that sit next to each other in the chain. It forms when the chain folds into its 3D shape, called tertiary structure. Folding brings amino acids that are far apart in the sequence right next to each other in space. In chymotrypsin, for example, the three key amino acids are numbers 57, 102 and 195 in the chain, yet they sit almost touching in the folded enzyme. That's why unfolding (denaturing) an enzyme kills its activity even though the sequence hasn't changed.

questions.q: An enzyme speeds up the forward reaction of A ⇌ B by 10⁶-fold. What happens to the rate of the reverse reaction?
o: It does not change
If only the forward rate rose, Keq would change, and catalysts can't change Keq.
It decreases 10⁶-fold
Catalysts never slow either direction.
It increases only once B accumulates
The speed-up comes from the lower hill, which is there whenever the enzyme is, from the start.
It also increases 10⁶-fold
Correct: both directions cross the same lowered hill, so both speed up 10⁶-fold and Keq stays the same.
questions.x: The forward and reverse reactions go over the same energy hill, just from opposite sides. The top of that hill is the transition state. An enzyme lowers the top of the hill, so both climbs get shorter by exactly the same amount. Same drop in height means the same speed-up, so the reverse reaction also speeds up 10⁶-fold. The equilibrium constant is the forward rate constant divided by the reverse one: Keq = kf ÷ kr. Multiply both by 10⁶ and the 10⁶ cancels, so Keq doesn't change.

questions.q: Peptide bond formation in the ribosome is catalyzed by ribosomal RNA. What does this show?
o: All enzymes are made of RNA
Most enzymes are proteins. This shows that some are RNA, not all.
Some biological catalysts are RNA molecules (ribozymes)
Correct: the part of the ribosome that makes peptide bonds is RNA, so RNA can be a catalyst.
Ribosomal proteins are not needed for translation
Ribosomal proteins still help with shape and assembly. They just don't do the chemistry.
RNA catalysts change a reaction's equilibrium
No catalyst, RNA or protein, changes the equilibrium.
questions.x: Inside the ribosome, the spot that actually links amino acids together with peptide bonds is called the peptidyl transferase center. It's made of ribosomal RNA (rRNA), not protein. So the ribosome is a ribozyme, an RNA molecule that acts as an enzyme. This shows that biological catalysts don't have to be proteins. Like every catalyst, a ribozyme speeds up a reaction without changing where its equilibrium sits.

questions.q: In Michaelis–Menten kinetics, how is Kₘ defined experimentally?
o: The maximum rate the enzyme can reach
The maximum rate is Vₘₐₓ, not Kₘ.
The substrate concentration at which v = Vₘₐₓ/2
Correct: putting [S] = Kₘ into the equation gives exactly half of Vₘₐₓ.
The number of substrate molecules converted per second per active site
Molecules converted per second per active site is kcat, the turnover number.
The substrate concentration at which v = Vₘₐₓ
The rate only approaches Vₘₐₓ and never quite reaches it.
questions.x: The Michaelis–Menten equation, v = Vₘₐₓ[S] ÷ (Kₘ + [S]), connects how much substrate there is ([S]) to how fast the enzyme works (v). Vₘₐₓ is the top speed, when every active site is busy. Kₘ is defined as the substrate concentration that gives half of that top speed. You can check it: put [S] = Kₘ into the equation and you get v = Vₘₐₓ × Kₘ ÷ (2 × Kₘ) = Vₘₐₓ ÷ 2. The curve only creeps closer and closer to Vₘₐₓ without ever reaching it, so no amount of substrate gives exactly Vₘₐₓ. That's why Kₘ is defined at the halfway point.

questions.q: An enzyme has Kₘ = 2 mM and Vₘₐₓ = 100 μmol/min. What is the initial rate at [S] = 6 mM?
o: 33 μmol/min
This flips the fraction: 100 × 2 ÷ 6. The right fraction is [S] ÷ (Kₘ + [S]).
50 μmol/min
50 is the rate when [S] = Kₘ = 2 mM. Here [S] is 6 mM, so it's faster.
75 μmol/min
300 μmol/min
The rate can never go above Vₘₐₓ, which is 100.
questions.x: Use the Michaelis–Menten equation: v = Vₘₐₓ × [S] ÷ (Kₘ + [S]). The values are Vₘₐₓ = 100 μmol/min, Kₘ = 2 mM and [S] = 6 mM. Plug in: v = 100 × 6 ÷ (2 + 6) = 600 ÷ 8 = 75 μmol/min. A quick check: 6 mM is 3 times Kₘ, so the enzyme runs at 3 ÷ (1 + 3) = 3/4 of top speed, and 3/4 of 100 is 75. Since [S] is bigger than Kₘ, the answer has to be between 50 (half of Vₘₐₓ) and 100 (Vₘₐₓ), which rules out 33 and 300.

questions.q: What substrate concentration is needed for an enzyme to reach 90% of Vₘₐₓ?
o: At 0.9 × Kₘ, the enzyme only reaches 0.9 ÷ 1.9 ≈ 47% of top speed.
9 × Kₘ
Correct: 0.9 = [S] ÷ (Kₘ + [S]) works out to [S] = 9 × Kₘ.
10 × Kₘ
At 10 × Kₘ, the enzyme reaches 10 ÷ 11 ≈ 91%, a bit more than asked.
90 × Kₘ
At 90 × Kₘ, the enzyme reaches about 99%, way more than needed.
questions.x: The share of top speed an enzyme reaches is v ÷ Vₘₐₓ = [S] ÷ (Kₘ + [S]). We want that to equal 0.9. Write 0.9 = [S] ÷ (Kₘ + [S]) and multiply both sides by (Kₘ + [S]): 0.9 × Kₘ + 0.9 × [S] = [S]. Take 0.9 × [S] away from both sides: 0.9 × Kₘ = 0.1 × [S]. Divide both sides by 0.1: [S] = 9 × Kₘ. Check: 9 ÷ (1 + 9) = 9/10. Getting close to top speed takes a lot of substrate: 9 × Kₘ gets you 90%, and even 90 × Kₘ only gets about 99%.

questions.q: At a substrate concentration of one-third of Kₘ, what fraction of Vₘₐₓ does an enzyme reach?
o: This leaves [S] out of the bottom of the fraction.
Half of Vₘₐₓ needs [S] = Kₘ, three times more substrate.
0.75 needs [S] = 3 × Kₘ. This flips the ratio.
questions.x: The share of top speed is v ÷ Vₘₐₓ = [S] ÷ (Kₘ + [S]). Here [S] = Kₘ ÷ 3. Plug in: (Kₘ ÷ 3) ÷ (Kₘ + Kₘ ÷ 3). Every term has Kₘ in it, so it cancels, leaving (1/3) ÷ (1 + 1/3) = (1/3) ÷ (4/3). Dividing by a fraction means flipping it and multiplying: 1/3 × 3/4 = 3/12 = 1/4 = 0.25. If you forget the [S] in the bottom, you get 1/3, which is only close to right when [S] is tiny compared with Kₘ.

questions.q: When [S] is far above Kₘ, what is the order of the enzyme reaction with respect to substrate?
o: First order
First order is the low-substrate end, when [S] is far below Kₘ.
Second order
Michaelis–Menten kinetics is never second order in substrate.
Negative first order
Adding substrate doesn't slow down a Michaelis–Menten enzyme.
Zero order
Correct: the enzyme is saturated, so v ≈ Vₘₐₓ no matter how much more substrate you add.
questions.x: Start from v = Vₘₐₓ[S] ÷ (Kₘ + [S]). When [S] is far bigger than Kₘ, adding Kₘ to [S] barely changes it, so Kₘ + [S] is about [S]. Then v ≈ Vₘₐₓ × [S] ÷ [S] = Vₘₐₓ. The enzyme is saturated: almost every active site is already busy, so adding more substrate doesn't speed it up. A rate that doesn't depend on the amount of a reactant is called zero order in that reactant. The rate still depends on how much enzyme there is, since more enzyme raises Vₘₐₓ.

questions.q: When [S] is far below Kₘ, the Michaelis–Menten equation reduces to which form?
o: v ≈ (Vₘₐₓ/Kₘ)[S]
Correct: Kₘ + [S] ≈ Kₘ, so the rate grows in direct proportion to [S].
v ≈ Vₘₐₓ
v ≈ Vₘₐₓ is the opposite end, when [S] is far above Kₘ.
v ≈ Vₘₐₓ/2
Half of Vₘₐₓ happens only at one point, [S] = Kₘ.
v ≈ Kₘ/[S]
This would make the rate go up as substrate goes down, which is impossible.
questions.x: Start from v = Vₘₐₓ[S] ÷ (Kₘ + [S]). When [S] is far smaller than Kₘ, adding it to Kₘ barely changes Kₘ, so Kₘ + [S] is about Kₘ. The equation becomes v ≈ (Vₘₐₓ ÷ Kₘ) × [S]. So the rate is directly proportional to [S]: most active sites are empty, and doubling the substrate doubles the rate. That's called first order in substrate. Divide the slope by the amount of enzyme and you get kcat ÷ Kₘ, the catalytic efficiency.

questions.q: An enzyme solution with 2 × 10⁻⁸ M active sites gives Vₘₐₓ = 2 × 10⁻⁴ M/s. What is kcat?
o: 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹
This divides the wrong way: [E]T ÷ Vₘₐₓ. Vₘₐₓ goes on top.
4 × 10⁻¹² s⁻¹
This multiplies the two numbers instead of dividing them.
10⁴ s⁻¹
Correct: kcat = (2 × 10⁻⁴) ÷ (2 × 10⁻⁸) = 1 × 10⁴ s⁻¹.
10¹² s⁻¹
Exponent slip: subtracting gives −4 − (−8) = +4, not 12.
questions.x: kcat, the turnover number, is how many substrate molecules one active site converts each second when it's working flat out. The formula is kcat = Vₘₐₓ ÷ [E]T, where [E]T is the total concentration of active sites. The values are Vₘₐₓ = 2 × 10⁻⁴ M/s and [E]T = 2 × 10⁻⁸ M. Divide the front numbers: 2 ÷ 2 = 1. Divide the powers of 10 by subtracting the exponents: −4 − (−8) = −4 + 8 = 4. So kcat = 1 × 10⁴ s⁻¹. The M on top and bottom cancel, leaving s⁻¹. Each active site handles about 10,000 molecules every second.

questions.q: Which enzyme has the highest catalytic efficiency?
o: kcat = 100 s⁻¹, Kₘ = 10⁻⁵ M
10² ÷ 10⁻⁵ = 10⁷ M⁻¹s⁻¹. Good, but 10 times lower than the best.
kcat = 1000 s⁻¹, Kₘ = 10⁻³ M
10³ ÷ 10⁻³ = 10⁶ M⁻¹s⁻¹. A big kcat alone doesn't make an enzyme efficient.
kcat = 10⁴ s⁻¹, Kₘ = 10⁻² M
10⁴ ÷ 10⁻² = 10⁶ M⁻¹s⁻¹. The fastest turnover, but the high Kₘ drags it down.
kcat = 10 s⁻¹, Kₘ = 10⁻⁷ M
Correct: 10¹ ÷ 10⁻⁷ = 10⁸ M⁻¹s⁻¹, the highest of the four.
questions.note: Efficiency is kcat/Kₘ, not kcat alone.
questions.x: Catalytic efficiency is kcat ÷ Kₘ, so you need to work it out for all four enzymes. A big kcat alone doesn't win: an enzyme also has to grab its substrate well, and a low Kₘ means it does. To divide powers of 10, subtract the exponents, and be careful with the minus signs: 10² ÷ 10⁻⁵ → 2 − (−5) = 7, so 10⁷. Doing the same for each gives 10⁷, 10⁶, 10⁶ and 10⁸ M⁻¹s⁻¹. The enzyme with kcat = 10 s⁻¹ and Kₘ = 10⁻⁷ M has the biggest ratio, so it's the most efficient, even though it's the slowest at turnover.

questions.q: Enzyme X has Kₘ = 0.1 mM and enzyme Y has Kₘ = 10 mM for the same substrate. At [S] = 5 mM, about what fraction of its Vₘₐₓ does enzyme Y reach?
o: Half of Vₘₐₓ needs [S] = Kₘ = 10 mM. Here [S] is only 5 mM.
This uses Kₘ ÷ (Kₘ + [S]) = 10 ÷ 15, the share of enzyme sitting empty.
98% is enzyme X's share: 5 ÷ 5.1. The question asks about Y.
questions.x: The share of top speed an enzyme reaches is v ÷ Vₘₐₓ = [S] ÷ (Kₘ + [S]), using that enzyme's own Kₘ. The question asks about enzyme Y, so use Kₘ = 10 mM and [S] = 5 mM. Plug in: 5 ÷ (10 + 5) = 5 ÷ 15 = 1/3 ≈ 33%. Enzyme X, with its tiny Kₘ of 0.1 mM, would be at 5 ÷ 5.1 ≈ 98% at the same substrate level. A low Kₘ means an enzyme gets close to full speed at a much lower substrate concentration.

questions.q: On a Lineweaver–Burk plot (1/v vs 1/[S]), what does the x-intercept equal?
o: 1/Vₘₐₓ
1/Vₘₐₓ is the y-intercept, not the x-intercept.
Kₘ/Vₘₐₓ
Kₘ/Vₘₐₓ is the slope of the line.
−1/Kₘ
Correct: setting 1/v = 0 gives 1/[S] = −1/Kₘ.
−Vₘₐₓ
Vₘₐₓ is never read straight off the x-axis. Both intercepts are flipped values.
questions.x: A Lineweaver–Burk plot takes the Michaelis–Menten curve and flips both axes: it plots 1/v against 1/[S]. That turns the curve into a straight line: 1/v = (Kₘ/Vₘₐₓ) × (1/[S]) + 1/Vₘₐₓ. The slope is Kₘ/Vₘₐₓ and the y-intercept is 1/Vₘₐₓ. The x-intercept is where the line crosses the x-axis, so set 1/v = 0: 0 = (Kₘ/Vₘₐₓ) × (1/[S]) + 1/Vₘₐₓ. Move 1/Vₘₐₓ over: (Kₘ/Vₘₐₓ) × (1/[S]) = −1/Vₘₐₓ. Multiply both sides by Vₘₐₓ/Kₘ: 1/[S] = −1/Kₘ.

questions.q: A Lineweaver–Burk plot has a y-intercept of 0.02 min/μM and an x-intercept of −0.25 μM⁻¹. What are Vₘₐₓ and Kₘ?
o: Vₘₐₓ = 0.02 μM/min, Kₘ = 0.25 μM
These are the intercepts copied straight. Both have to be flipped.
Vₘₐₓ = 50 μM/min, Kₘ = 4 μM
Correct: Vₘₐₓ = 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50 μM/min and Kₘ = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4 μM.
Vₘₐₓ = 50 μM/min, Kₘ = 0.25 μM
Vₘₐₓ is right, but Kₘ wasn't flipped: 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4 μM.
Vₘₐₓ = 4 μM/min, Kₘ = 50 μM
This swaps them. The y-axis gives Vₘₐₓ and the x-axis gives Kₘ.
questions.x: On a Lineweaver–Burk plot, the y-intercept is 1/Vₘₐₓ and the x-intercept is −1/Kₘ. So flip each one. Vₘₐₓ = 1 ÷ y-intercept = 1 ÷ 0.02 min/μM = 50 μM/min (0.02 is 1/50, so flipping it gives 50). For Kₘ: −1/Kₘ = −0.25 μM⁻¹, so 1/Kₘ = 0.25 and Kₘ = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4 μM (0.25 is 1/4). The usual mistake is reading the intercepts as Vₘₐₓ and Kₘ themselves instead of flipping them.

questions.q: On a Lineweaver–Burk plot, lines with and without an inhibitor cross on the x-axis. Which type of inhibition is this?
o: Pure noncompetitive
Correct: sharing the x-intercept means Kₘ is unchanged, while Vₘₐₓ drops.
Competitive
Competitive inhibitor lines cross on the y-axis, because Vₘₐₓ doesn't change.
Uncompetitive
Uncompetitive inhibitor lines are parallel, so they never cross.
Mixed, binding E more tightly than ES
These mixed inhibitor lines cross left of the y-axis but above the x-axis, not on it.
questions.x: On a Lineweaver–Burk plot, the x-intercept is −1/Kₘ. If the lines with and without inhibitor cross on the x-axis, they share the same x-intercept, so Kₘ didn't change. The inhibited line sits higher on the y-axis, and the y-intercept is 1/Vₘₐₓ, so a bigger 1/Vₘₐₓ means a smaller Vₘₐₓ. Same Kₘ with lower Vₘₐₓ is the signature of pure noncompetitive inhibition. Competitive inhibition shares the y-intercept instead, and uncompetitive inhibition gives parallel lines that never cross.

questions.q: Why does a pure noncompetitive inhibitor lower Vₘₐₓ but leave Kₘ unchanged?
o: It binds the active site and blocks substrate
Blocking the active site is competitive inhibition, which raises Kₘ.
It binds only the ES complex
Binding only the enzyme–substrate complex is uncompetitive inhibition, which lowers Kₘ.
It binds free enzyme and the ES complex with equal affinity
Correct: binding both forms equally takes enzymes out of action without changing how well substrate binds.
It permanently destroys substrate
Inhibitors act on the enzyme, not by destroying substrate.
questions.x: A pure noncompetitive inhibitor binds at a spot away from the active site, and it binds the free enzyme (E) and the enzyme–substrate complex (ES) equally well. Because it doesn't care whether substrate is there, it doesn't change how easily substrate binds, so Kₘ stays the same. But any enzyme with inhibitor stuck on it can't make product, and adding more substrate can't push the inhibitor off. So it's as if you had less enzyme, and Vₘₐₓ drops.

questions.q: An inhibitor binds only to the enzyme–substrate complex. How do the apparent Kₘ and Vₘₐₓ change?
o: Both decrease
Correct: this is uncompetitive inhibition. Trapping ES lowers both Kₘ and Vₘₐₓ by the same factor.
Kₘ increases; Vₘₐₓ unchanged
Kₘ up with Vₘₐₓ unchanged is competitive inhibition.
Kₘ unchanged; Vₘₐₓ decreases
Kₘ unchanged with Vₘₐₓ down is pure noncompetitive inhibition.
Kₘ increases; Vₘₐₓ decreases
Kₘ up with Vₘₐₓ down is mixed inhibition that prefers free enzyme.
