questions.x: An inhibitor that binds only the enzyme–substrate complex (ES) is called uncompetitive. It traps ES as a dead-end complex (ESI) that can't make product, so Vₘₐₓ drops. At the same time, pulling ES out of the picture makes more E and S combine to replace it (Le Châtelier's principle). The enzyme then looks like it's grabbing substrate more easily, so the apparent Kₘ drops too, by the same factor. On a Lineweaver–Burk plot, that gives parallel lines.

questions.q: A mixed inhibitor binds free enzyme much more tightly than the ES complex. How does it change the kinetic parameters?
o: Kₘ decreases and Vₘₐₓ decreases
Both going down happens when a mixed inhibitor prefers ES, not free enzyme.
Kₘ increases and Vₘₐₓ is unchanged
Vₘₐₓ stays the same only for a purely competitive inhibitor, which can't bind ES at all.
Kₘ and Vₘₐₓ are both unchanged
An inhibitor that binds both E and ES has to lower Vₘₐₓ.
Kₘ increases and Vₘₐₓ decreases
Correct: preferring free E raises Kₘ, and binding ES too lowers Vₘₐₓ.
questions.x: A mixed inhibitor can bind both the free enzyme (E) and the enzyme–substrate complex (ES). Because it can sit on ES, where extra substrate can't push it off, it always lowers Vₘₐₓ. What happens to Kₘ depends on which form it likes better. If it prefers free E, it's partly competing with substrate for the enzyme, so the enzyme seems to grab substrate less easily and Kₘ goes up. If it preferred ES, Kₘ would go down. Only an inhibitor that binds free E alone (competitive) leaves Vₘₐₓ unchanged.

questions.q: Methanol poisoning can be treated with ethanol, which is a substrate of the same alcohol dehydrogenase. Why does this work?
o: Ethanol irreversibly destroys the enzyme
Ethanol is a normal substrate. It binds, gets converted, and leaves. It doesn't destroy the enzyme.
Ethanol competes for the active site and slows the formation of toxic methanol products
Correct: ethanol fills the active site, so methanol is turned into toxic products much more slowly.
Ethanol converts methanol back into harmless glucose
No reaction in the body turns methanol into glucose.
Ethanol binds an allosteric site and raises Vₘₐₓ
Speeding the enzyme up would make more toxic products and worsen the poisoning.
questions.x: Methanol itself isn't very toxic. The danger comes when the liver enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) turns it into formaldehyde, which is then turned into formic acid, and that harms the eyes and makes the blood acidic. Ethanol is also a substrate for ADH, and the enzyme grabs it more readily. With lots of ethanol around, it fills most of the active sites, so methanol has to wait its turn. That's competitive inhibition: the toxic products form slowly while methanol leaves the body unchanged. The drug fomepizole works the same way.

questions.q: An irreversible inhibitor permanently inactivates half of the enzyme molecules in a sample. How do the kinetic parameters of the sample change?
o: Kₘ doubles and Vₘₐₓ is unchanged
Kₘ rising with Vₘₐₓ unchanged is the competitive pattern.
Vₘₐₓ is halved and Kₘ is unchanged
Correct: half the working enzyme means half the Vₘₐₓ, and the survivors bind substrate normally.
Both Kₘ and Vₘₐₓ are halved
Both dropping by the same factor is the uncompetitive pattern.
Neither parameter changes
Losing working enzyme has to lower Vₘₐₓ.
questions.x: An irreversible inhibitor permanently knocks out enzyme molecules, so it's like using less enzyme. Top speed depends on how much working enzyme you have: Vₘₐₓ = kcat × [E]T. Halve the working enzyme and Vₘₐₓ is halved. The enzymes that weren't hit are completely normal, so they grab substrate just as easily as before, and Kₘ stays the same. On a graph this looks like pure noncompetitive inhibition: a lower top, but the same half-speed point.

questions.q: Rates (μM/s) without and with inhibitor: [S] = 1 μM: 33 vs 17; [S] = 10 μM: 83 vs 67; [S] = 100 μM: 98 vs 95. What type of inhibition is this?
o: Pure noncompetitive
Noncompetitive inhibition would cut the rate by the same share at every [S], even high.
Uncompetitive
Uncompetitive inhibition lowers Vₘₐₓ, so lots of substrate wouldn't overcome it.
Irreversible
Losing working enzyme would keep the rate low even at high [S].
Competitive
Correct: the inhibitor matters at low [S] but fades at high [S], so Vₘₐₓ is unchanged.
questions.x: The trick is to compare the inhibitor's effect at low and high substrate. Divide the inhibited rate by the normal rate at each [S]. At 1 μM: 17 ÷ 33 ≈ 0.52, so the rate is cut about in half. At 10 μM: 67 ÷ 83 ≈ 0.81. At 100 μM: 95 ÷ 98 ≈ 0.97, almost normal. The inhibitor's effect fades as substrate rises, so lots of substrate beats it, and the top speed (Vₘₐₓ) is unchanged. That's the fingerprint of competitive inhibition. A noncompetitive or irreversible inhibitor would still drag the rate down at high substrate.

questions.q: With an inhibitor present, an enzyme's apparent Kₘ rises from 2 to 5 μM and its Vₘₐₓ falls from 100 to 60 μM/s. What type of inhibition is this?
o: Mixed
Correct: both numbers changed, with Kₘ going up, so the inhibitor prefers free enzyme.
Competitive
Competitive inhibition doesn't change Vₘₐₓ.
Uncompetitive
Uncompetitive inhibition lowers Kₘ, but here Kₘ went up.
Pure noncompetitive
Pure noncompetitive inhibition leaves Kₘ unchanged, but here it changed.
questions.x: Each kind of inhibitor leaves its own fingerprint. Competitive: Kₘ up, Vₘₐₓ unchanged. Uncompetitive: both down. Pure noncompetitive: Vₘₐₓ down, Kₘ unchanged. Here Kₘ went up (2 → 5 μM) and Vₘₐₓ went down (100 → 60 μM/s). None of those three fit, and only mixed inhibition can do both. Vₘₐₓ dropping means the inhibitor can bind the enzyme–substrate complex, and Kₘ rising means it binds the free enzyme even more tightly.

questions.q: An enzyme has Kₘ = 3 μM. A competitive inhibitor is added at a concentration equal to 2 Ki. What is the apparent Kₘ?
o: 1 μM
This divides by the factor. A competitive inhibitor makes Kₘ bigger, not smaller.
3 μM
A competitive inhibitor does raise the apparent Kₘ.
6 μM
This uses 2 as the factor and forgets the 1: it should be 1 + 2 = 3.
9 μM
Correct: Kₘ,app = 3 × (1 + 2) = 3 × 3 = 9 μM.
questions.x: A competitive inhibitor raises the apparent Kₘ by a factor of (1 + [I]/Ki), where [I] is the inhibitor concentration and Ki is how tightly it binds. The formula is Kₘ,app = Kₘ × (1 + [I]/Ki). The values: Kₘ = 3 μM and [I] = 2 × Ki, so [I]/Ki = 2. Plug in: Kₘ,app = 3 × (1 + 2) = 3 × 3 = 9 μM. Vₘₐₓ doesn't change. A common slip is forgetting the 1 and using just 2 as the factor, which gives 6.

questions.q: How does a plot of v versus [S] for an allosteric enzyme with cooperative subunits differ from a Michaelis–Menten plot?
o: It is a straight line through the origin
A straight line would mean the enzyme never fills up. Every enzyme levels off.
It decreases as [S] increases
Activity still goes up as substrate goes up.
It is sigmoidal instead of hyperbolic
Correct: cooperative binding gives an S-shaped curve instead of a simple bend.
It is identical to the hyperbolic plot
Cooperativity is exactly what changes the curve's shape.
questions.x: An allosteric enzyme usually has several subunits, and with cooperativity, substrate binding on one subunit makes the others grab substrate more easily. So at low [S], the rate climbs slowly, because few sites are filled and the grip is weak. Once binding gets going, the grip improves and the rate shoots up. Finally all sites fill and the rate levels off at Vₘₐₓ. That gives an S-shaped (sigmoidal) curve. A Michaelis–Menten enzyme, whose sites work independently, gives a simple bend (a hyperbola) instead.

questions.q: What does an allosteric activator do to a cooperative enzyme?
o: It binds the active site and is converted into product
A molecule that binds the active site and becomes product is a substrate, not an activator.
It shifts the equilibrium toward T, moving the curve right
Favoring the T state and sliding the curve right is what an inhibitor does.
It changes the reaction's ΔG
Regulators change how fast a reaction goes, not its ΔG.
It shifts the T ⇌ R equilibrium toward R, moving the v vs [S] curve left
Correct: favoring the high-grip R state means less substrate is needed, so the curve slides left.
questions.x: Allosteric enzymes flip between two shapes: a low-activity T state (tense) and a high-activity R state (relaxed), which grabs substrate more easily. An allosteric activator binds a regulatory spot away from the active site and holds the enzyme in the R state. With more enzyme in R, less substrate is needed to reach a given speed, so the S-shaped curve slides to the left. An allosteric inhibitor does the opposite: it favors T and slides the curve right. Neither one changes ΔG; they only change speed.

questions.q: The final product of a biosynthetic pathway inhibits the enzyme for the pathway's first committed step. What is this called?
o: Feedforward activation
Feedforward activation is an early molecule switching on a later enzyme.
Zymogen activation
Zymogen activation is switching on an enzyme precursor by cutting it.
Feedback inhibition
Correct: the end product signals that there's enough and shuts down the first step.
Substrate-level phosphorylation
Substrate-level phosphorylation is a way of making ATP, not a control system.
questions.x: A biosynthetic pathway is a chain of reactions that builds something, one step at a time. In feedback inhibition, the final product of the chain binds a regulatory spot on the enzyme for the first committed step (the first one-way step that only this pathway uses) and slows it down. When enough product has piled up, the whole pathway slows right at its entrance, so the cell doesn't waste material or energy making more. When the product gets used up, the brake comes off. Feedforward activation runs the other way: an early molecule switches on a later enzyme.

questions.q: In the concerted (MWC) model of allostery, how do the subunits change state?
o: Each subunit changes state one at a time as it binds ligand
Subunits changing one at a time is the sequential (KNF) model.
All subunits switch between T and R together, so mixed states do not exist
Correct: all subunits switch together, so there are no half-T, half-R molecules.
Subunits never change conformation
Both models depend on subunits changing shape.
Only the catalytic subunit changes, never the regulatory subunit
The concerted model doesn't treat some subunits differently. All switch together.
questions.x: Allosteric proteins with several subunits flip between a low-grip T state (tense) and a high-grip R state (relaxed). The concerted model, also called the MWC model, says all the subunits flip together: the whole molecule is either all T or all R, never a mix. Each time a ligand binds, it tips the balance a little more toward the all-R form, which makes the empty sites grab ligand more easily. The other model, the sequential (KNF) model, lets subunits change one at a time, so mixed molecules can exist.

questions.q: When a substrate binding to one active site increases binding at other active sites of the same enzyme, what is this effect called?
o: A homotropic allosteric effect
Correct: the molecule causing the effect is the substrate itself.
A heterotropic allosteric effect
Heterotropic effects come from a molecule that isn't the substrate.
Competitive inhibition
Here binding helps other sites bind. Competitive inhibition blocks binding.
Covalent modification
No covalent bond forms or breaks when substrate binds.
questions.x: Allosteric effects are named by what molecule causes them. If the molecule causing the effect is the protein's own substrate, it's called homotropic ('homo' means same). If it's a different molecule, it's heterotropic ('hetero' means different). Here, the substrate binding at one active site makes the other active sites bind substrate more easily. The effector is the substrate itself, so it's a homotropic effect, also called positive cooperativity. O₂ binding to hemoglobin is the classic example.

questions.q: Why does the pancreas secrete its proteases as inactive zymogens?
o: Because zymogens digest proteins faster
Zymogens are inactive. They don't digest anything until they're switched on.
To keep them from being denatured by stomach acid
Pancreatic juice goes to the small intestine, not the stomach.
To prevent the proteases from digesting the pancreas itself
Correct: keeping them inactive until they reach the intestine protects the pancreas.
Because the proteases need a coenzyme only found in the gut
Zymogens are switched on by cutting off a piece, not by a coenzyme.
questions.x: Proteases are enzymes that cut proteins. If the pancreas made them in active form, they'd start digesting the pancreas itself, since it's made of protein too. So it makes them as zymogens: inactive versions like trypsinogen and chymotrypsinogen. They travel down a duct into the small intestine, and only there are they switched on, by having a piece cut off. If they get switched on too early, inside the pancreas, they damage it, causing pancreatitis.

questions.q: Enteropeptidase in the duodenum activates trypsinogen. Why does this one step activate many digestive proteases?
o: Trypsin cleaves and activates the other pancreatic zymogens
Correct: trypsin cuts and switches on the other pancreatic zymogens, setting off a cascade.
Enteropeptidase activates each zymogen separately
Enteropeptidase mainly switches on trypsinogen, not each zymogen.
Trypsin acts as an allosteric activator of the other proteases
Zymogens are switched on by cutting bonds, not by a molecule binding a regulatory spot.
The zymogens activate themselves in acidic conditions
Acid switching on its own precursor is pepsinogen in the stomach, not the pancreatic zymogens.
questions.x: Enteropeptidase is an enzyme stuck to the lining of the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine. It has basically one job: cut trypsinogen into active trypsin. Trypsin is itself a protease, and it goes on to cut and switch on the other pancreatic zymogens, like chymotrypsinogen and proelastase, plus more trypsinogen. So one small trigger sets off a chain reaction (a cascade) that switches on the whole set of digestive enzymes, right where they're needed.

questions.q: Which form of enzyme regulation is irreversible?
o: Phosphorylation by a kinase
Phosphatases can remove the phosphate, so it can be undone.
Binding of an allosteric inhibitor
Allosteric inhibitors bind by weak attractions and come off again.
Competitive inhibition by a substrate analog
Competitive inhibitors can be pushed out by more substrate or washed away.
Proteolytic activation of a zymogen
Correct: a cut peptide bond can't be rejoined to switch the enzyme back off.
questions.x: Switching on a zymogen means cutting a peptide bond, and cells have no way to glue that bond back together. So once the enzyme is on, it can't be turned back into the inactive form. It can only be stopped by an inhibitor protein or by being broken down. The other choices can all be undone. A phosphatase removes the phosphate a kinase added. Allosteric and competitive inhibitors stick by weak attractions and float off. One-way switching suits processes that should run to the end once started, like digestion and blood clotting.

questions.q: Two isozymes catalyze the same reaction in different tissues. How do they usually differ?
o: In the reaction they catalyze
By definition, isozymes run the same reaction.
In amino acid sequence and kinetic or regulatory properties
Correct: isozymes are different proteins, each tuned to its tissue's needs.
In the equilibrium constant they produce
No enzyme changes the equilibrium constant.
In nothing; they are identical molecules
Identical molecules would just be the same enzyme, not isozymes.
questions.x: Isozymes are different versions of an enzyme that run the same reaction. They're made from different genes (or different versions of one gene), so their amino acid sequences differ. That lets each tissue get a version tuned to its own needs: a different Kₘ, Vₘₐₓ or regulation. For example, glucokinase in the liver needs much more glucose to reach half speed than hexokinase in muscle does. But no enzyme can change the equilibrium constant, so all isozymes reach the same equilibrium.

questions.q: Which assumption is central to the steady-state derivation of the Michaelis–Menten equation?
o: Enzyme concentration greatly exceeds substrate concentration
It's the other way around: substrate is assumed to far outnumber enzyme.
[ES] stays roughly constant during the initial-rate period
Correct: ES forms as fast as it breaks down, so its amount stays roughly constant.
The reaction has reached chemical equilibrium
Starting rates are measured far from equilibrium, when little product exists.
The product rapidly converts back into ES
Product turning back into ES is assumed to be negligible.
questions.x: The Michaelis–Menten equation comes from a model where enzyme (E) and substrate (S) form a complex (ES), which then makes product (P). The key shortcut, called the steady-state assumption, is that during the first moments of the reaction, the amount of ES stays about constant. That's because ES is being made just as fast as it breaks down. This works when there's far more substrate than enzyme and almost no product yet, so the reverse reaction doesn't matter. Solving for [ES] with this shortcut gives the Michaelis–Menten equation.

questions.q: Kₘ equals (k₋₁ + kcat)/k₁. When is Kₘ a good approximation of the substrate's dissociation constant (Kd)?
o: When kcat is much larger than k₋₁
If kcat is much bigger, Kₘ is mostly kcat ÷ k₁ and comes out much larger than Kd.
When k₁ is zero
If k₁ were zero, ES would never form at all.
Always, by definition
Kₘ and Kd differ whenever kcat isn't tiny.
When kcat is much smaller than k₋₁
Correct: with kcat much smaller than k₋₁, Kₘ ≈ k₋₁ ÷ k₁ = Kd.
questions.note: Low Kₘ means high affinity only roughly.
questions.x: Two numbers get mixed up here. Kd = k₋₁ ÷ k₁ measures pure binding: how easily ES falls apart compared with how easily it forms. Kₘ = (k₋₁ + kcat) ÷ k₁ adds in kcat, the rate ES turns into product. ES can leave in two ways: falling apart (k₋₁) or reacting (kcat). If kcat is much smaller than k₋₁, ES falls apart many times before it ever reacts, so k₋₁ + kcat is about k₋₁, and Kₘ ≈ Kd. Then a low Kₘ really does mean tight binding. If kcat is big, Kₘ comes out larger than Kd.

questions.q: Why are enzyme kinetics measured as initial rates?
o: Substrate is nearly at its starting level and product has not built up
Correct: substrate is still at its starting level and product hasn't built up yet.
Enzymes are only active for the first few seconds
Enzymes keep working. The rate drops because the concentrations change, not because the enzyme quits.
Vₘₐₓ can be measured only at time zero
Vₘₐₓ comes from many starting rates measured at different [S].
The enzyme has not yet bound any substrate
Substrate binds within milliseconds of mixing.
questions.x: The starting rate (initial rate, v₀) is measured in the first moments after you mix enzyme and substrate. At that point, [S] is still basically what you put in, so you know exactly which [S] the rate goes with. And there's almost no product yet. That avoids three problems that grow with time: substrate running low, product turning back into substrate, and product getting in the enzyme's way. Measure v₀ at many different [S] values and you can work out Kₘ and Vₘₐₓ.

questions.q: Raising [S] from 10 mM to 20 mM leaves an enzyme's initial rate unchanged. What can be concluded?
o: The enzyme is denatured
A denatured enzyme would show almost no activity, not a steady top rate.
[S] is well below Kₘ
Below Kₘ, doubling [S] would nearly double the rate.
The enzyme is saturated, with [S] well above Kₘ
Correct: the enzyme is saturated, so extra substrate can't speed it up.
A competitive inhibitor must be present
More substrate can overcome a competitive inhibitor, so the rate would go up.
questions.x: Normally, doubling the substrate speeds up an enzyme a lot, unless the enzyme is already nearly maxed out. If going from 10 mM to 20 mM changes nothing, almost every active site is already busy. That means the enzyme is saturated: [S] is far above Kₘ and the rate is about Vₘₐₓ. For example, if Kₘ were 1 mM, the enzyme would be at 10 ÷ 11 ≈ 91% of top speed at 10 mM and 20 ÷ 21 ≈ 95% at 20 mM, a change too small to notice. A denatured enzyme would barely work at all.

questions.q: An enzyme has kcat/Kₘ ≈ 10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹. What does this suggest?
o: It binds substrate very weakly
Weak binding would mean a high Kₘ and a small kcat ÷ Kₘ, not a huge one.
Its reaction has a large positive ΔG
kcat ÷ Kₘ is about speed. It says nothing about ΔG.
Its rate is limited by how fast substrate diffuses to it
Correct: 10⁸ to 10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹ is about as fast as molecules can diffuse together.
It must be allosterically regulated
Being efficient doesn't tell you whether an enzyme is regulated.
questions.x: kcat ÷ Kₘ, the catalytic efficiency, tells you how fast free enzyme meets free substrate and turns it into product. There's a ceiling: an enzyme can't work faster than molecules can drift into each other in water, which is about 10⁸ to 10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹. That drifting is called diffusion. An enzyme at about 10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹ turns nearly every substrate molecule it bumps into into product. Its speed is limited by diffusion, not by its chemistry. Triose phosphate isomerase is a famous example, sometimes called a 'perfect' enzyme.

questions.q: Protein kinase A is a tetramer of two regulatory and two catalytic subunits. How does cAMP activate it?
o: cAMP phosphorylates the catalytic subunits
cAMP is a signaling molecule, not a phosphate donor. The phosphate comes from ATP.
cAMP binds the regulatory subunits, releasing active catalytic subunits
Correct: cAMP binds the regulatory subunits, which release the working catalytic subunits.
cAMP cleaves the regulatory subunits
Nothing is cut. cAMP binds and later comes off, so it can be switched off again.
cAMP binds the active site as a substrate
cAMP binds the regulatory subunits, not the active site, and isn't turned into product.
questions.x: Protein kinase A (PKA) is made of four parts: two regulatory subunits and two catalytic subunits (the ones that actually do the work of adding phosphates). When it's off, each regulatory subunit sits in a catalytic subunit's active site and blocks it. cAMP binds the regulatory subunits, which changes their shape so they let go. The freed catalytic subunits are now active and add phosphates to serine and threonine on target proteins. When cAMP is broken down, the regulatory subunits grab the catalytic ones again and PKA switches off.

questions.q: On a Lineweaver–Burk plot, an inhibitor increases the slope without changing the y-intercept. What is most likely true of the inhibitor?
o: It resembles the substrate and binds the active site
Correct: this is competitive inhibition, so Vₘₐₓ stays the same and Kₘ goes up.
It binds only the enzyme–substrate complex
Binding only the enzyme–substrate complex gives parallel lines.
It covalently destroys enzyme molecules
Destroying enzyme lowers Vₘₐₓ, which would raise the y-intercept.
It binds an allosteric site on E and ES equally
Binding E and ES equally gives lines that cross on the x-axis.
questions.x: On a Lineweaver–Burk plot, the y-intercept is 1/Vₘₐₓ and the slope is Kₘ/Vₘₐₓ. If the y-intercept didn't change, Vₘₐₓ didn't change. If the slope got steeper while Vₘₐₓ stayed the same, then Kₘ went up. Same Vₘₐₓ with higher Kₘ is competitive inhibition. That usually comes from a molecule that looks like the substrate and competes for the active site. Enough substrate pushes it out, which is why Vₘₐₓ stays the same.

questions.q: A suicide (mechanism-based) inhibitor works by which mechanism?
o: It binds reversibly at an allosteric site
Binding reversibly at a regulatory spot describes an allosteric inhibitor.
It competes with substrate and is easily displaced
Being easily pushed out describes a reversible competitive inhibitor.
The enzyme converts it into a reactive form that covalently inactivates the enzyme
Correct: the enzyme's own chemistry turns the inhibitor into something reactive that bonds to it permanently.
It denatures the enzyme by raising the temperature
Inhibitors act chemically. They don't work by heating the enzyme.
questions.x: A suicide inhibitor (also called a mechanism-based inhibitor) looks like a harmless substrate at first. The enzyme grabs it and starts its normal chemistry on it. But that chemistry turns the inhibitor into a reactive molecule right there in the active site. The reactive molecule then forms a covalent bond with the enzyme and disables it permanently. The enzyme basically does itself in. Since only the target enzyme can 'arm' the inhibitor, these are very specific.

questions.q: Which way of regulating enzyme activity usually takes longest to take effect?
o: Changing transcription of the enzyme's gene
Correct: making new enzyme takes hours. The other controls work in seconds or less.
Allosteric inhibition by a metabolite
Allosteric binding happens in milliseconds.
Phosphorylation by an existing kinase
Adding a phosphate to enzyme that's already there takes seconds to minutes.
Competitive inhibition by an existing molecule
An inhibitor that's already there binds almost instantly.
questions.x: Cells can control enzymes in fast ways and slow ways. Allosteric regulators and competitive inhibitors just bind and unbind, which takes milliseconds. Adding a phosphate with a kinase that's already there changes existing enzymes in seconds to minutes. Changing how much the enzyme's gene is transcribed means making new mRNA, translating it into protein and folding that protein, or waiting for old enzyme to be broken down. That takes hours. So controlling transcription is the slowest, though its effects last the longest.

questions.q: An enzyme has Kₘ = 2 μM and Vₘₐₓ = 90 μM/s. A competitive inhibitor is present at [I] = Ki. What is v at [S] = 4 μM?
o: 30 μM/s
This halves Vₘₐₓ, treating the inhibitor as noncompetitive. Competitive doubles Kₘ instead.
45 μM/s
Correct: Kₘ,app = 4 μM, so v = 90 × 4 ÷ (4 + 4) = 45 μM/s.
60 μM/s
60 is the rate with no inhibitor: 90 × 4 ÷ (2 + 4).
90 μM/s
The rate only gets close to Vₘₐₓ when there's far more substrate.
questions.x: A competitive inhibitor only changes Kₘ. First fix Kₘ: Kₘ,app = Kₘ × (1 + [I]/Ki). Here Kₘ = 2 μM and [I] = Ki, so [I]/Ki = 1 and Kₘ,app = 2 × (1 + 1) = 2 × 2 = 4 μM. Vₘₐₓ stays 90 μM/s. Now use Michaelis–Menten: v = Vₘₐₓ × [S] ÷ (Kₘ,app + [S]) = 90 × 4 ÷ (4 + 4) = 360 ÷ 8 = 45 μM/s. Notice [S] now equals the new Kₘ, so the enzyme runs at exactly half of Vₘₐₓ. Halving Vₘₐₓ instead would treat it as noncompetitive and give 30.

questions.q: An enzyme has Vₘₐₓ = 120 μM/s. A pure noncompetitive inhibitor is added at [I] = Ki. What is v at [S] = Kₘ?
o: 30 μM/s
Correct: Vₘₐₓ,app = 120 ÷ 2 = 60, and at [S] = Kₘ, v = 60 ÷ 2 = 30 μM/s.
40 μM/s
This treats it as competitive: Kₘ doubled instead of Vₘₐₓ halved.
60 μM/s
60 uses only one of the two halvings, not both.
120 μM/s
This ignores both the inhibitor and the fact that [S] = Kₘ gives half speed.
questions.x: A pure noncompetitive inhibitor lowers Vₘₐₓ by a factor of (1 + [I]/Ki) and leaves Kₘ alone. With [I] = Ki, the factor is 1 + 1 = 2, so Vₘₐₓ,app = 120 ÷ 2 = 60 μM/s. Kₘ didn't change, so at [S] = Kₘ the enzyme still runs at half of its (new) top speed: v = 60 × Kₘ ÷ (Kₘ + Kₘ) = 60 × 1/2 = 30 μM/s. Two halvings: one from the inhibitor, one from [S] = Kₘ. Putting the factor of 2 on Kₘ instead (the competitive way) gives 40.

questions.q: More enzyme is added to an assay. How does its Lineweaver–Burk line change?
o: The x-intercept moves and the y-intercept stays the same
A moving x-intercept with a fixed y-intercept means Kₘ changed, the competitive pattern.
The line shifts parallel to itself
A parallel shift is the uncompetitive pattern, where Kₘ and Vₘₐₓ change together.
Nothing changes
Vₘₐₓ depends on how much enzyme there is, so the line must change.
The y-intercept falls and the x-intercept stays the same
Correct: Vₘₐₓ goes up (so 1/Vₘₐₓ goes down) while Kₘ stays the same.
questions.x: Top speed depends on how much enzyme you have: Vₘₐₓ = kcat × [E]T. So adding enzyme raises Vₘₐₓ, which lowers the y-intercept of a Lineweaver–Burk plot (the y-intercept is 1/Vₘₐₓ). Kₘ belongs to each enzyme molecule and doesn't depend on how many molecules there are, so the x-intercept (−1/Kₘ) stays put. The line swings down around the same x-intercept and gets less steep.

questions.q: Substrates A (kcat/Kₘ = 10⁶ M⁻¹s⁻¹) and B (kcat/Kₘ = 10⁴ M⁻¹s⁻¹) are present at equal, low concentrations with one enzyme. What is the ratio of their rates, A : B?
o: Equal concentrations don't mean equal rates when the enzyme handles one substrate better.
Correct: the rate ratio equals the kcat/Kₘ ratio, 10⁶ ÷ 10⁴ = 100.
This compares the exponents (6 and 4) instead of the actual numbers.
questions.x: When two substrates compete for the same enzyme at low concentration, each one's rate is v = (kcat/Kₘ) × [E] × [S]. Both share the same free enzyme, so [E] cancels when you divide one rate by the other: vA ÷ vB = (kcat/Kₘ)A × [A] ÷ ((kcat/Kₘ)B × [B]). The concentrations are equal, so they cancel too, leaving 10⁶ ÷ 10⁴. Dividing powers of 10 means subtracting exponents: 6 − 4 = 2, so 10² = 100. The rates are 100 : 1. That's why kcat/Kₘ is called the specificity constant.

questions.q: Most kinases actually use a complex of ATP with which ion as their substrate?
o: Na⁺
Na⁺ binds ATP only weakly and isn't kinases' usual partner.
Mg²⁺
Correct: Mg²⁺ cancels some of ATP's negative charge and holds it in the right shape.
Cl⁻
Cl⁻ is negative, so it would be pushed away by ATP's negative phosphates.
Fe³⁺
Iron's usual job is moving electrons, not partnering with ATP.
questions.x: Inside cells, ATP is mostly found stuck to a magnesium ion, as Mg²⁺–ATP. ATP's phosphate groups carry several negative charges that push on each other. Mg²⁺, with its two positive charges, sits between two of the phosphates. It cancels some of that negative charge and holds the phosphates in a set shape the kinase can work with. That makes the last phosphate easier to move onto the target. So kinases, and most other enzymes that use ATP, need Mg²⁺.

questions.q: What is an allosteric site?
o: The site where substrate is converted to product
Where substrate becomes product is the active site.
The site where a protease cleaves a zymogen
The spot a protease cuts in a zymogen is a cleavage site.
The DNA sequence that controls the enzyme's expression
A DNA stretch controlling the gene is a promoter, not part of the enzyme.
A regulatory binding site separate from the active site
Correct: a regulatory binding spot away from the active site that changes the enzyme's shape and activity.
questions.x: An allosteric site is a binding spot on an enzyme that's separate from the active site. The name comes from Greek: 'allos' means other, so it's literally 'the other site.' When a regulator molecule (an effector) binds there, it changes the enzyme's shape, and that change travels to the active site and turns activity up or down. The effector isn't turned into product, unlike a substrate in the active site, and it can come and go.

questions.q: Phosphofructokinase-1 is inhibited by ATP and activated by AMP. What does a high AMP level signal to it?
o: The cell is low on energy, so glycolysis should speed up
Correct: high AMP means ATP is running low, so PFK-1 speeds up glycolysis.
The cell has plenty of energy, so glycolysis should slow down
Plenty of energy is signaled by high ATP, not high AMP.
AMP is PFK-1's main substrate
PFK-1's substrates are fructose-6-phosphate and ATP. AMP is a regulator.
Glycolysis should be replaced by gluconeogenesis
When energy is low, the cell needs to make ATP, not spend it making glucose.
questions.x: Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) runs the first committed step of glycolysis, the pathway that breaks down glucose to make ATP, and it keeps track of the cell's energy level. When the cell uses ATP faster than it makes it, AMP (ATP with two phosphates removed) builds up. AMP binds a regulatory spot on PFK-1 and switches it on, speeding up glycolysis so the cell makes more ATP. When ATP is plentiful, ATP binds a different, inhibitory spot and slows PFK-1 down. So ATP is both PFK-1's substrate and its brake.

questions.q: Why does the reaction rate level off at high substrate concentrations?
o: The substrate becomes a competitive inhibitor
Typical enzymes aren't blocked by their own substrate. That would make the rate fall, not level off.
The equilibrium constant decreases
The equilibrium constant doesn't change with [S].
Nearly all active sites are occupied
Correct: once nearly every active site is busy, extra substrate has nowhere to go.
The enzyme is denatured by substrate
A saturated enzyme is working at top speed. Denatured enzymes stop working.
questions.x: How fast an enzyme works depends on how many of its active sites are holding substrate. At low [S], most sites are empty, so adding substrate fills more of them and the rate climbs. At high [S], nearly every site is already busy. Extra substrate has no free enzyme to grab, so the rate levels off at Vₘₐₓ. This is called saturation. The enzyme isn't damaged or denatured; it's working as fast as it can.

questions.q: A pure noncompetitive inhibitor is added to an enzyme assay. What happens to the enzyme's apparent kcat/Kₘ?
o: It increases
An inhibitor can't make the enzyme more efficient.
It is unchanged
kcat/Kₘ stays the same in uncompetitive inhibition, where both drop together.
It becomes zero
Reversible inhibition is partial. Some enzyme always stays free and working.
It decreases
Correct: apparent kcat drops while Kₘ stays the same, so kcat/Kₘ drops.
questions.x: kcat/Kₘ (catalytic efficiency) is kcat divided by Kₘ. A pure noncompetitive inhibitor takes enzymes out of action, so the apparent kcat drops (just like Vₘₐₓ does). But it leaves Kₘ unchanged. A smaller top number divided by the same bottom number gives a smaller result, so kcat/Kₘ goes down. At [I] = Ki, for example, it's cut in half. That means this inhibitor slows the enzyme even when substrate is scarce. An uncompetitive inhibitor is different: it lowers kcat and Kₘ by the same factor, so their ratio stays the same.

questions.q: During an enzyme purification, total protein falls from 500 mg to 5 mg while total activity falls only from 1000 to 500 units. What happens to specific activity?
o: It falls by half
Halving is the change in total activity, not activity per mg.
It rises 100-fold
100-fold is the drop in protein alone. It ignores the enzyme that was lost.
It rises 50-fold, from 2 to 100 units/mg
Correct: 1000 ÷ 500 = 2 and 500 ÷ 5 = 100 units/mg, a 50-fold rise.
It stays the same
Removing other proteins makes the enzyme a bigger share of what's left.
questions.x: Specific activity is enzyme activity divided by total protein, and it tells you how pure the enzyme is. The formula: specific activity = total activity ÷ total protein. Before: 1000 units ÷ 500 mg = 2 units/mg. After: 500 units ÷ 5 mg = 100 units/mg. Divide to compare: 100 ÷ 2 = 50, so it rose 50-fold. Half the enzyme was lost along the way (500 out of 1000 units), but the other proteins were removed much faster, so what's left is much purer.

questions.q: After mild treatment with a mercury compound, an allosteric enzyme gives a hyperbolic v vs [S] curve, still catalyzes, and no longer responds to its allosteric inhibitor. What most likely happened?
o: The active site was destroyed
The enzyme still works, so the active site is fine.
Catalytic subunits separated from regulatory subunits
Correct: freed catalytic subunits still work but lose cooperativity and regulation.
The enzyme's primary structure was hydrolyzed
Mild mercury treatment doesn't cut peptide bonds.
The inhibitor became covalently attached to the active site
An inhibitor stuck in the active site would stop the enzyme from working.
questions.x: Some allosteric enzymes, like aspartate transcarbamoylase (ATCase), are built from separate catalytic subunits (which do the chemistry) and regulatory subunits (which bind the regulators). Mercury compounds react with the -SH groups of cysteines and can make those subunits fall apart, without cutting any peptide bonds. The freed catalytic subunits still make product, but they've lost their partners. So they no longer show cooperativity (the curve becomes a simple bend instead of an S), and they ignore the inhibitor, which binds the regulatory subunits.

questions.q: Mendel's law of segregation is best explained by which meiotic event?
o: Separation of sister chromatids in anaphase II
Sister chromatids are copies of one homolog with the same allele. The allele pair splits when homologs separate.
Crossing over during prophase I
Crossing over swaps pieces between homologs. It mixes alleles but doesn't separate a pair.
Cytokinesis after telophase II
Cytokinesis just splits the cytoplasm. The alleles were already separated before this.
Separation of homologous chromosomes in anaphase I
Correct: each homolog carries one allele, so the pair splits when homologs separate in anaphase I.
questions.note: Segregation = homologs part in meiosis I.
questions.x: Mendel's law of segregation says your two copies of a gene (your two alleles) split up, so each egg or sperm gets just one. You carry one allele on each chromosome of a matching pair. Those matching chromosomes are called homologs: one came from mom, one from dad. In anaphase I of meiosis, the homologs get pulled to opposite ends of the cell, so the two alleles land in different cells. That's segregation. Sister chromatids are the two identical copies of ONE homolog, made when the DNA was copied. They carry the same allele, so splitting them in anaphase II doesn't separate an allele pair.

questions.q: Two carriers of an autosomal recessive disorder have two children. What is the probability that exactly one child is affected?
o: This counts only one birth order. Affected-first and affected-second both count, so double it.
That's the chance for one child. It ignores the two-child setup.
This treats affected and unaffected as equally likely. They're 1/4 and 3/4.
questions.note: Exactly one of n: multiply by the number of orders.
questions.x: Two carriers (Aa × Aa) have a 1/4 chance of an affected child (aa) each time, and a 3/4 chance of an unaffected one. 'Exactly one affected' can happen two ways: affected then unaffected, or unaffected then affected. Each way is 1/4 × 3/4 = 3/16. Add the two ways: 3/16 + 3/16 = 6/16, and 6/16 reduces to 3/8 (divide top and bottom by 2). Forgetting the second birth order gives 3/16, which is the most common slip on this kind of question.

questions.q: An unaffected woman whose brother has an autosomal recessive disease (parents unaffected) has a child with a man who is a known carrier. What is the probability the child is affected?
o: This uses 1/2 for her carrier chance. She's unaffected, so it's 2/3.
This assumes she's definitely a carrier. She's only a carrier with probability 2/3.
Correct: P(she's a carrier) 2/3 × P(aa from two carriers) 1/4 = 2/12 = 1/6.
This tacks on an extra 1/2. The 1/4 already covers both parents passing the allele.
questions.x: Her brother is affected (aa) and her parents aren't, so both parents must be carriers (Aa). Their kids come out AA, Aa, Aa or aa. She's unaffected, so aa is off the table, leaving 3 equally likely options, 2 of which are carriers: her carrier chance is 2/3. If she is a carrier, two carriers have an affected child 1/4 of the time. Both have to be true, so multiply: 2/3 × 1/4 = 2/12 = 1/6. Using 1/2 for her carrier chance gives 1/8, the classic mistake.

questions.q: Mendel's law of independent assortment applies most strictly to genes that are:
o: Tightly linked on the same chromosome
Linked genes ride together on one chromosome, so they break independent assortment.
Alternative alleles of the same gene
Alleles of one gene separate from each other. That's segregation; assortment is about different genes.
Found only on the X chromosome
Being on the X doesn't help. Two X-linked genes share one chromosome and can be linked.
Located on different nonhomologous chromosomes
Correct: different chromosome pairs line up independently in metaphase I.
questions.x: Independent assortment means the alleles of different genes get sorted into gametes without affecting each other. It happens because, in metaphase I, each pair of homologs (matching chromosomes) lines up on its own, no matter how the other pairs line up. So genes on different chromosomes sort independently, and every combination of their alleles shows up equally often. Genes sitting close together on the same chromosome are physically tied, so they travel together unless crossing over separates them. That's called linkage, and it breaks the law.

questions.q: Of 100 people with a genotype for an autosomal dominant disease, 80 show signs of the disease and 20 show none. This describes:
o: 80% expressivity
Expressivity is how severe the trait is in people who show it, not how many show it.
Codominance
Codominance means both alleles show up in one heterozygote, like AB blood. Not described here.
A 20% mutation rate
The 20 people with no signs still have the mutant genotype, so no mutation rate is involved.
80% penetrance
Correct: penetrance = 80 ÷ 100 × 100% = 80% of carriers show the phenotype.
questions.note: Penetrance = whether; expressivity = how much.
questions.x: Penetrance is the percent of people with a genotype who show the phenotype (the visible trait) at all. Formula: penetrance = (number showing it) ÷ (number with the genotype) × 100%. Here 80 people show signs and 100 have the genotype, so penetrance = 80 ÷ 100 × 100% = 0.8 × 100% = 80%. Expressivity is a different idea: among the people who do show the trait, how severe is it? The 20 people without signs still carry the allele, so this has nothing to do with a mutation rate.

questions.q: A woman with normal vision has a color-blind father (X-linked recessive). She has a child with a man with normal vision. What is the probability their first child is a color-blind son?
o: That's the risk once you know the child is a boy. The question also needs the chance it's a boy.
Correct: she's a sure carrier, so P(son) 1/2 × P(he gets her mutant X) 1/2 = 1/4.
This treats her carrier chance as 1/2. Her father gave her his mutant X for sure.
She carries the allele from her father and can pass it on, so it isn't zero.
questions.x: Color blindness here is X-linked recessive. Her father is color-blind, and a father gives his only X to every daughter, so she definitely carries one mutant X. She's a sure carrier. Now two things must both happen: the child must be a boy (chance 1/2), and he must get her mutant X instead of her normal one (chance 1/2). Multiply: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. Answering 1/2 answers a different question: the risk once you already know the baby is a boy.

questions.q: Siblings born to a mother with a mitochondrial DNA mutation vary widely in severity of the resulting disease. The best explanation is that:
o: Each oocyte received a different proportion of mutant mitochondria
Correct: with a mix of mitochondria (heteroplasmy), each egg gets a different mutant share by chance.
Paternal mitochondria compensate in some children
Dad's mitochondria are basically never passed on, so they can't make up the difference.
mtDNA recombines with nuclear DNA during meiosis
mtDNA is a separate genome and doesn't cross over with nuclear chromosomes.
X-inactivation differs between siblings
X-inactivation shuts off an X chromosome. It has nothing to do with mitochondrial genes.
questions.note: Heteroplasmy explains variable severity in mitochondrial disease.
questions.x: Each cell holds many mitochondria, and each one has its own little DNA (mtDNA). A mother can carry a mix of normal and mutant mtDNA in her cells. That mix is called heteroplasmy. When her eggs form, the mitochondria get handed out at random, so each egg ends up with a different share of mutant ones. Symptoms show up only once the mutant share passes a threshold, and they get worse as it climbs. That's why siblings from the same mother can range from mild to severe. Dad's mitochondria basically never get passed on, so they can't help.

questions.q: Deleting the same region of chromosome 15 causes one syndrome when inherited from the father and a different syndrome when inherited from the mother. This best illustrates:
o: X-inactivation
X-inactivation shuts off an X. Chromosome 15 is an autosome, not a sex chromosome.
Mitochondrial inheritance
The defect is in a nuclear chromosome that either parent can pass, not in mitochondria.
Incomplete dominance
Incomplete dominance is a blend of two alleles. It doesn't depend on which parent gave the allele.
Genomic imprinting
Correct: some genes are silenced based on the parent of origin, so the working copy differs.
questions.x: This is genomic imprinting. For a few genes, a chemical tag switches off one parent's copy, so only the other parent's copy works. Which copy is silenced depends on whether it came from mom or dad. On chromosome 15, some genes only work on dad's copy and others only on mom's. Lose dad's region and you lose the working paternal genes: that's Prader-Willi syndrome. Lose mom's region and you lose the working maternal genes: that's Angelman syndrome. The giveaway is that the same deletion causes different diseases depending on the parent it came from.

questions.q: Two genes show a recombination frequency of 50% in testcrosses. This indicates that the genes:
o: Assort independently, as if unlinked
Correct: 50% recombinants is the maximum and looks just like independent assortment.
Are adjacent on the same chromosome
Genes right next to each other would almost never cross over, so RF would be near 0%.
Are exactly 100 map units apart
Measured RF can't go above 50%, so it can't show a distance of 100 map units.
Are linked in the repulsion phase
Phase changes which classes count as recombinant, not the RF value.
questions.x: Recombination frequency (RF) is the percent of offspring that carry a new mix of alleles, made by crossing over. It tops out at 50%. Even if a crossover happens between two genes every single time, it only involves two of the four chromatids, so only half the gametes come out recombinant. An RF of 50% means parental and recombinant offspring show up in equal numbers, which is exactly what you'd see for genes on different chromosomes. So the genes act unlinked: they're either on different chromosomes or very far apart on the same one.

questions.q: In a three-point testcross, the parental classes are ABC and abc, and the two rarest classes are AbC and aBc. Which gene is in the middle?
o: A
In the rare classes, A still sits with C just like in the parentals, so A is on an end.
C
C keeps its parental partner A in the rare classes, so C is on an end.
B
Correct: a double crossover swaps only the middle gene, and only B is switched.
It cannot be determined without map distances
The rarest (double crossover) classes alone tell you the middle gene.
questions.note: Rarest class = double crossover; the swapped gene is in the middle.
questions.x: In a three-point testcross you follow three linked genes at once. The most common offspring are the parentals (here ABC and abc). The rarest are double crossovers, which need two crossovers at once. A double crossover swaps only the middle gene, while the two genes on the ends stay with their original partners. So line up a rare class next to the parental it most resembles: ABC versus AbC. Only B has changed, so B is in the middle. You don't need map distances for this.

questions.q: A dihybrid with genes linked in repulsion (Ab/aB) and little recombination is testcrossed to ab/ab. Which progeny classes are most frequent?
o: AB and ab (recombinant types)
With a parent in repulsion (Ab/aB), AB and ab are the recombinant classes.
All four classes equally
Four equal classes happen only with independent assortment, not tight linkage.
AB only
A testcross shows every gamete the dihybrid makes, and AB is a rare recombinant here.
Ab and aB (parental types)
Correct: the parent's chromosomes are Ab and aB, so those classes dominate.
questions.x: Linked genes sit on the same chromosome, so they're usually inherited together. The parental (non-recombinant) offspring always match the allele combos on the dihybrid's own chromosomes. 'Repulsion' means the parent is Ab/aB: one chromosome carries A with b, the other a with B. So the parental gametes are Ab and aB. With little crossing over, most gametes are copies of those two chromosomes, so Ab and aB offspring are the most common. AB and ab only appear when crossing over happens, so here they're the rare recombinants.

questions.q: Genes A and B are 20 cM apart. Two dihybrids with coupling-phase chromosomes (AB/ab) are crossed. What fraction of offspring are ab/ab?
o: Correct: each parent makes ab at (1 − 0.20) ÷ 2 = 0.40, and 0.40 × 0.40 = 0.16.
That's 1/16, the answer for unlinked genes. Linkage makes ab more common.
This assumes no recombination at all, so ab would be 50%. Here it's 40%.
This squares a recombinant gamete (0.10). In coupling, ab is a parental gamete.
questions.note: Linked genes: parental gametes = (1 − RF)/2 each; recombinant = RF/2 each.
questions.x: 20 cM apart means 20% of gametes are recombinant and 80% are parental. In coupling (AB/ab), the parental gametes are AB and ab, split evenly. Formula: P(ab gamete) = (1 − RF) ÷ 2. Values: RF = 0.20. Plug in: (1 − 0.20) ÷ 2 = 0.80 ÷ 2 = 0.40. An ab/ab child needs an ab gamete from each parent, so multiply: 0.40 × 0.40 = 0.16 = 16%. Using the recombinant share (0.10) would only fit parents in repulsion (Ab/aB).

questions.q: Recombination frequencies between distant genes underestimate their true map distance mainly because:
o: Distant genes are never separated by crossing over
Distant genes are separated by crossing over most often, not never.
Even numbers of crossovers between them restore parental combinations
Correct: double crossovers swap the alleles back, go uncounted, and RF levels off near 50%.
Crossover frequency decreases toward chromosome ends
That isn't the general reason RF levels off for distant genes.
Recombinant gametes fail to fertilize eggs
Recombinant gametes work fine. If they failed, RF would be low for close genes too.
questions.note: Map from short intervals added together, not one long measurement.
questions.x: One crossover between two genes makes a recombinant. But a second crossover in the same stretch swaps the alleles right back, so the offspring looks parental. Any even number of crossovers hides itself that way. Genes that are far apart get multiple crossovers a lot, and many go uncounted. So the measured recombination frequency (RF) comes out lower than the true distance and levels off around 50%. That's why accurate maps are built by adding up short distances, where double crossovers are rare.

questions.q: A child with trisomy 21 has two different maternal alleles at a marker very close to the chromosome 21 centromere. Nondisjunction most likely occurred in:
o: Maternal meiosis II
A meiosis II error puts sister chromatids in the egg, which carry identical alleles near the centromere.
Paternal meiosis I
The extra alleles are maternal, so the extra chromosome came from the mother.
Maternal meiosis I
Correct: two different maternal alleles means both maternal homologs went into the egg.
Mitosis after fertilization
An error after fertilization copies a chromosome already there, giving identical alleles.
questions.note: Different homologs = MI error; identical copies = MII error.
questions.x: Nondisjunction means chromosomes fail to separate. Homologs (mom's and dad's versions of a chromosome) separate in meiosis I. Sister chromatids (two identical copies) separate in meiosis II. Right next to the centromere, crossing over almost never mixes alleles, so a marker there tells you which whole chromosome went into the egg. Two DIFFERENT maternal alleles mean both of the mother's homologs ended up in the egg, which is a meiosis I error. A meiosis II error would give two IDENTICAL alleles, because sister chromatids are copies.

questions.q: A normal egg is fertilized by sperm produced after nondisjunction of the sex chromosomes in paternal meiosis I. What karyotypes can result?
o: 47,XYY or 45,X
YY sperm come from a meiosis II error, when the two Y chromatids fail to split.
47,XXY or 45,X
Correct: a meiosis I error gives XY sperm or sperm with no sex chromosome.
47,XXX or 45,X
XX sperm come from a meiosis II error, not meiosis I.
47,XXY only
The partner cell gets no sex chromosome, and its sperm gives 45,X too.
questions.x: A father has one X and one Y. In meiosis I, they're supposed to split into different cells. If they don't (nondisjunction), one cell gets both X and Y and the other gets no sex chromosome. So the sperm end up either XY or with no sex chromosome at all. A normal egg always brings one X. XY sperm + X egg = 47,XXY (Klinefelter syndrome). Empty sperm + X egg = 45,X (Turner syndrome). XX or YY sperm only come from errors in meiosis II, after X and Y have already split.

questions.q: A compound causes reversion in the Ames test only when rat liver extract is added; extract alone causes no reversion. The best interpretation is:
o: Liver extract itself is the mutagen
The extract alone caused no reversion, so it isn't the mutagen.
The compound is mutagenic only to mammals
The bacteria did mutate once the compound was activated, so it isn't mammal-only.
Liver enzymes convert it into a mutagenic metabolite
Correct: liver enzymes turn the compound into a mutagenic product.
Liver enzymes repair the bacterial DNA
Repair would lower the number of revertants, not raise it.
questions.x: The Ames test uses bacteria that can't make the amino acid histidine. A mutagen (something that damages DNA) can flip that broken gene back, so they grow again. That's called reversion. Some chemicals are harmless until liver enzymes, like the cytochrome P450 family, turn them into reactive, DNA-damaging products. That's called metabolic activation. Adding rat liver extract mimics it. Here the compound only causes reversion with the extract, and the extract alone does nothing. So the liver enzymes are turning the compound into a mutagen.

questions.q: A cytosine in a C–G base pair is deaminated to uracil and not repaired. After two rounds of replication, one descendant DNA molecule will carry what at that site?
o: A G–C pair, no change
The strand copied from the original G stays normal, but the U strand's line doesn't.
A T–A pair, a C→T transition
Correct: U pairs with A in round one, then A pairs with T in round two.
A G–T mismatch
A mismatch only lasts until the next copy, which turns each strand into a full base pair.
An A–T transversion from purine to pyrimidine
C to T swaps one pyrimidine for another, so it's a transition, not a transversion.
questions.x: Deamination means a base loses its amino group (an NH₂). When cytosine loses it, it turns into uracil (U), and uracil pairs with adenine (A), not guanine (G). Follow the U strand. First replication: U is copied, and an A goes in across from it, giving a U–A pair. Second replication: that A is copied, and a T goes in across from it, giving a T–A pair. So one descendant molecule has T–A where C–G used to be. C and T are both pyrimidines, so this is a transition. Cells use an enzyme called uracil-DNA glycosylase to remove U before this can happen.

questions.q: In a population at equilibrium, ABO allele frequencies are Iᴬ = 0.3, Iᴮ = 0.1 and i = 0.6. What fraction of people have type A blood?
o: This counts only IᴬIᴬ. Iᴬi people are type A too.
This counts only Iᴬi, and it happens to match type O (0.6² = 0.36).
That's the Iᴬ allele frequency, not the share of type A people.
questions.x: Type A comes from two genotypes, IᴬIᴬ and Iᴬi, because Iᴬ is dominant to i. With more than two alleles, Hardy–Weinberg works the same way: a homozygote is its allele frequency squared, and a heterozygote is 2 × the two allele frequencies. Formula: type A = p² + 2pr. Values: p (Iᴬ) = 0.3, r (i) = 0.6. Plug in: 0.3² + 2 × 0.3 × 0.6 = 0.09 + 0.36 = 0.45. So 45% of people are type A.

questions.q: In a population with strong positive assortative mating for a trait controlled by one gene, what happens over generations without other forces?
o: Allele frequencies shift toward the dominant allele
Who mates with whom doesn't add or remove alleles, so allele frequencies don't shift.
Homozygotes increase and heterozygotes decrease, with allele frequencies unchanged
Correct: like-with-like mating changes genotype mix, not allele counts.
Heterozygotes increase
Backwards: similar mates make more homozygotes, not heterozygotes.
Genotype frequencies remain at Hardy–Weinberg values
Hardy–Weinberg needs random mating, and this isn't random.
questions.x: Positive assortative mating means individuals pick mates that look like themselves. So like genotypes tend to pair up: AA with AA, aa with aa. Those pairings make more homozygotes (two matching alleles) and fewer heterozygotes (two different alleles) each generation. But nobody's alleles are being added or taken away, just shuffled into different pairings. So allele frequencies stay the same. Only genotype frequencies drift away from the Hardy–Weinberg values, because Hardy–Weinberg assumes random mating.

questions.q: Two unaffected parents with no family history have two children with the same fully penetrant autosomal dominant disorder. The best explanation is:
o: Two independent new mutations
Possible, but two new mutations in the same gene in one family is extremely unlikely.
Both parents are carriers of a recessive allele
This is a dominant disorder, so recessive carrier parents don't fit.
Incomplete penetrance in both children
The children are affected and penetrance is full, so this doesn't explain anything.
Germline mosaicism in one parent
Correct: a mutation in part of one parent's germline can reach several children.
questions.x: Germline mosaicism is the best fit. It means a mutation popped up in some of a parent's egg- or sperm-making cells early in that parent's own development, but not in the rest of their body. So the parent looks completely healthy, with no family history, yet a share of their eggs or sperm carry the dominant allele. That one event can reach more than one child. Two separate new mutations in the same gene in one family would be very unlikely. And 'fully penetrant' means anyone who carries the allele in their body cells shows the disease.

questions.q: A phenotypically normal woman's brother has hemophilia A (X-linked recessive); her parents are unaffected. If she has a son with an unaffected man, what is the probability the son has hemophilia?
o: This assumes she's definitely a carrier. Her chance is only 1/2.
This multiplies in another 1/2 for the baby's sex, but we already know it's a son.
Correct: she's a carrier with chance 1/2, then 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
This borrows the autosomal 2/3 carrier rule, which doesn't apply to X-linked traits.
questions.x: Hemophilia A is X-linked recessive. A boy gets his only X from his mother, so an affected brother with unaffected parents means their mother is a carrier. The woman got one of her mother's two X's at random, so her carrier chance is 1/2. If she is a carrier, her son gets her mutant X with chance 1/2. Formula: P(son affected) = P(she's a carrier) × P(son gets mutant X). Plug in: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. The child is already known to be a son, so don't multiply by another 1/2.

questions.q: In a population at Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, 9% of people show a recessive phenotype. What fraction of people with the dominant phenotype are heterozygous?
o: That's heterozygotes out of everyone, not out of dominant-phenotype people.
That's p², the share of homozygous dominant people.
That's pq, missing the 2 in 2pq.
Correct: 2pq = 0.42, dominant phenotype = 0.91, and 0.42 ÷ 0.91 = 6/13.
questions.note: Conditional: divide by the dominant phenotype frequency, 1 − q².
questions.x: Start with what you can see. Recessive phenotype = q² = 0.09, so q = √0.09 = 0.3 and p = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7. Heterozygotes: 2pq = 2 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.42 of everyone. People with the dominant phenotype: 1 − q² = 1 − 0.09 = 0.91. The question asks only about that group, so divide: 0.42 ÷ 0.91 = 42/91. Both divide by 7, giving 6/13 ≈ 0.46. Answering 0.42 forgets to shrink the group to dominant-phenotype people.

questions.q: In a diploid population of N individuals, what is the probability that a single new neutral mutation will eventually become fixed by genetic drift?
o: A single copy among 2N is far more likely to be lost than kept.
Zero, since neutral alleles never fix
Drift can carry a neutral allele all the way to 100% by chance.
1/(2N), its starting frequency
Correct: a neutral allele's chance of fixing equals its starting frequency, 1/(2N).
1/N²
The starting frequency is 1/(2N), not 1/N².
questions.x: Diploid means each person has two copies of every gene, so N people carry 2N copies. A brand-new mutation is just 1 of those 2N copies, so it starts at a frequency of 1 ÷ 2N. Genetic drift is random change in allele frequency by chance. For a neutral allele, one that doesn't help or hurt, drift is equally likely to favor any copy. So the chance that this one copy's descendants eventually take over the whole population (fixation) equals its starting frequency: 1/(2N). That's tiny, so most new neutral mutations get lost.

questions.q: A tetraploid plant arises from a diploid ancestor. It cannot produce fertile offspring with the diploid because:
o: Tetraploid pollen cannot fertilize diploid ovules
Fertilization can happen. The barrier is that the hybrid is sterile.
The tetraploid has different genes than the diploid
It has the same genes as the diploid, just twice as many sets.
Their triploid hybrids have unpaired chromosomes in meiosis and are sterile
Correct: triploid hybrids can't pair chromosomes evenly in meiosis, so they're sterile.
Tetraploids reproduce only asexually
Many polyploid plants reproduce sexually just fine.
questions.note: Polyploidy can create a new species in a single generation.
questions.x: Ploidy is the number of chromosome sets. A tetraploid (4 sets) makes gametes with 2 sets, and a diploid (2 sets) makes gametes with 1 set. So their hybrid has 2 + 1 = 3 sets: it's triploid. In meiosis, chromosomes have to pair up in twos. With three copies of each, one is always left over, so most gametes get lopsided chromosome sets and don't work. The hybrid is sterile. That cuts the tetraploid off from its parent species in a single generation, a common way new plant species form.

questions.q: Certain flowers and their specific pollinators show matching adaptations, each having evolved in response to the other. This is:
o: Convergent evolution
Convergence is unrelated species evolving similar traits on their own, not in response to each other.
Coevolution
Correct: each species evolves in response to the other.
Genetic drift
Drift is random. Matching adaptations come from selection.
Allopatric speciation
No geographic split or new species is described.
questions.x: Coevolution is when two species that interact keep evolving in response to each other. A change in one puts new selective pressure on the other, and back again. Flowers whose shape fits one pollinator, and pollinators whose mouthparts fit that flower, are the classic example. Predator and prey, or host and parasite, locked in an arms race are others. Convergent evolution sounds similar but isn't: there, unrelated species end up looking alike on their own because they live in similar conditions, not because they're shaping each other.

questions.q: Guppies moved from a stream with many predators to a stream with few predators evolve brighter-colored males over several generations. The best interpretation is that:
o: Bright color was caused by the new stream's diet in each fish
A diet effect in each fish isn't inherited, and this change built up over generations.
Reduced predation let sexual selection for bright males outweigh natural selection against them
Correct: with predators rare, sexual selection for bright males outweighs the cost of being seen.
Predators prefer bright guppies, so color increased
Backwards: fewer predators means less selection against bright males, not more.
Genetic drift produced the same change by chance
Drift is random. A steady change in one direction points to selection.
questions.x: Two forces pull on a male guppy's color. Sexual selection favors bright males, because females prefer them. Natural selection favors dull males, because predators spot bright ones more easily. In a stream with lots of predators, dull wins. Move the fish to a stream with few predators, and being bright costs much less, so females' preference takes over and bright males leave more offspring. The change built up over generations, in one steady direction, which points to selection acting on inherited color, not diet or chance.

questions.q: Where two closely related species meet, their hybrids have low fitness, and over time mating preferences that avoid hybridization become stronger. This process is called:
o: Reinforcement
Correct: selection against weak hybrids strengthens barriers to mating.
Gene flow
Gene flow mixes populations together. Here they're being kept apart.
Hybrid vigor
Hybrid vigor means hybrids are fitter. Here they're less fit.
Genetic drift
Drift is random. This change is driven by selection against hybrids.
questions.x: This is reinforcement. Picture two populations that started drifting apart and now meet again. Their hybrids (offspring from mating across the two groups) don't do well. So individuals that mate with their own kind leave more healthy offspring than those that mix. Over generations, selection makes the mating preferences that prevent mixing stronger. Barriers that act before an embryo forms, like mate preference, are called prezygotic barriers. Reinforcement strengthens them and helps finish splitting the two into separate species.

questions.q: In a fish species, individuals with the rarer of two mouth shapes always have higher feeding success. Over many generations this will most likely:
o: Fix the more common form
The common form is the one at a disadvantage, so it shrinks.
Eliminate both forms
Selection favors whichever form is rare, so it never removes both.
Fix whichever form is rare now
Once the rare form becomes common, it loses its advantage.
Keep both forms present near a stable intermediate frequency
Correct: whichever form is rare is favored, so both stay near a steady balance.
questions.x: This is negative frequency-dependent selection: a trait does better when it's rare and worse when it's common. Suppose one mouth shape is rare, so it feeds better. It spreads. Once it becomes the common shape, it loses the edge, and the other shape, now rare, starts doing better instead. That back-and-forth pushes the two shapes toward a steady balance where both stick around. Neither can take over completely, because winning makes it common, and being common makes it lose. Keeping two or more forms like this is called a balanced polymorphism.

questions.q: A neutral allele tightly linked to a strongly favored allele rises in frequency along with it. The best explanation is:
o: The neutral allele is itself favored
It's neutral, so by definition it has no effect on fitness.
Independent assortment
Tightly linked genes are inherited together, so they don't assort independently.
Mutation repeatedly creates the neutral allele
Mutation is far too slow to cause a rise like this.
Genetic hitchhiking, since linkage keeps the two alleles together
Correct: linkage keeps the two together, so the neutral allele rides the selective sweep.
questions.x: This is genetic hitchhiking. 'Neutral' means the allele doesn't help or hurt survival at all. 'Tightly linked' means it sits very close to the favored allele on the same chromosome, so crossing over almost never separates them, and they're inherited as one block. When selection pushes the favored allele up in frequency (a selective sweep), the neutral allele rides along. Selection isn't acting on it; it's just stuck to something that's being selected. One side effect: sweeps wipe out a lot of variation near the favored gene.

questions.q: A population has 10 breeding males and 90 breeding females. Using Nₑ = 4(Nm)(Nf)/(Nm + Nf), what is its effective population size?
o: That's the head count of breeders, not Nₑ. An uneven sex ratio makes Nₑ smaller.
This averages the two sexes. The formula multiplies them, so the rarer sex counts a lot.
This is just twice the number of males and leaves the females out.
questions.note: A skewed sex ratio lowers Nₑ and strengthens drift.
questions.x: Effective population size (Nₑ) is the size of an ideal population that would have the same amount of genetic drift as the real one. Formula: Nₑ = 4NₘN_f ÷ (Nₘ + N_f). Values: Nₘ = 10 males, N_f = 90 females. Plug in: 4 × 10 × 90 = 40 × 90 = 3600 on top, and 10 + 90 = 100 on the bottom. Then 3600 ÷ 100 = 36. Every offspring gets half its genes from a father, and only 10 males are passing those on, so the few males drag Nₑ way below the 100 breeders you'd count.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane?
o: Two continuous protein sheets sandwich a central lipid layer
That's the older Davson–Danielli 'sandwich' model, which freeze-fracture images disproved.
Phospholipids flip freely and rapidly between the two leaflets
Flip-flop is slow without flippases. Sideways movement is the fast one.
Proteins are locked in fixed positions by a rigid lipid lattice
The bilayer is fluid, and experiments show many proteins drift sideways.
Lipids and many proteins diffuse laterally within a phospholipid bilayer
Correct: the bilayer acts like a flat liquid where lipids and proteins slide sideways.
questions.note: Fast: lateral diffusion. Slow: flip-flop between leaflets.
questions.x: The fluid mosaic model says the cell membrane behaves like a thin, flat liquid. It's a phospholipid bilayer: two layers of lipids, each layer called a leaflet. Lipids and many proteins slide sideways within their own leaflet, and the proteins are scattered through it like tiles in a mosaic. What lipids don't do easily is flip from one leaflet to the other. That's called flip-flop, and it's slow because the lipid's water-loving head would have to cross the oily middle. Enzymes called flippases speed it up.

questions.q: How does cholesterol affect an animal cell membrane at low temperature?
o: It makes the membrane even more rigid than it would be without it
That's cholesterol's effect at high temperature. In the cold it does the opposite.
It greatly raises the bilayer's permeability to ions
Cholesterol actually lowers permeability to ions and small polar molecules.
It catalyzes rapid flip-flop of phospholipids
Cholesterol isn't an enzyme. Flippases handle flip-flop.
It disrupts tight packing of acyl tails, helping keep the membrane fluid
Correct: its rigid ring wedges between tails and stops them packing into a gel.
questions.note: Cholesterol is a fluidity buffer: less fluid when hot, more fluid when cold.
questions.x: Cholesterol acts like a fluidity buffer: it keeps the membrane from getting too stiff or too loose. In the cold, phospholipid tails want to pack tightly together and turn the membrane into a stiff gel. Cholesterol's flat, rigid ring wedges between the tails and stops that tight packing, so the membrane stays more fluid than it would without it. In the heat, the same ring does the opposite: it holds the tails back and makes the membrane less fluid. The tempting wrong answer describes the hot-temperature effect.

questions.q: Why is spontaneous flip-flop of a phospholipid from one leaflet to the other very slow?
o: Its polar head group would have to pass through the hydrophobic core
Correct: dragging a polar head through the oily core takes a lot of energy.
Phospholipids are covalently bonded to neighboring membrane proteins
Most phospholipids aren't chemically bonded to proteins.
Lateral diffusion is equally slow, so all lipid motion is slow
Sideways diffusion is fast, about a micrometer per second.
The cytoskeleton anchors every phospholipid in place
The cytoskeleton anchors some proteins, not each lipid.
questions.x: A phospholipid has a polar (water-loving) head and oily tails. In the bilayer, the heads face the water on each side and the tails form an oily core in the middle, about 3 nm thick. To flip to the other leaflet, the head would have to drag through that oily core, and that takes a lot of energy. So spontaneous flip-flop is very slow, taking hours to days, unless flippase enzymes help. Sliding sideways is the opposite: the head stays in water the whole time, so it's fast.

questions.q: Uptake of solute X rises with external [X] but levels off at high [X], is unaffected by blocking ATP synthesis, and never builds [X] inside above outside. X enters by:
o: Simple diffusion through the bilayer
Simple diffusion rises in a straight line and never levels off.
Primary active transport
That needs ATP and could pile X up inside.
Secondary active transport
That could push X uphill using an ion gradient, which ATP maintains.
Facilitated diffusion through a carrier
Correct: saturable, needs no energy, and only moves X downhill.
questions.note: Saturation means a protein is involved; no uphill movement means no energy.
questions.x: Read the three clues one at a time. Uptake levels off at high [X]: that means a limited number of protein carriers are all busy (saturation), so it isn't simple diffusion. Blocking ATP changes nothing: no energy is being used, directly or indirectly. X never gets higher inside than outside: it only moves downhill, from high to low concentration. Saturable, no energy, downhill only: that's facilitated diffusion. Secondary active transport also uses a carrier, but it can push X uphill, and it fails once ATP runs out and ion gradients fade.

questions.q: Red blood cells (about 300 mOsm inside) are placed in a 300 mM urea solution. Urea crosses the membrane readily. What happens?
o: Nothing, because the solution is isosmotic
Isosmotic isn't the same as isotonic when the solute can cross the membrane.
The cells shrink and crenate
Shrinking needs a solute that can't get in, at higher concentration outside.
The cells swell and lyse
Correct: urea enters freely, so it can't hold water out, and water follows into the cell.
The cells shrink briefly, then stay smaller
Urea doesn't stay outside, so it can't keep water out of the cell.
questions.note: Tonicity counts only solutes that cannot cross the membrane.
questions.x: Osmolarity counts all dissolved particles. Tonicity counts only the particles that can't cross the membrane, because only those can hold water on one side. The red cells sit at about 300 mOsm, and the solution is 300 mM urea, so the totals match: it's isosmotic. But urea crosses red cell membranes easily. It flows in until it's equal on both sides, so it adds no lasting pull on water. Meanwhile the cell's own trapped solutes keep pulling water in. The cell swells and bursts (lyses). The solution is isosmotic but hypotonic.

questions.q: Intestinal cells absorb glucose against its gradient through a Na⁺–glucose symporter. What is the immediate energy source for this step?
o: The Na⁺ electrochemical gradient across the apical membrane
Correct: Na⁺ moving downhill drives glucose uphill (secondary active transport).
ATP hydrolysis by the symporter itself
The symporter doesn't break down ATP. That would be primary active transport.
The glucose concentration gradient
Glucose is moving against its own gradient, so that can't power it.
The proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane
That gradient runs ATP synthase in mitochondria, not this transporter.
questions.note: ATP is spent indirectly by the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase.
questions.x: The Na⁺–glucose symporter (called SGLT1) carries Na⁺ and glucose into the cell together. Na⁺ is much more concentrated outside the cell, and the inside is negative, so Na⁺ 'wants' to rush in. That downhill rush releases energy, and the symporter uses it to drag glucose in against glucose's own gradient. That's secondary active transport. The symporter never breaks down ATP itself. ATP is used indirectly: the Na⁺/K⁺ pump on the other side of the cell (the basolateral side) spends ATP to keep Na⁺ low inside.

questions.q: A vesicular transporter loads neurotransmitter into synaptic vesicles while H⁺ leaves the vesicle. This transporter is best described as a(n):
o: Symporter performing primary active transport
The two move in opposite directions, and no ATP is used directly.
Uniporter performing facilitated diffusion
It moves two substances, and pushes transmitter uphill.
Antiporter performing secondary active transport
Correct: opposite directions, powered by the H⁺ gradient.
ATP-driven pump
The H⁺ gradient powers it, not ATP broken down by this protein.
questions.x: Sort transporters with two questions. First: which way do things move? Transmitter goes into the vesicle while H⁺ comes out, so they move in opposite directions. That's an antiporter. Second: where does the energy come from? A different protein, a V-type ATPase, spends ATP to pump H⁺ into the vesicle ahead of time. This transporter just uses that H⁺ gradient: H⁺ flows out downhill and drives transmitter in uphill. Using a gradient made by another pump is secondary active transport. It isn't a pump itself, because it doesn't break down ATP.

questions.q: A toxin makes a resting cell's membrane far more permeable to Na⁺ than to any other ion. The membrane potential will move toward:
o: 0 mV, where no ions move
At 0 mV, Na⁺ would still flow in, so 0 mV isn't an equilibrium for Na⁺.
About −90 mV, near E_K
K⁺ is no longer the main ion crossing, so Vm won't stay near E_K.
−70 mV, because the pump fixes Vm
The pump can't hold Vm in place when permeability changes this much.
About +60 mV, near E_Na
Correct: Vm moves toward the equilibrium potential of the most permeable ion.
questions.note: Goldman logic: Vm is a weighted average set by relative permeability.
questions.x: Each ion has an equilibrium potential: the voltage where its concentration push and electrical push cancel out. For Na⁺ (E_Na) that's about +60 mV, and for K⁺ (E_K) about −90 mV. The membrane potential (Vm) gets pulled toward the equilibrium potential of whichever ion crosses most easily. At rest that's K⁺, which is why Vm sits near −70 mV. If a toxin makes Na⁺ by far the most permeable ion, Vm heads toward E_Na, about +60 mV. That's what briefly happens at the peak of an action potential.

questions.q: During a single action potential in a large neuron, intracellular [Na⁺]:
o: Roughly doubles and must be restored before the next spike
One spike moves far too few ions to change bulk concentrations much.
Barely changes, because very few ions must cross to change Vm
Correct: a tiny number of ions crossing changes the voltage a lot.
Becomes equal to extracellular [Na⁺]
The gradient stays nearly intact. Thousands of spikes can fire without the pump.
Falls, because Na⁺ leaves during depolarization
Na⁺ comes in during depolarization, not out.
questions.x: Barely changes. The membrane acts like a tiny capacitor, a thin layer that stores charge on its two sides.
