Only a very thin sheet of ions right next to the membrane has to cross to swing the voltage by about 100 mV. In a large neuron, the Na⁺ that rushes in during one spike is a tiny fraction of the Na⁺ already inside, so the concentration hardly moves. That's why a neuron can fire thousands of spikes even with the Na⁺/K⁺ pump blocked. The pump fixes the small drift slowly, over the long run, not after each spike.

questions.q: A membrane protein is released into solution by a high-salt wash, with no detergent needed. It is most likely a(n):
o: Multipass transmembrane protein
Multipass proteins are buried in the bilayer and need detergent to come out.
Peripheral protein held by ionic interactions
Correct: high salt breaks the charge attractions holding it to the surface.
Protein with a covalent lipid anchor
Its lipid anchor stays stuck in the bilayer, so detergent is needed.
Single-pass transmembrane receptor
Its oily helix keeps it in the bilayer no matter how much salt you add.
questions.note: Salt or pH strips peripheral proteins; integral proteins need detergent.
questions.x: Membrane proteins come in two main kinds. Integral proteins have oily (hydrophobic) parts buried inside the bilayer. Peripheral proteins just sit on the surface, held on by ionic and hydrogen bonds to lipid heads or to other proteins. High salt shields those charges and breaks the attraction, so peripheral proteins come off without harming the bilayer. Anything with a part buried in the oily core, including proteins held by a lipid anchor, stays put. Freeing those takes a detergent, which dissolves the bilayer itself.

questions.q: A small fluorescent dye injected into one cardiac muscle cell quickly appears in neighboring cells. Which junction allows this?
o: Tight junctions
Tight junctions seal the gap between cells. They don't connect the insides.
Desmosomes
Desmosomes hold cells together for strength, with no channel between them.
Hemidesmosomes
Hemidesmosomes attach a cell to the basement membrane, not to a neighbor.
Gap junctions
Correct: connexon channels link cytoplasms and pass ions and small molecules.
questions.x: Gap junctions. They're made of connexons, little channels built from proteins called connexins. A connexon in one cell lines up with one in the cell next door, forming a tunnel that connects the two cytoplasms directly. Ions and small molecules, up to about 1 kDa, pass right through, so a small dye spreads from cell to cell. The same tunnels let electrical signals spread through heart muscle so it beats together. Tight junctions also link cells, but they seal the space between them rather than opening a path from one inside to the other.

questions.q: In a photobleaching experiment, protein X recovers 90% of its fluorescence but protein Y recovers only 30%. The best explanation is that Y:
o: Is a peripheral protein, not an integral one
Peripheral proteins are often quite mobile, so that doesn't predict low recovery.
Is in a more fluid region of the membrane
A more fluid region would make recovery bigger, not smaller.
Is smaller than X
Smaller proteins tend to diffuse faster, which would raise recovery.
Is largely anchored to the cytoskeleton
Correct: tethered molecules can't move in to refill the bleached spot.
questions.x: In FRAP (fluorescence recovery after photobleaching), a laser bleaches the glow out of one spot on the membrane. Then you watch whether glowing proteins from nearby drift in to refill it. How much the spot recovers tells you what share of the protein can move (the mobile fraction). How fast it recovers tells you how quickly they diffuse. X recovers 90%, so most of it moves. Y recovers only 30%, so most Y molecules are stuck, usually because they're tied to the cytoskeleton or another fixed structure.

questions.q: K⁺ channels conduct K⁺ about 1000 times better than the smaller Na⁺ ion because:
o: The pore is too narrow for Na⁺ to fit
Na⁺ is smaller than K⁺, so a pore that's too narrow can't explain it.
Na⁺ carries a larger charge than K⁺
Both ions carry the same +1 charge.
Carbonyl oxygens in the filter fit dehydrated K⁺ but are too far apart for Na⁺
Correct: the filter's oxygens fit a bare K⁺ but are too far apart for Na⁺.
K⁺ channels use ATP to reject Na⁺
Channels are passive. Selectivity comes from the filter's structure.
questions.x: In water, every ion wears a coat of water molecules (a hydration shell). To get through the K⁺ channel's narrowest part, the selectivity filter, an ion has to take that coat off. The filter is lined with carbonyl oxygens (C=O groups from the protein backbone) spaced to hug a bare K⁺ exactly the way water did, so K⁺ loses nothing by swapping. Na⁺ is smaller, so it can't touch all those oxygens at once. Taking off its water would cost energy it doesn't get back, so it stays out. It's about fit, not about the pore being too narrow.

questions.q: After receptor-mediated endocytosis, LDL separates from its receptor in the endosome mainly because:
o: Lysosomal enzymes digest the receptor
Normally the receptor is recycled to the surface, not digested.
The endosome's acidic pH lowers receptor binding affinity
Correct: the endosome's low pH weakens the grip, and the receptor recycles.
The clathrin coat pulls the LDL away
The clathrin coat falls off soon after the vesicle forms.
The endosome is more alkaline than the blood
Endosomes are acidic, not alkaline.
questions.x: LDL (the particle that carries cholesterol in the blood) binds its receptor tightly at the neutral pH of blood. After the cell pulls them in together (receptor-mediated endocytosis), they end up in an endosome, a sorting bubble inside the cell. Pumps in the endosome membrane push H⁺ in, making it acidic. The low pH changes the receptor's shape, so it loosens its grip and lets go of LDL. LDL moves on to a lysosome to be broken down, and the empty receptor is sent back to the surface to be used again.

questions.q: Clathrin knockdown sharply reduces transferrin uptake but leaves uptake of a fluid-phase dye by macropinocytosis unchanged. This suggests that:
o: Transferrin enters by clathrin-mediated endocytosis
Correct: only the clathrin-dependent route was disrupted, and transferrin used it.
Transferrin enters by simple diffusion
A big protein can't diffuse across the bilayer, and its uptake fell without clathrin.
Macropinocytosis requires clathrin
Dye uptake by macropinocytosis didn't change, so it doesn't need clathrin.
All endocytosis requires clathrin
Macropinocytosis kept going without clathrin, so not all routes need it.
questions.x: A knockdown lowers the amount of one protein. If a process stops, it needs that protein. If it keeps going, it doesn't. Clathrin is the protein that forms the coat on one kind of endocytic vesicle. Transferrin (the protein that carries iron in blood) is taken up much less without clathrin, so it enters by clathrin-mediated endocytosis. Dye uptake by macropinocytosis, where the cell gulps big sips of fluid using actin, didn't change, so that route doesn't need clathrin. Cells clearly have more than one way in.

questions.q: Inside-out vesicles containing Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase are prepared in a buffer with Na⁺ and K⁺, and ATP is then added to the outside medium. The pump will move:
o: Na⁺ out of the vesicle and K⁺ into it
That's the normal cell direction. Inside-out vesicles flip it.
Both ions into the vesicle
The pump is an antiporter, so the two ions move in opposite directions.
Nothing, because ATP cannot reach the pump
The ATP-binding face now faces the medium, so the added ATP reaches it.
Na⁺ into the vesicle and K⁺ out into the medium
Correct: the cytoplasmic face now faces the medium, so Na⁺ goes in and K⁺ comes out.
questions.note: Track which face of the pump touches the ATP.
questions.x: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump always works relative to its own two faces. On its cytoplasmic face (the side that normally faces the inside of the cell), it binds ATP and Na⁺ and releases K⁺. On its other face, it releases Na⁺ and picks up K⁺. In an inside-out vesicle, the cytoplasmic face points out toward the medium. So ATP added to the medium can reach it, and the pump grabs Na⁺ from the medium and pushes it into the vesicle, while it moves K⁺ out of the vesicle into the medium. Always ask which side the ATP-binding face is on.

questions.q: Replacing most extracellular Na⁺ with impermeant choline barely changes a neuron's resting potential. This indicates that:
o: Resting membrane permeability to Na⁺ is low
Correct: if Na⁺ barely shapes Vm at rest, taking it away changes little.
Choline is highly permeant at rest
The question says choline is impermeant, so it can't cross.
Na⁺ is the main determinant of resting potential
If Na⁺ ran the show, removing it would make the cell noticeably more negative.
The Na⁺/K⁺ pump stops at low Na⁺
Nothing points to the pump, and it wouldn't explain a steady voltage.
questions.x: The resting potential depends on each ion's gradient, weighted by how easily that ion crosses the membrane (its permeability). That's the idea behind the Goldman equation. At rest, lots of K⁺ channels are open and very few Na⁺ channels are, so K⁺ has a big say and Na⁺ a tiny one. Taking away most of the Na⁺ outside barely moved the voltage, which tells you Na⁺ wasn't contributing much: resting Na⁺ permeability is low. Choline is just a stand-in that can't cross, used to keep the total solute level steady.

questions.q: A protein reconstituted into liposomes moves glucose into them only when the outside has more Na⁺ than the inside. The protein is most likely a:
o: GLUT uniporter
A uniporter moves glucose on its own, with no need for a Na⁺ gradient.
Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase
The Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves Na⁺ and K⁺, not glucose.
Na⁺–glucose symporter
Correct: glucose moves only with an inward Na⁺ gradient, both going the same way.
Glucose-gated ion channel
Ion channels carry ions, and glucose isn't an ion.
questions.x: A liposome is a tiny artificial bubble of lipid with nothing in its membrane except the protein you put there. So whatever rules you see must come from that protein alone. Glucose only moves in when Na⁺ is higher outside, meaning only when Na⁺ can also flow in. So the protein couples the two, moving them in the same direction: a Na⁺–glucose symporter, like SGLT. Na⁺ flowing downhill powers glucose's trip in. A GLUT uniporter would move glucose down its own gradient whether or not there was any Na⁺ gradient.

questions.q: A 90-kDa cytosolic protein moves into the nucleus after a short stretch of basic residues (PKKKRKV) is added to it. This stretch acts as a:
o: Signal sequence for the ER
ER signal sequences are oily (hydrophobic) stretches, usually at the start.
Nuclear localization signal
Correct: importins recognize a short basic stretch and carry cargo through nuclear pores.
Mitochondrial targeting sequence
Mitochondrial signals are helices with one charged face and one oily face.
Nuclear export signal
An export signal would send the protein out of the nucleus, not in.
questions.note: Proteins too large to diffuse through the pore need an NLS.
questions.x: Nuclear pores let small things drift through, but proteins bigger than about 40 to 60 kDa need a pass. That pass is a nuclear localization signal (NLS). The classic NLS is a short run of basic amino acids, lysine (K) and arginine (R). PKKKRKV, from a virus protein called SV40 large T antigen, is the textbook example. Carrier proteins called importins recognize it and escort the cargo through the pore, with energy from a gradient of Ran-GTP. A 90-kDa protein is too big to drift in, so adding the NLS is what got it inside.

questions.q: Cells unable to add mannose-6-phosphate to lysosomal enzymes would most likely:
o: Retain the enzymes in the rough ER
The enzymes leave the ER normally. It's the Golgi sorting step that fails.
Send the enzymes into the nucleus
M6P has nothing to do with getting into the nucleus.
Secrete the enzymes, leaving lysosomes full of undigested material
Correct: untagged enzymes take the default path and are secreted.
Degrade the enzymes in proteasomes immediately
The untagged enzymes fold fine. They're just sent to the wrong place.
questions.note: This is I-cell disease: high lysosomal enzyme levels in the blood.
questions.x: Lysosomes are bags of digestive enzymes. Those enzymes are made in the rough ER, then travel to the Golgi (the cell's sorting center). In the Golgi, they get a tag: mannose-6-phosphate (M6P). Receptors in the trans Golgi grab M6P-tagged enzymes and ship them off to lysosomes. Without the tag, the enzymes take the default route, which is out of the cell. So lysosomes end up with no enzymes and fill with undigested junk, while enzyme levels in the blood rise. That's I-cell disease. Leaving the ER still works fine.

questions.q: Bafilomycin A1 inhibits the V-type H⁺-ATPase. Treated cells would most likely show:
o: Lower lysosomal pH and faster digestion
Blocking the H⁺ pump can't make lysosomes more acidic.
Loss of ATP synthesis in mitochondria
Mitochondria use the F-type ATP synthase, not V-type pumps.
Higher lysosomal pH and slower breakdown of endocytosed proteins
Correct: without H⁺ pumping, lysosomes lose their acid and their enzymes slow down.
Faster mannose-6-phosphate tagging in the Golgi
M6P tagging happens in the Golgi and doesn't depend on lysosome pH.
questions.note: V-type pumps acidify lysosomes and endosomes.
questions.x: A V-type H⁺-ATPase is a pump that spends ATP to push H⁺ (acid) into lysosomes and endosomes, keeping lysosomes around pH 5. The digestive enzymes inside, called acid hydrolases, work best in that acid. Bafilomycin blocks the pump, so H⁺ stops coming in and the pH rises (less acidic). The enzymes slow down, and proteins brought in by endocytosis get broken down more slowly. Mitochondria make ATP with a different machine, the F-type ATP synthase, so they aren't the direct target.

questions.q: A secretory protein's N-terminal signal sequence is deleted. The protein will most likely:
o: Be secreted faster than normal
Without the signal, it can't enter the secretory pathway, so it can't be secreted.
Be sent to the lysosome
Lysosome proteins also have to enter the ER first.
Stay in the cytosol, made on free ribosomes
Correct: with no signal for SRP to grab, translation never moves to the ER.
Insert into the plasma membrane
Getting into the plasma membrane also starts with ER entry.
questions.x: The signal sequence is a short stretch at the start (N-terminus) of a protein that says 'send me to the ER'. As it comes out of the ribosome, a particle called SRP (signal recognition particle) grabs it and steers the whole ribosome to the rough ER, where the protein is fed inside. Delete the signal and SRP has nothing to grab, so the ribosome stays free in the cytosol and the protein ends up there. Every route through the secretory pathway, whether to secretion, lysosomes or the plasma membrane, starts with getting into the ER.

questions.q: N-linked glycosylation of a secreted protein begins in the:
o: Lumen of the rough ER
Correct: a premade sugar chain is added to asparagine as the protein enters the ER.
Golgi apparatus
The Golgi trims N-linked sugars and adds O-linked ones, but doesn't start N-linked.
Cytosol
Secreted proteins get their sugars inside the ER, not in the cytosol.
Lysosome
Lysosomes break sugars down; they don't add them.
questions.x: Glycosylation means attaching sugar chains to a protein. In N-linked glycosylation, the sugars attach to the nitrogen (N) on the side chain of asparagine. It starts in the lumen (inside space) of the rough ER. An enzyme called oligosaccharyltransferase moves a ready-made chain of 14 sugars onto asparagines that sit in an Asn-X-Ser/Thr sequence, often while the protein is still being made. The Golgi later trims and remodels those sugars and adds O-linked sugars. That's why the Golgi is tempting, but it doesn't start N-linked ones.

questions.q: An ER-resident chaperone loses its C-terminal KDEL retrieval sequence. It will most likely:
o: Stay in the ER, unaffected
KDEL is needed to bring back the copies that leak to the Golgi.
Move into the nucleus
Losing KDEL doesn't create a signal for the nucleus.
Be secreted from the cell
Correct: without KDEL, it isn't brought back from the Golgi and gets secreted.
Be degraded in the cytosol right after synthesis
It still enters the ER through its signal sequence.
questions.note: Secretion is the default for lumenal proteins with no other signal.
questions.x: Some soluble proteins that belong in the ER, like the chaperone BiP, keep leaking forward to the Golgi with everything else. To get them back, they carry a 'return' tag at their C-terminal end: the four amino acids KDEL. KDEL receptors in the early (cis) Golgi grab any protein with that tag and ship it back to the ER in COPI vesicles. Without KDEL, the leaked chaperone isn't returned, so it follows the default route for soluble proteins in the pathway: out of the cell. KDEL doesn't hold proteins in the ER; it brings back escapees.

questions.q: Most proteins inside mitochondria are:
o: Encoded by nuclear genes, made in the cytosol and then imported
Correct: mtDNA codes only a few proteins; the rest are imported through TOM/TIM.
Encoded by mitochondrial DNA and made in the matrix
Human mtDNA codes only 13 proteins, a tiny share of what mitochondria need.
Made on the rough ER and delivered by vesicles
Mitochondria aren't part of the ER-to-Golgi vesicle system.
Taken up from the blood by endocytosis
Mitochondrial proteins are made inside the cell, not taken from the blood.
questions.x: Mitochondria have their own small DNA (mtDNA), but in humans it codes for only 13 proteins, all parts of the electron transport chain, plus some rRNAs and tRNAs. The other 1,000 or so mitochondrial proteins are coded by genes in the nucleus. They're made on free ribosomes in the cytosol, then pulled into the mitochondrion through protein channels called TOM (in the outer membrane) and TIM (in the inner membrane), usually guided by a targeting sequence at their start. Mitochondria don't get proteins by vesicles from the ER.

questions.q: In hepatocytes, the final step that releases free glucose from glucose-6-phosphate occurs in the:
o: Mitochondrial matrix
Gluconeogenesis starts in the matrix, but this last step happens elsewhere.
Cytosol, by a soluble phosphatase
G6P has to be moved into the ER. The enzyme sits in the ER membrane.
Lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum
Correct: glucose-6-phosphatase sits in the ER membrane with its active site in the lumen.
Peroxisome
Peroxisomes don't release glucose.
questions.x: Glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) is glucose with a phosphate attached, and that phosphate traps it inside the cell. To send glucose out into the blood, the liver has to cut the phosphate off. The enzyme that does it, glucose-6-phosphatase, sits in the ER membrane with its working end facing the ER lumen (the inside space). A transporter moves G6P into the ER, the phosphate is removed there, and the free glucose then leaves the cell through GLUT2. Gluconeogenesis does start in the mitochondria, but this last step happens in the ER.

questions.q: Brown fat produces heat because its mitochondria contain a protein that:
o: Blocks electron transport at complex IV
Blocking electron flow would stop both heat and ATP production.
Lets H⁺ flow back into the matrix without passing through ATP synthase
Correct: thermogenin lets H⁺ bypass ATP synthase, so the energy becomes heat.
Speeds ATP synthase to make extra ATP
Uncoupling lowers ATP output. The energy is released as heat.
Pumps H⁺ out of the intermembrane space using ATP
The heat comes from H⁺ leaking back in, not from pumping it out.
questions.x: Normally, the electron transport chain pumps H⁺ out of the matrix, building up a gradient. H⁺ flows back in through ATP synthase, and that flow makes ATP. Brown fat mitochondria have an extra protein, thermogenin (also called UCP1), that opens a side path: H⁺ flows back into the matrix without going through ATP synthase. The gradient's energy then comes out as heat instead of ATP. This is called uncoupling. The chain actually runs faster, because the gradient never builds up enough to slow it down.

questions.q: Unlike microtubules and actin filaments, intermediate filaments:
o: Lack polarity and are not used as tracks by motor proteins
Correct: their subunits line up in opposite directions, so the filament has no direction.
Are built from globular subunits that bind GTP
Globular subunits that bind GTP describes tubulin in microtubules.
Turn over rapidly by dynamic instability
Intermediate filaments are the most stable cytoskeletal fibers, not the fastest-changing.
Drive cell crawling by polymerizing at the leading edge
Actin polymerizing at the front edge is what drives cell crawling.
questions.x: The cytoskeleton has three kinds of fibers: microtubules, actin filaments, and intermediate filaments. Intermediate filament subunits pair up, and then two pairs line up facing opposite ways (antiparallel). Because of that, both ends of the filament look the same: there's no plus end or minus end. Motor proteins need a direction to walk, so they can't use intermediate filaments as tracks. Intermediate filaments also don't bind GTP or ATP, and they're very stable, acting like ropes that resist pulling. GTP and dynamic instability belong to microtubules.

questions.q: Paclitaxel (Taxol) stabilizes microtubules and prevents them from shrinking. It blocks cell division mainly because:
o: It prevents tubulin from polymerizing at all
Blocking assembly is how colchicine works. Paclitaxel stabilizes microtubules instead.
It breaks down actin in the contractile ring
Paclitaxel targets tubulin, not actin.
Spindle microtubules must shorten to pull sister chromatids apart
Correct: frozen spindle microtubules can't shorten to pull chromatids apart.
It stops DNA replication in S phase
Its block is in mitosis, not in DNA copying.
questions.x: Microtubules are constantly growing and shrinking, which is called dynamic instability, and mitosis depends on it. In anaphase, the microtubules attached to chromosomes (at a spot called the kinetochore) shorten, pulling the sister chromatids (the two identical copies of each chromosome) to opposite ends of the cell. Paclitaxel locks microtubules in place so they can't shrink. The spindle can't pull, and the cell gets stuck in mitosis. Colchicine and vinca drugs do the opposite, blocking microtubules from forming, but they cause the same mitotic arrest.

questions.q: Plant cells lack centrioles yet still build working mitotic spindles. This shows that:
o: Plant spindles are made of actin
Plant spindles are made of microtubules too.
Plant cells separate chromosomes without microtubules
Plant mitosis still uses a microtubule spindle.
Centrioles are needed only in prokaryotes
Prokaryotes don't have centrioles at all.
Centrioles are not required to nucleate spindle microtubules
Correct: other organizing centers can start spindle microtubules without centrioles.
questions.x: Centrioles are small barrel-shaped structures found in the centrosomes of animal cells. A microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) is any spot that starts new microtubules growing, using a protein called γ-tubulin. Plant cells have no centrioles, but they still build normal spindles out of microtubules, started by γ-tubulin at other MTOCs, like the surface of the nucleus. So centrioles aren't required to start spindle microtubules. Even animal cells can build a spindle if their centrioles are removed. Plant spindles are still made of microtubules, just like animal ones.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts bacterial flagella with sperm flagella?
o: Both are built from tubulin in a 9 + 2 arrangement
Bacterial flagella are made of flagellin, not tubulin.
Sperm flagella rotate; bacterial flagella whip back and forth
This swaps them: bacterial flagella rotate, sperm flagella bend.
Bacterial flagella rotate using a H⁺ gradient; sperm flagella bend using dynein and ATP
Correct: the bacterial motor spins using H⁺ flow; the sperm tail bends using dynein and ATP.
Both are powered directly by ATP hydrolysis at the base
The bacterial motor runs on H⁺ flowing in, not directly on ATP.
questions.x: Bacterial flagella and sperm flagella share a name but not much else; they evolved separately. A bacterial flagellum is a stiff, corkscrew-shaped filament made of a protein called flagellin. A rotary motor at its base spins it like a propeller, powered by H⁺ (sometimes Na⁺) flowing into the cell. A sperm flagellum is a bundle of microtubules in a '9 + 2' pattern (nine pairs around two in the middle), called the axoneme. The motor protein dynein uses ATP to slide neighboring pairs past each other, which makes the whole tail bend in waves.

questions.q: Mutations in keratins 5 and 14 cause basal skin cells to tear apart with minor friction. This shows that intermediate filaments mainly:
o: Give cells tensile strength against mechanical stress
Correct: keratin networks hooked into desmosomes spread out mechanical force.
Move vesicles to the cell surface
Moving vesicles is done by motor proteins on microtubules.
Form the contractile ring in cytokinesis
The contractile ring is made of actin and myosin.
Seal the paracellular space
Tight junction proteins seal the space between cells.
questions.x: Intermediate filaments are the cell's ropes: they help it stand up to pulling and rubbing. Keratins are the intermediate filaments in skin cells. In the bottom (basal) layer of skin, keratins 5 and 14 form a tough network that hooks into desmosomes (rivets between neighboring cells) and hemidesmosomes (rivets to the layer below). That spreads any force across the whole tissue instead of letting it tear one cell. When these keratins are mutated, in a disease called epidermolysis bullosa simplex, cells break open and the skin blisters from minor friction.

questions.q: Carcinoma cells that lose E-cadherin expression are more likely to metastasize mainly because:
o: They detach more easily from neighboring cells
Correct: E-cadherin holds epithelial cells together, so losing it lets them break free.
They stop dividing
Losing cadherin doesn't stop cells from dividing.
They lose all integrins
Integrins are a separate system, and E-cadherin loss doesn't remove them.
They form more gap junctions
Gap junctions aren't what keeps cells from escaping.
questions.x: E-cadherin is the main 'glue' protein holding epithelial cells to each other. It forms adherens junctions between neighbors and, inside the cell, links to actin through helper proteins called catenins. When carcinoma cells lose E-cadherin, they let go of their neighbors, get more mobile, and can wander off into other tissues. This change is part of what's called the epithelial–mesenchymal transition. Losing cadherin doesn't slow cell division, and integrins, which grip the surrounding matrix instead of other cells, are a separate system.

questions.q: In kidney tubule cells, the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is located mainly on which surface?
o: Basolateral membrane
Correct: pumping Na⁺ toward the blood keeps cell Na⁺ low, so more flows in from the urine.
Apical membrane
A pump on the apical side would push Na⁺ back into the urine.
Tight junctions
Tight junctions seal the gaps between cells and hold no pumps.
Nuclear envelope
The pump works in the plasma membrane, not around the nucleus.
questions.x: Kidney tubule cells have two different sides. The apical side faces the tubular fluid (the urine being made). The basolateral side faces the blood. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase sits on the basolateral side. It pumps Na⁺ out of the cell toward the blood, which keeps Na⁺ inside the cell low. That low inside level gives Na⁺ in the urine a downhill path into the cell through channels and symporters on the apical side. Net result: Na⁺ moves from urine to blood. A pump on the apical side would just shove Na⁺ back into the urine.

questions.q: Glycine must occupy every third position in a collagen chain because:
o: It forms the disulfide bonds that link the chains
Glycine has no sulfur. Cysteine makes disulfide bonds.
It is the residue that vitamin C hydroxylates
Vitamin C helps add OH groups to proline and lysine, not glycine.
Its tiny side chain fits in the crowded center of the triple helix
Correct: only glycine's tiny side chain fits in the crowded center of the helix.
Its charged side chain binds water
Glycine's side chain is a single hydrogen, not charged.
questions.x: Collagen is three protein chains twisted tightly into a triple helix. Its sequence repeats as Gly-X-Y: glycine, then two other amino acids (often proline and hydroxyproline). Because of how the chains twist, every third residue points straight into the crowded center where the three chains meet. Only glycine fits there, because its side chain is just a single hydrogen atom, the smallest possible. Swap one of those glycines for a bigger amino acid, and the helix can't wind tightly. That kind of mutation causes osteogenesis imperfecta, or 'brittle bone disease'.

questions.q: Tumor cells that overexpress matrix metalloproteinases tend to be more invasive because they:
o: Make more collagen to wall themselves off
MMPs break collagen down; they don't make it.
Degrade the basement membrane and surrounding matrix
Correct: cutting through the basement membrane and matrix lets cells move into nearby tissue.
Strengthen their own adherens junctions
MMPs act on the matrix, and stronger adhesion would make cells less invasive.
Speed up DNA repair
MMPs are protein-cutting enzymes outside the cell, not DNA repair enzymes.
questions.x: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) are enzymes, using zinc, that cut up collagen and other proteins in the extracellular matrix, the mesh around cells. That includes the basement membrane, a thin sheet mostly made of type IV collagen that sits under epithelial cells and acts like a fence. A carcinoma has to break through that fence to invade. So tumor cells making lots of MMPs can cut their way out into nearby tissue and blood vessels. Building more matrix or gripping neighbors more tightly would hold tumor cells in, not help them spread.

questions.q: Which part of a typical neuron is specialized mainly for receiving synaptic input from other cells?
o: Dendrites
Correct: dendrites are covered in receptors and collect incoming signals.
Axon terminals
Axon terminals are the sending end. They release neurotransmitter, they don't receive it.
Axon hillock
The hillock adds up inputs and starts the spike, but it isn't the main receiving surface.
Nodes of Ranvier
Nodes of Ranvier are gaps in the myelin where the signal gets boosted along the axon.
questions.x: Dendrites are the receiving end of a neuron. Signals in a neuron travel one way: they come in at the dendrites and the cell body, get added up at the axon hillock, travel down the axon, and leave from the axon terminals. Dendrites branch out like a tree, which gives them lots of surface covered in receptors (proteins that catch incoming neurotransmitter). The axon hillock is the tempting wrong answer, because it handles the incoming signals too. But its job is to add them up and decide whether to fire, not to collect them.

questions.q: A neuron receives many small excitatory and inhibitory inputs. Where is the decision to fire an action potential normally made?
o: At each dendritic spine independently
Spines make small local voltage bumps. They don't make the all-or-none firing decision.
At the axon hillock/initial segment, which has a high density of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
Correct: the summed inputs reach threshold here, where voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are densest.
At the axon terminal, where Ca²⁺ channels open
Terminals respond to a spike that already fired. They don't start it.
At the nucleus, which controls membrane voltage
The nucleus runs gene expression, not split-second electrical decisions.
questions.note: Trap: the soma integrates, but the trigger zone is the axon hillock.
questions.x: The decision to fire happens at the axon hillock, also called the initial segment, where the axon leaves the cell body. Inputs on the dendrites are small graded potentials: little voltage bumps that can be up (excitatory) or down (inhibitory) and fade as they spread. They all flow toward the hillock and add up there. The hillock is packed with voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, so it has the lowest threshold. If the total reaches threshold, an all-or-none action potential starts right there. A single dendritic spine only makes a small local bump, so it can't decide anything alone.

questions.q: The extracellular K⁺ concentration around a neuron is experimentally raised. What happens to the resting membrane potential?
o: It becomes more negative (hyperpolarizes)
More outside K⁺ means less K⁺ leaks out, so the cell gets less negative, not more.
It does not change because the pump compensates
The pump can't cancel a change in the K⁺ equilibrium potential.
It becomes less negative (depolarizes)
Correct: a smaller K⁺ gradient makes E_K less negative, and the resting potential follows it.
It reverses to about +60 mV
+60 mV is about E_Na. The cell is still dominated by K⁺, so it just moves toward 0.
questions.note: EK shifts with [K⁺]out, so resting Vm tracks extracellular K⁺.
questions.x: At rest, the membrane leaks mostly K⁺, so the resting potential sits close to the K⁺ equilibrium potential (E_K), the voltage where K⁺ stops moving overall. K⁺ normally leaks out because there's much more of it inside. Raise K⁺ outside and that gradient shrinks, so less K⁺ leaks out and the inside loses less positive charge. E_K becomes less negative, and the resting potential follows it toward 0. That's depolarization. This is why high blood K⁺ (hyperkalemia) is dangerous for the heart. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump can't undo it, because the pump doesn't change E_K.

questions.q: During the absolute refractory period, no second action potential can be fired no matter how strong the stimulus. What is the cause?
o: The neuron has run out of releasable neurotransmitter
Running out of neurotransmitter affects the synapse, not whether the axon can fire.
The Na⁺ concentration gradient has been abolished
One spike moves very few ions, so the Na⁺ gradient is basically unchanged.
Voltage-gated K⁺ channels are inactivated and closed
K⁺ channels are open at this point. That's what brings the voltage back down.
Most voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are inactivated and cannot reopen yet
Correct: inactivated Na⁺ channels must reset at a negative voltage before they can open again.
questions.x: The cause is Na⁺ channel inactivation. When voltage-gated Na⁺ channels (channels that open at a certain voltage) open during a spike, each one quickly gets plugged by an inactivation gate. That plug won't reset until the membrane goes back to a negative voltage. While most Na⁺ channels are plugged, no stimulus, however strong, can start another spike. That's the absolute refractory period. It's not about running out of anything: one spike moves so few ions that the Na⁺ gradient barely changes.

questions.q: A stimulus applied during the relative refractory period can trigger an action potential only if it is larger than normal. Why?
o: All Na⁺ channels are inactivated, so a larger stimulus forces them open
If every Na⁺ channel were inactivated, nothing would work. That's the absolute period.
The membrane is hyperpolarized and extra K⁺ channels are still open, so more depolarization is needed
Correct: open K⁺ channels fight depolarization, and some Na⁺ channels are still inactivated.
The threshold voltage rises to about +30 mV
Threshold rises only a little. It doesn't climb anywhere near the +30 mV peak.
Myelin temporarily blocks current at that site
Myelin doesn't change during the refractory period.
questions.x: In the relative refractory period, some Na⁺ channels have reset and could open again. But lots of K⁺ channels are still open, letting positive K⁺ leave, and the cell is often hyperpolarized (more negative than its usual rest). So the cell starts farther from threshold, and the leaking K⁺ fights any push upward. A bigger stimulus than normal can still get it there. If all the Na⁺ channels were still inactivated, no stimulus would work at all, and that's the absolute refractory period instead.

questions.q: Many neurons briefly become more negative than resting potential right after an action potential. What causes this afterhyperpolarization?
o: Voltage-gated K⁺ channels close slowly, so K⁺ permeability stays elevated
Correct: K⁺ keeps leaving through slow-closing channels, pulling the voltage toward E_K.
The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase moves 3 K⁺ into the cell per cycle
The pump moves 2 K⁺ in and 3 Na⁺ out, and it isn't the main cause.
Na⁺ channels open a second time
Na⁺ coming in would make the cell more positive, not more negative.
Cl⁻ is pumped out of the cell
Cl⁻ leaving would make the inside more positive, and it isn't the mechanism here.
questions.x: Afterhyperpolarization comes from slow K⁺ channels. The voltage-gated K⁺ channels that bring the voltage back down after a spike open late and close slowly. So for a few milliseconds, K⁺ can leave even more easily than at rest. That pulls the voltage closer to E_K, the K⁺ equilibrium potential, which is below the normal resting value. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump is the tempting wrong answer, but it moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in, and its direct effect on voltage is small and slow.

questions.q: Two unmyelinated axons differ only in diameter. Why does the wider axon conduct action potentials faster?
o: It has a more negative resting potential
Axon width doesn't set the resting potential.
It has a higher threshold, so it fires less often
Threshold doesn't decide how fast the signal travels.
It contains more mitochondria to power the spike
The spike runs on ion gradients, not directly on ATP from mitochondria.
Its larger cross-section lowers internal resistance, so current spreads farther along the axon
Correct: lower internal resistance lets current spread farther, so the next patch fires sooner.
questions.note: Speed up conduction two ways: wider axon or myelin.
questions.x: A spike travels because current flowing inside the axon spreads ahead and brings the next patch of membrane to threshold. The farther that current spreads before it fades, the faster the signal moves. A wider axon has more room inside, so there's less internal (axial) resistance, meaning less to fight the current. Current reaches farther down the axon and triggers distant membrane sooner. Diameter doesn't set the resting potential or the threshold, and the spike is powered by ion gradients, not directly by ATP.

questions.q: A neuromuscular preparation is bathed in Ca²⁺-free solution, and the motor nerve is stimulated. Nerve action potentials are recorded normally. What happens at the muscle?
o: It contracts more strongly because Ca²⁺ normally inhibits release
Ca²⁺ is needed for release. It doesn't hold release back.
It contracts normally because the nerve still fires
The nerve fires, but without Ca²⁺ coming in, no transmitter gets released.
It fails to contract because acetylcholine is not released
Correct: ACh release needs outside Ca²⁺ flowing into the nerve terminal.
It contracts continuously because acetylcholinesterase is inactive
Acetylcholinesterase doesn't need outside Ca²⁺, and no ACh is released anyway.
questions.note: The nerve fires, but the synapse fails without Ca²⁺.
questions.x: The muscle won't contract. The nerve still fires normally because the action potential in the axon runs on Na⁺ and K⁺, not Ca²⁺. But when the spike reaches the nerve terminal, voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open, and Ca²⁺ flowing in from outside is what makes vesicles (little sacs of neurotransmitter) release acetylcholine (ACh). With no Ca²⁺ outside, nothing flows in, no ACh is released, and the muscle never gets the message. So the step that needs Ca²⁺ is the synapse, not the axon.

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter do most postganglionic sympathetic neurons release onto their target organs?
o: Acetylcholine
Preganglionic fibers release ACh. Most sympathetic postganglionic fibers don't.
Norepinephrine
Correct: most sympathetic postganglionic fibers release norepinephrine.
Epinephrine
Epinephrine is mostly a hormone from the adrenal medulla, not a nerve-ending transmitter.
Dopamine
Dopamine is a building block for norepinephrine, not the main transmitter released here.
questions.note: Exception: sympathetic fibers to sweat glands release ACh.
questions.x: Most sympathetic postganglionic neurons release norepinephrine. The autonomic nervous system uses a two-neuron chain. The first neuron (preganglionic) releases acetylcholine (ACh) in a ganglion, a cluster of nerve cell bodies. The second neuron (postganglionic) runs to the organ, and in the sympathetic system it usually releases norepinephrine. Epinephrine is the tempting wrong answer because of fight or flight, but it's mostly a hormone that the adrenal medulla pours into the blood. One exception to know: sympathetic fibers to sweat glands release ACh.

questions.q: Acetylcholine excites skeletal muscle but inhibits cardiac pacemaker cells. What best explains these opposite effects?
o: Acetylcholine is converted to norepinephrine in the heart
ACh is broken down into choline and acetate, not turned into norepinephrine.
The heart releases more acetylcholinesterase
Faster breakdown would shorten the effect, not reverse it.
Skeletal muscle has a more negative resting potential
Resting potential doesn't explain excitation versus inhibition here.
The two tissues express different receptor types linked to different responses
Correct: the receptor, not the transmitter, decides whether a cell is excited or inhibited.
questions.x: A neurotransmitter isn't excitatory or inhibitory by itself. What it does depends on the receptor it binds. Skeletal muscle has nicotinic receptors, which are ion channels that let positive ions in and excite the cell. Heart pacemaker cells have M2 muscarinic receptors, which work through a G protein (Gi) to open K⁺ channels. K⁺ leaving makes the cell more negative, so it fires more slowly. Changing how fast ACh is broken down would change how long the effect lasts, not flip it from excite to inhibit.

questions.q: Ouabain irreversibly blocks the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Over the next several hours, what happens to an isolated neuron's resting potential?
o: It immediately becomes strongly positive
The pump adds only a few millivolts directly, and the gradients fade slowly.
It hyperpolarizes as Na⁺ accumulates outside
Without the pump, Na⁺ builds up inside the cell, not outside.
It slowly depolarizes as the Na⁺ and K⁺ gradients run down
Correct: leaks keep running without the pump, so the gradients and E_K slowly collapse.
It stays exactly the same because leak channels set Vm
Leak channels only work because the pump keeps the gradients up.
questions.note: The pump's main role is keeping gradients, not directly setting Vm.
questions.x: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in. Its direct effect on voltage is only a few millivolts. Its real job is keeping the Na⁺ and K⁺ gradients (the differences between inside and outside) in place. Ouabain blocks it, but the leak channels keep working: Na⁺ keeps drifting in and K⁺ keeps drifting out. Over hours, K⁺ inside falls and Na⁺ inside rises, so E_K becomes less negative and the cell slowly depolarizes. Nothing happens instantly, because the gradients take time to run down.

questions.q: Chloride is about 10 times more concentrated outside a neuron than inside. Using the Nernst equation (61 mV per decade), what is ECl?
o: About +61 mV
Right size, wrong sign. Cl⁻ is negative, so z = −1 flips +61 to −61.
About −61 mV
About −6 mV
log(10) is 1, so the answer is 61 mV in size, not 6.1 mV.
About +122 mV
There's no factor of 2 here, and the sign should be negative for Cl⁻.
questions.note: Anion higher outside → negative equilibrium potential.
questions.x: Use the Nernst equation, which gives the voltage that exactly balances one ion's concentration gradient. Formula: E = (61 mV ÷ z) × log([out]/[in]). Values: Cl⁻ has charge z = −1, and [out]/[in] = 10. Plug in: E = (61 ÷ −1) × log(10). log just reads off the exponent of 10, so log(10) = log(10¹) = 1. That gives E = −61 × 1 = −61 mV. The negative charge flips the sign; forgetting it gives +61 mV.

questions.q: In a voltage-clamp experiment, a depolarizing step produces an early inward current followed by a sustained outward current. Adding tetraethylammonium (TEA) abolishes only the outward current. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: The outward current is carried by K⁺ through voltage-gated channels
Correct: TEA blocks K⁺ channels, so the late outward current is K⁺ leaving.
The inward current is carried by K⁺
The early inward current survived TEA. In neurons it's Na⁺ coming in, not K⁺.
TEA blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
The early inward Na⁺ current was untouched, so TEA didn't block Na⁺ channels.
The outward current is caused by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump
Pump currents are tiny and aren't blocked by TEA.
questions.x: The outward current is K⁺ leaving through voltage-gated K⁺ channels. A voltage clamp holds the membrane at a set voltage and measures the current that flows. When you step the voltage up, Na⁺ channels open first, and Na⁺ rushing in gives the early inward current. Then slower K⁺ channels open, and K⁺ flowing out gives the late outward current. TEA (tetraethylammonium) is a K⁺ channel blocker, so if TEA wipes out only the outward current, that current must be K⁺. The early inward current survived, which fits Na⁺, blocked by a different drug, TTX.

questions.q: Myelin increases conduction velocity partly because it changes the electrical properties of the internodal membrane. Which change is correct?
o: Membrane resistance decreases and capacitance increases
That's backward. It would make the internode leakier and slower to charge.
Both resistance and capacitance increase
Thicker insulation lowers capacitance, like moving capacitor plates apart.
Membrane resistance increases and capacitance decreases
Correct: less current leaks out and less charge is needed to change voltage.
Internal axial resistance increases
Myelin doesn't change resistance inside the axon. That depends on diameter.
questions.x: Myelin raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance. Myelin is many layers of fatty membrane wrapped around the axon. Resistance is how hard it is for current to pass through, so more layers mean higher resistance and less current leaking out. Capacitance is how much charge the membrane has to store to change its voltage. Thicker insulation is like pulling a capacitor's two plates farther apart, so capacitance drops. Less leak and less charge needed both let current spread farther and charge the next node faster. Axial resistance, inside the axon, depends on diameter, not myelin.

questions.q: In the stretch reflex, the quadriceps contracts while the hamstrings relax. How does the hamstring motor neuron become inhibited?
o: The spindle afferent releases GABA directly onto the hamstring motor neuron
Sensory afferents release glutamate and excite. Inhibition needs an interneuron in between.
The quadriceps motor neuron releases glycine onto the hamstrings
Motor neurons release ACh onto muscle, not glycine onto other neurons.
The brain sends a voluntary relaxation command
Reciprocal inhibition is a spinal reflex. The brain doesn't need to send anything.
The spindle afferent excites an inhibitory interneuron that synapses on the hamstring motor neuron
Correct: the afferent excites an inhibitory interneuron that quiets the hamstring motor neuron.
questions.note: An afferent can't inhibit directly; it needs an inhibitory interneuron.
questions.x: Sensory neurons (afferents) can only excite; they release glutamate. So to shut off the opposing muscle, the spindle afferent excites a small inhibitory interneuron in the spinal cord. That interneuron releases glycine onto the hamstring motor neuron and quiets it. This is called reciprocal inhibition: the quadriceps contracts and the hamstrings relax so they don't fight each other. It all happens in the spinal cord, with no command from the brain.

questions.q: Sympathetic fibers to eccrine sweat glands are an exception to the usual autonomic pattern. What is unusual about them?
o: Their postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors
Correct: they're sympathetic in origin but release ACh onto muscarinic receptors.
They have no preganglionic neuron
They still use the normal two-neuron chain, preganglionic neuron included.
They release epinephrine directly into sweat
Sweat glands are switched on by a transmitter, not by epinephrine released into sweat.
They originate from the sacral spinal cord
Sacral outflow is parasympathetic. These come from the thoracolumbar cord.
questions.x: Sympathetic fibers to sweat glands break the usual rule. Most sympathetic postganglionic neurons (the second neuron in the two-neuron chain) release norepinephrine. But the ones going to eccrine sweat glands release acetylcholine (ACh) onto muscarinic receptors. They're still sympathetic: they leave the thoracic and lumbar spinal cord and use the normal two-neuron chain. That's why atropine, a drug that blocks muscarinic receptors, cuts down sweating and can make people overheat.

questions.q: Pressing on a closed eye can make a person "see" flashes of light even though no light enters. What principle does this illustrate?
o: The perceived modality depends on which pathway is activated, not on the stimulus type
Correct: any signal on the optic pathway gets read as light, whatever caused it.
Photoreceptors respond only to pressure
Photoreceptors respond best to light. Pressure is just an unusual way to set them off.
Sensory adaptation
Adaptation is a fading response to a steady stimulus. That isn't what's happening.
Mechanoreceptors in the eye convert pressure to light
No receptor makes light. The brain interprets the signal as light.
questions.x: This shows labeled-line coding. Each sense has its own pathway into the brain, and the brain reads any activity on that pathway as that sense, no matter what set it off. Pressing on the eye squeezes the retina and fires off signals along the optic pathway. The brain only knows that the light line is active, so you see flashes of light, called phosphenes. No light came in, and nothing in the eye makes light. The sensation comes from which line is active, not from what kind of stimulus caused it.

questions.q: After a complete spinal cord transection at the mid-thoracic level and recovery from spinal shock, what is expected for the legs?
o: Voluntary movement and sensation are lost, but spinal stretch reflexes still occur
Correct: the reflex arcs below the cut still work without the brain.
Voluntary movement returns but reflexes are lost
That's backward. The motor tracts are cut, so voluntary movement is what's lost.
Both reflexes and voluntary movement remain normal
Voluntary movement needs the tracts that were cut.
Arm movement is lost but leg movement is preserved
A mid-back cut is below the arm nerves, so the arms are spared.
questions.x: Cutting the spinal cord completely in the mid-back severs the tracts that carry sensation up to the brain and movement commands down from it. So the legs lose feeling and voluntary movement. But the reflex arcs for the legs run through the lower spinal cord on their own: sensor to cord to muscle, no brain needed. Once spinal shock wears off (a temporary period when everything below the cut goes quiet), stretch reflexes come back, often stronger than normal because the brain no longer calms them down. The arms are fine, since their nerves leave the cord above the cut.

questions.q: A patient has weakness, muscle atrophy and absent reflexes in one arm. Damage to which structure best explains this pattern?
o: Upper motor neurons in the motor cortex
Upper motor neuron damage usually gives stiffness and brisk reflexes, not absent ones.
The cerebellum
Cerebellar damage causes clumsiness, not muscle wasting and lost reflexes.
Lower motor neurons in the ventral horn or their axons
Correct: losing the last link to muscle gives limp weakness, atrophy and no reflexes.
Dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons only
Losing sensation alone wouldn't cause weakness and wasting.
questions.x: This points to the lower motor neurons. Their cell bodies sit in the ventral (front) horn of the spinal cord, and their axons run straight to the muscle. They're the last link, the only way to tell a muscle to contract. Lose them and the muscle goes limp and weak, shrinks from lack of nerve input (atrophy), and has no reflexes, because the reflex arc's output wire is gone. Upper motor neuron damage, in the brain, looks different: stiff muscles and brisk reflexes, because the lower motor neurons are still there and lose the brain's calming signals.

questions.q: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies reduce the number of functional nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction. Why do acetylcholinesterase inhibitors improve strength?
o: They let acetylcholine persist longer, increasing binding to the remaining receptors
Correct: ACh lasts longer, so it binds the remaining receptors more often.
They create new nicotinic receptors
These drugs don't change how many receptors there are.
They remove the antibodies from the end plate
They act on an enzyme, not on the antibodies or the immune system.
They block muscarinic receptors on skeletal muscle
Skeletal muscle uses nicotinic receptors, not muscarinic ones.
questions.x: In myasthenia gravis, the immune system makes antibodies that block and destroy nicotinic receptors on muscle, the receptors acetylcholine (ACh) binds to make the muscle contract. With fewer receptors, the signal can fall short, especially with repeated use. Acetylcholinesterase is the enzyme that breaks ACh down. Blocking it with a drug like pyridostigmine lets ACh hang around longer, so each molecule gets more chances to bind the receptors that are left. That makes the signal stronger. It treats the symptoms but doesn't add receptors or stop the antibodies.

questions.q: Most organs receive both sympathetic and parasympathetic input. Which target is controlled mainly by the sympathetic division alone?
o: The heart
The heart gets both: the vagus nerve slows it and sympathetic nerves speed it up.
Most systemic blood vessels
Correct: vessel width is set by turning sympathetic firing up or down.
The iris of the eye
The iris has a sympathetic dilator muscle and a parasympathetic sphincter muscle.
The salivary glands
Salivary glands get input from both divisions.
questions.x: Most blood vessels get sympathetic nerves and little or no parasympathetic input. The body controls how wide they are with just that one signal. More sympathetic firing onto α₁ receptors squeezes the vessels narrower (constriction). Less firing lets them relax and widen (dilation). The heart, the iris of the eye and the salivary glands all get input from both divisions. The heart is the tempting pick because it's the famous autonomic organ, but the vagus nerve slows it, so it isn't sympathetic-only.

questions.q: In untreated type 1 diabetes, ketone bodies accumulate in the blood. What is the reason?
o: High insulin drives fat synthesis into ketones
Insulin is missing in type 1 diabetes, and insulin actually blocks ketone production.
Glucose is converted directly into ketones
Ketones come from breaking down fat, not straight from glucose.
Without insulin, lipolysis and hepatic fatty-acid oxidation increase, producing excess acetyl-CoA that becomes ketones
Correct: low insulin and high glucagon drive fat breakdown and ketone production.
The kidney stops excreting ketones
The kidney does excrete ketones. The problem is making too many.
questions.x: Insulin normally tells the body there's plenty of sugar, so store fat and don't make ketones. In type 1 diabetes there's no insulin, and glucagon is high, so the body acts like it's starving. Fat tissue breaks fat into fatty acids (lipolysis). The liver burns those fatty acids into acetyl-CoA, a small two-carbon fuel unit, faster than the citric acid cycle can use it. The extra acetyl-CoA gets turned into ketone bodies (acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate). These are acids, so they cause ketoacidosis. Glucose itself doesn't become ketones.

questions.q: A patient makes large volumes of dilute urine. After injection of desmopressin (an ADH analog), urine becomes concentrated. Where is the defect most likely?
o: In kidney ADH receptors
If the kidney's receptors were broken, desmopressin wouldn't work. It did.
In ADH production or release from the hypothalamus–posterior pituitary
Correct: the kidney responds to an ADH substitute, so the problem is ADH supply. That's central DI.
In pancreatic β cells
β-cell failure causes diabetes mellitus, with sugar in the urine.
In the adrenal cortex
The adrenal cortex doesn't make ADH, and desmopressin wouldn't fix a defect there.
questions.note: Response to ADH analog = central DI; no response = nephrogenic DI.
questions.x: The defect is in making or releasing ADH, so this is central diabetes insipidus. ADH (antidiuretic hormone) is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. It tells the kidney to put water channels into its collecting ducts so it can save water and make concentrated urine. Desmopressin is a lab-made ADH. If it works, the kidney's ADH receptors and water channels are fine, so the missing piece is the body's own ADH. If the kidney itself ignored ADH (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), desmopressin would do little.

questions.q: A pituitary tumor compresses the stalk and blocks hypothalamic signals to the anterior pituitary. Which hormone level is most likely to RISE?
o: Prolactin
Correct: dopamine normally holds prolactin back, so blocking the stalk lets it rise.
ACTH
ACTH needs CRH to push it, so it falls.
TSH
TSH needs TRH to push it, so it falls.
GH
GH is driven mostly by GHRH, so it falls.
questions.note: Prolactin is the one anterior pituitary hormone under tonic inhibition.
questions.x: Prolactin rises. The hypothalamus controls the anterior pituitary by sending hormones down tiny blood vessels in the pituitary stalk. Most of those signals say make more: CRH for ACTH, TRH for TSH, GHRH for GH. Cut them off and those hormones fall. Prolactin is the one that's held back instead. The hypothalamus sends dopamine, which says stop making prolactin. Block the stalk and that brake disappears, so prolactin goes up while the others go down.

questions.q: A patient with high cortisol and high ACTH is given high-dose dexamethasone. Cortisol falls substantially. What is the most likely source of excess ACTH?
o: An ectopic ACTH-secreting tumor in the lung
Tumors outside the pituitary usually ignore dexamethasone, so cortisol wouldn't fall.
A pituitary adenoma
Correct: pituitary adenomas still partly obey feedback, so a high dose lowers ACTH.
An adrenal tumor secreting cortisol
A cortisol-making adrenal tumor would push ACTH low, not high.
Primary adrenal insufficiency
Adrenal insufficiency means low cortisol, not high.
questions.x: The source is most likely a pituitary adenoma, a benign tumor of the pituitary. Dexamethasone is a strong lab-made version of cortisol. Normally, cortisol tells the pituitary to make less ACTH (negative feedback), and ACTH is the signal that tells the adrenal glands to make cortisol. A pituitary adenoma still listens to that feedback a little, so a high dose of dexamethasone turns its ACTH down, and cortisol falls. An ACTH-making tumor somewhere else, like the lung, usually ignores feedback. An adrenal tumor would leave ACTH low, not high.

questions.q: A male athlete uses high doses of anabolic steroids for a year. What changes in his testes are expected?
o: Shrinkage and reduced sperm production due to suppressed LH and FSH
Correct: the extra androgen shuts down GnRH, LH and FSH, so the testes go quiet.
Enlargement due to increased LH
LH falls from negative feedback. It doesn't rise.
Increased sperm production due to more testosterone
Testosterone inside the testes falls when LH is shut off, so sperm drop.
No change because the testes ignore feedback
The testes depend on LH and FSH, so they do change.
questions.x: Expect shrinking testes and fewer sperm. The brain checks testosterone levels to decide how much to ask for. Steroids flood the blood with androgen, so the hypothalamus cuts back on GnRH, and the pituitary cuts back on LH and FSH. LH is what tells the testes' Leydig cells to make testosterone, so testosterone inside the testes drops, even though blood levels are high. Sperm production needs FSH plus that high local testosterone. Without them, sperm production falls and the testes shrink.

questions.q: A hormone's effect is blocked by an antibody that cannot cross membranes but binds the hormone's receptor. What does this suggest?
o: The receptor is in the nucleus
An antibody can't cross the membrane, so it couldn't reach a receptor in the nucleus.
The hormone is a steroid that acts on DNA
Steroid receptors are inside the cell, out of the antibody's reach.
The receptor is on the cell surface
Correct: an antibody that can't enter the cell can only reach surface receptors.
The hormone acts without any receptor
If a receptor antibody blocks the effect, a receptor must be involved.
questions.x: The receptor is on the cell surface. An antibody is a big protein that can't get through the cell membrane, so it can only grab things sticking out on the outside of the cell. If an antibody against the receptor blocks the hormone, the receptor must be somewhere the antibody can reach: the surface. That fits peptide hormones, like insulin, and catecholamines, like epinephrine. Steroid and thyroid hormones use receptors inside the cell, which the antibody couldn't touch.

questions.q: An adrenal tumor secretes excess aldosterone. Which pattern is expected?
o: Hypotension, high K⁺ and high renin
Low pressure and high K⁺ fit too little aldosterone, the opposite situation.
Hypertension, high K⁺ and high renin
Extra aldosterone pushes K⁺ down and turns renin off.
Normal pressure, low Na⁺ and high renin
Aldosterone holds on to Na⁺ and raises pressure, which turns renin off.
Hypertension, low K⁺ and low renin
Correct: kept Na⁺ raises pressure, which turns renin off, while K⁺ is lost in urine.
questions.x: Expect high blood pressure, low K⁺ and low renin. Aldosterone tells the kidney's collecting duct to hold on to Na⁺ and get rid of K⁺. Water follows Na⁺, so blood volume and pressure go up. The kidney senses the high pressure and stops releasing renin, the enzyme that normally starts the chain leading to aldosterone. Meanwhile, K⁺ keeps getting dumped into the urine, so blood K⁺ falls. If renin were high instead, you'd suspect something pushing the adrenal from outside, like a narrowed kidney artery, not a tumor.

questions.q: Increasing doses of a hormone increase a target-cell response until the response plateaus. Further doses produce no additional effect. What is the best explanation?
o: The hormone is degraded only at high doses
Faster breakdown wouldn't make a clean ceiling. A fixed number of receptors would.
The hormone becomes inhibitory at low doses
The response rises at low doses, so the hormone stimulates there.
The hormone's receptors are saturated
Correct: once every receptor is occupied, more hormone can't add more signal.
The response is not receptor-mediated
A plateau points to a limited number of receptors, which supports a receptor.
questions.x: The receptors are saturated. A hormone works by binding to receptors, and each cell has only so many. At low doses, more hormone fills more receptors, so the response grows. Once nearly every receptor has a hormone stuck in it, extra hormone has nowhere to bind, and the response levels off. That ceiling is actually evidence that the hormone works through a limited number of specific receptors.

questions.q: During exercise, sympathetic activity inhibits insulin secretion. What advantage does this provide?
o: It causes glucose to be stored in fat
Storing glucose as fat would take fuel out of the blood.
It helps keep blood glucose available as fuel
Correct: low insulin means less storage and more glucose released into the blood.
It increases glucose uptake by the brain
The brain takes up glucose mostly without insulin.
It stimulates protein synthesis in muscle
Lower insulin doesn't boost protein building, and that isn't the goal during exercise.
questions.x: Lowering insulin keeps fuel in the blood. Insulin is the store-it signal: it tells cells to pull glucose out of the blood and save it as glycogen and fat. During exercise you want the opposite. Sympathetic nerves act on α₂ receptors on the pancreas's β cells to cut insulin release. With insulin low, the liver releases glucose and fat tissue releases fatty acids, so fuel stays available. Working muscle doesn't need insulin to take up glucose, because contraction itself moves GLUT4 glucose transporters to the cell surface.

questions.q: An XY individual has female external genitalia and high testosterone because androgen receptors do not work. What does this demonstrate?
o: High testosterone directly causes female development
Testosterone doesn't cause female development. The tissues just can't respond to it.
The individual lacks testes
The testes are there and are making the testosterone.
Hormone effects require functional receptors, even when hormone levels are high
Correct: target cells can't respond without working receptors, however high the hormone.
Estrogen cannot be made in XY individuals
Testosterone can be turned into estrogen, so XY people can make estrogen.
questions.x: This shows that a hormone only works if its receptor works, no matter how much hormone there is. This is androgen insensitivity syndrome. The person is XY and has testes that make plenty of testosterone, but the androgen receptor is broken, so the body's cells can't respond to it. Without that signal, the external genitalia develop along the female pattern. The testes also still make anti-Müllerian hormone, so the uterus and upper vagina don't form.

questions.q: Thyroid hormone increases the number of β-adrenergic receptors on heart cells, so the same epinephrine level produces a larger response. This is an example of:
o: An antagonistic effect
Antagonistic hormones push the same thing in opposite directions.
Negative feedback
Negative feedback means a hormone's effect turns down its own release.
A tropic effect
A tropic hormone tells another gland to release its hormone.
A permissive effect
Correct: one hormone makes the target respond more strongly to another.
questions.x: This is a permissive effect: one hormone sets up a tissue so a second hormone can have its full effect, often by adding more receptors. Thyroid hormone raises the number of β-adrenergic receptors on heart cells. Those are the receptors epinephrine binds. More receptors means the same amount of epinephrine produces a bigger response. That's why people with an overactive thyroid often have a fast heart rate. It isn't tropic, because no gland is being told to release a hormone.
